teile.einleitung: The forest dung beetle is a beetle with a shiny blue-black body that crawls about mainly on paths in the forest. It eats the droppings of animals and buries them as food for its larvae. In this way it is an important helper that keeps the forest floor clean and fertile.
wichtigste: The forest dung beetle lives mainly in forests, especially beech woods.
Its scientific name is Anoplotrupes stercorosus.
It grows to about 12 to 19 millimetres long.
Its underside shines metallic blue, violet or green.
It feeds mainly on droppings, and sometimes on fungi.
It digs tunnels in the ground and stores droppings there for its larvae.
It develops in complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, beetle.

abschnitte.text: The forest dung beetle is 12 to 19 millimetres long and has a domed, shiny blue-black body. The underside shimmers **metallic** blue, violet or green. On the wing cases you can see seven fine lengthwise grooves. It looks very similar to the common dung beetle, but stays smaller.

The forest dung beetle is found all over Europe, in the east as far as western Siberia. It lives from the lowlands up to about 2000 metres and is also common in Switzerland. You find it especially often in **beech woods**. In summer and autumn you often see the beetles crawling singly across forest paths.

The beetle eats mainly the **droppings** of animals such as roe deer, red deer, wild boar or foxes. Sometimes it also eats fungi or tree sap. It belongs to the dung beetle family, but does not roll balls like the scarab beetles. Instead it pulls the dung down into the ground.

In spring, males and females dig a vertical **tunnel** into the ground together. Side tunnels branch off from this passage and end in small chambers. The female works underground, and the male carries the dug-out earth outside. Into each chamber goes an egg together with a store of droppings.

A **larva** hatches from the egg and eats the store of droppings in its chamber. The larva grows for about a year and spends the winter in the ground. In spring it turns into a pupa, and in summer the finished beetle hatches. But it can only breed itself the following spring.

Forest dung beetles are important **recyclers** in the forest. By burying droppings, they bring nutrients into the soil, and the forest floor is loosened. In this way animal droppings and the fly larvae living in them also disappear faster. On the underside of the beetle you often see small mites that let it carry them to the next dung heap.

begriffe.erklaerung: A beetle family whose members feed on animal droppings.
Everything that parent animals do so that their young grow up well.
Making chirping sounds by rubbing two parts of the body together.
The hard front wings of a beetle, which protect the delicate hind wings.

gewusst: Forest dung beetles can make chirping sounds by rubbing parts of the body together.
If a forest dung beetle lies on its back, it often has trouble getting back on its feet.

teile.einleitung: The Western honey bee is the bee that beekeepers keep all over the world. It collects nectar and pollen and makes honey from them. In doing so it pollinates countless flowers and is one of the most important farm animals of all.
wichtigste: The honey bee is an insect with 6 legs and 4 wings.
It has 5 eyes in all.
With its antennae it smells and feels.
It is usually brown and yellow with dark stripes.
When flying it makes a buzzing sound.
It collects nectar and pollen from flowers.
A bee colony is made up of a queen, workers and drones.

abschnitte.text: The honey bee is about 11 to 13 millimetres long, so smaller than a fingernail is wide. It is usually brown and yellow with dark stripes and has a hairy body. Like all insects it has 6 legs and a body made of head, thorax and abdomen. Added to this are 4 wings, which beat so fast that a **buzzing** is produced. Workers have a sting with barbs.

The honey bee has 5 eyes in all: two large **compound eyes** and three small simple eyes on the forehead. It sees ultraviolet light, but not red. With the **antennae** it smells and feels. In this way it finds flowers by their scent and recognises its nestmates.

In summer a colony has about 30,000 to 60,000 bees. There is one **queen**, who can lay up to 2,000 eggs a day. The workers are females and do all the jobs, from cleaning and feeding to collecting. The male **drones** mate only with young queens. A summer bee lives only about five to six weeks.

The collectors fetch **nectar** and **pollen** from flowers. They carry the pollen home in small baskets on their hind legs, and it is protein food for the larvae. From the nectar they make honey by letting water evaporate and mixing in substances. With the waggle dance they show other bees where good sources of food are.

The Western honey bee originally comes from Europe, Africa and western Asia. In Switzerland, about 17,000 beekeepers keep bees (as of about 2023). The original subspecies here is the dark bee, and today the Carniolan bee is also widespread. A great danger is the introduced **varroa mite**, a parasite.

begriffe.erklaerung: An eye made of many thousands of small single eyes.
The sweet juice in flowers from which bees make honey.
The flower dust that bees collect as protein food.
A male honey bee without a sting.
A dance with which a bee shows the direction and distance of a food source.

gewusst: For one kilogram of honey, bees fly in all a distance that would go round the Earth several times.
Whether a larva becomes a queen depends on the food: she gets only royal jelly.

teile.einleitung: The western lowland gorilla is a large ape from the rainforests of central Africa. It is the most common gorilla subspecies and the one you see in zoos. Despite its enormous strength, it is a peaceful plant eater.
wichtigste: It is a subspecies of the western gorilla.
It lives mainly in the Congo Basin in central Africa.
A male can weigh over 150 kilograms.
Older males have a silver-grey back.
Gorillas live in family groups.
They eat mainly plants and fruit.
The species is critically endangered.

abschnitte.text: The western lowland gorilla has dark, often brownish fur. Males grow to about 1.7 metres upright and can weigh over 150 kilograms. Females are only about half as heavy. From about 12 years old, males get a silver-grey back and are then called **silverbacks**. Gorillas usually walk on all fours and support themselves on their knuckles.

It lives mainly in the **Congo Basin** in central Africa. It is found in Cameroon, Gabon, the Republic of the Congo, the Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea and Angola. There it inhabits tropical **rainforests** and swamp forests in the lowlands. Every night it builds itself a new sleeping nest from branches and leaves.

Gorillas are almost pure **plant eaters**. The western lowland gorilla eats an especially large amount of fruit, as well as leaves, stems and bark. Sometimes it adds ants and termites to its menu. A large male eats many kilograms of food a day.

Gorillas live in groups of about 5 to 15 animals. A silverback leads the group and protects several females and their young. After a pregnancy of about eight and a half months, a female usually has one young one. The young stay with the mother for several years. In danger, the silverback drums on his chest to threaten.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature, IUCN, classes the western gorilla as **critically endangered**. The dangers are poaching, the felling of forests and diseases such as Ebola fever. Protected areas such as the Odzala-Kokoua National Park in the Congo are important. In Switzerland, western lowland gorillas live, for example, in Zurich Zoo and Basel Zoo, where they take part in breeding programmes.

begriffe.erklaerung: An adult male gorilla with grey fur on his back, the leader of the group.
Large apes without a tail, close relatives of humans, such as the gorilla, chimpanzee and orang-utan.
A group within an animal species that lives in a particular area and differs slightly.
Walking on all fours with the hands resting on the knuckles.

gewusst: Gorillas share about 98 per cent of their genes with humans.
Gorillas do the chest drumming with the flat hand, not with fists.

teile.einleitung: Alveoli are tiny air sacs in the lungs at the ends of the finest airways. This is where gas exchange takes place: oxygen passes from the air into the blood, and carbon dioxide is given off. Without the alveoli we could not breathe.
wichtigste: Alveoli are the smallest sacs in the lungs.
A human lung contains about 300 million alveoli.
In the alveoli, oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide is given off.
Each sac is surrounded by a fine network of blood vessels.
The wall between air and blood is extremely thin.
All the alveoli together have a very large surface area.
Smoking and some diseases can destroy the alveoli.

abschnitte.text: The word **alveolus** comes from Latin and means “small hollow”. The alveoli sit like bunches of grapes at the ends of the finest airways, the **bronchioles**. A single sac is only about 0.2 millimetres across. Adults have about 300 million of them in both lungs together.

When you breathe in, the alveoli fill with fresh air. The oxygen travels through the thin wall into the blood, which is called **diffusion**. At the same time, carbon dioxide travels from the blood into the sacs and is breathed out. Gases always move from the side with more gas to the side with less.

Around each alveolus lies a dense network of hair-thin blood vessels, the **capillaries**. The dividing wall between air and blood is less than one thousandth of a millimetre thick. Haemoglobin, the red blood protein, picks up the oxygen. After that, the blood carries the oxygen through the heart to the whole body.

Because there are so many sacs, the total area for gas exchange is huge. It is estimated at about 80 to 140 square metres, which is roughly as much as half a tennis court. A large area means that a lot of oxygen can get into the blood at once. A substance called **surfactant** stops the sacs from collapsing.

Cigarette smoke and fine dust damage the delicate walls of the sacs. In the disease **emphysema**, the walls burst and many small sacs become a few large ones. This makes the surface area smaller, and people with it find it hard to get enough air. Pneumonia can also fill the alveoli with fluid and make breathing harder.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny air sac in the lungs in which gas exchange takes place.
The way particles move by themselves from where there are many to where there are few.
A hair-thin blood vessel with a very thin wall.
A substance that keeps the air sacs of the lungs open.

gewusst: If you could spread out all the alveoli, they would cover about half a tennis court.
Premature babies often still have too little surfactant and therefore need help with breathing.

teile.einleitung: Anosmia means that you can no longer smell anything. The sense of smell can be lost through infections, injuries or old age. Because smelling and tasting are closely linked, food then also tastes different.
wichtigste: Anosmia is the loss of the sense of smell.
A weakened sense of smell is called hyposmia.
When smells are distorted and often seem unpleasant, it is called parosmia.
From 2020, many people suddenly lost their sense of smell because of COVID-19.
A head injury can also lead to anosmia.
People with anosmia cannot smell smoke, gas or spoiled food.
In smell training, you regularly sniff rose, lemon, eucalyptus and clove.

abschnitte.text: The word **anosmia** comes from Greek and means roughly “without smell”. It means the complete **loss of the sense of smell**. If smelling is only weakened, it is called **hyposmia**. In **parosmia**, smells are perceived in a distorted way. Coffee, for example, may suddenly smell of something burnt or rotten.

Common causes are **infections** of the nose and airways, such as a bad cold. From **2020**, many people suddenly lost their sense of smell because of **COVID-19**. A **head injury** can also damage the fine nerves of smell. Other reasons are long-lasting inflammation of the sinuses or nasal polyps. In **old age**, the sense of smell gets weaker in most people anyway.

The sense of smell warns us of dangers. People with anosmia cannot smell **smoke**, escaping **gas** or **spoiled food**. This is why **smoke alarms** are especially important for them. Food is also less enjoyable, because a large part of what we feel as taste is really smell. With the tongue alone you can only tell sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

Often the sense of smell comes back by itself after an infection, but sometimes this takes months. **Smell training** can help. In it, you deliberately sniff certain scents several times a day. **Rose, lemon, eucalyptus and clove** are often used. This is meant to teach the brain to recognise smells again.

gewusst: Some people are born without a sense of smell and only notice late.
If you hold your nose while eating, apple and raw onion taste much more alike.

teile.einleitung: Warmbloods are horses that lie, in build and temperament, between the fiery thoroughbreds and the heavy, calm cold-bloods. Today they are the most important horses in equestrian sport, for example in show jumping and dressage.
wichtigste: Warmblood is a type of horse and not a single breed.
The name has nothing to do with body temperature, but with temperament.
Warmbloods arose from crossing heavy farm horses with thoroughbreds.
Slimmer warmbloods are used today mainly for riding and sport.
Well-known breeds are the Hanoverian, Holsteiner, Trakehner and Oldenburg.
In Switzerland the Swiss Warmblood is bred.
Warmbloods are usually about 160 to 175 centimetres tall, measured at the withers.

abschnitte.text: Horses are often divided by type into three groups: **thoroughbred**, warmblood and **cold-blood**. Thoroughbreds such as the English Thoroughbred are light, fast and spirited. Cold-bloods are heavy, strong and very calm. The warmblood lies in between and combines strength, stamina and willingness to perform with a character that is easy to guide.

Warmbloods have a strong but elegant body with long legs and a well-shaped neck. Their size, called the **height at the withers**, is usually between about 160 and 175 centimetres. Common coat colours are bays, chestnuts, blacks and greys. Their movements are lively and ground-covering, which is especially important in dressage.

In the past, warmbloods were needed mainly as **carriage horses**, in farming and in the army. For this, strong but also fast animals were needed. When tractors and cars replaced horses in the 20th century, the breeding aim changed. More thoroughbred blood was crossed in so that the horses became lighter and more athletic.

Today slimmer warmbloods are the typical **sport horses**. They jump high obstacles in show jumping, show exact movements in dressage and run across country in eventing. They are also popular in carriage driving and as leisure horses. At the Olympic Games, most horses in these disciplines are warmbloods.

The **Swiss Warmblood** is a line of breeding of its own that is aimed at sport. The Swiss National Stud in **Avenches** in the canton of Vaud supports horse breeding in the country. Better known as a Swiss breed, however, is the Franches-Montagnes horse from the Jura, which is built somewhat heavier. Many Swiss show jumpers ride warmbloods from Germany, Belgium or the Netherlands.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very light, fast and spirited type of horse, for example the English Thoroughbred.
A heavy, strong and calm type of horse, used in the past for heavy work.
The size of a horse, measured from the ground to the withers.
The raised spot where the neck joins the back of a horse.

gewusst: Warmbloods are not warmer than other horses, and all horses have a body temperature of about 38 degrees.
Many warmblood breeds carry a brand by which you can tell their line of breeding.
The Trakehner originally comes from East Prussia.

teile.einleitung: Migratory locusts are grasshoppers that join together into huge swarms and fly long distances. A single swarm can consist of billions of animals and eat whole fields bare in a few hours. Such plagues occur especially often in Africa, the Middle East and southern Asia.
wichtigste: A migratory locust is a grasshopper that travels in huge swarms.
Especially large swarms of locusts often occur in Africa.
Well-known species are the desert locust and the migratory locust of Europe.
At high density, grasshoppers that live singly turn into swarming animals.
A swarm can include billions of animals.
A desert locust eats about as much each day as it weighs itself.
Plagues of locusts can lead to famines.

abschnitte.text: Migratory locusts are not a species of their own, but several species of grasshopper that can form **swarms**. The best known are the **desert locust** and the European migratory locust. They belong to the short-horned grasshoppers, like many grasshoppers in our meadows. Mostly they live singly and unnoticed.

After heavy rain, a lot of grass grows in dry areas, and the locusts multiply strongly. When it gets crowded and the animals often touch each other, they change. They become more sociable, change colour and get a stronger body for long flights. This change is called **phase change**, and the solitary phase turns into the swarming phase.

A large swarm can cover several hundred square kilometres and consist of billions of animals. With the wind, the swarms often fly over a hundred kilometres in a day. Especially large swarms often occur in **Africa**, but also in the Middle East and in India. In 2019 and 2020, the worst swarms for decades moved over Kenya, Ethiopia and Somalia in East Africa.

A desert locust eats about as much each day as it weighs itself, so about two grams. With billions of animals, whole harvests disappear in a short time. For farmers in poor countries, a **plague of locusts** can mean hunger and hardship. Even in the Bible, locusts are described as one of the ten plagues of Egypt.

The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the **FAO**, monitors the locusts with satellites and reports from many countries. In this way an early warning can be given when swarms form. The animals are mostly fought with insect poison that is sprayed from aircraft or vehicles. More friendly to the environment is a fungus that attacks only locusts.

In the past, swarms of the European migratory locust sometimes also reached central Europe. Today there are no plagues of locusts in Switzerland. In many countries of the world, however, locusts are a popular, protein-rich **food**. Since 2017, migratory locusts have also been allowed to be sold as food in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very large group of animals that moves together.
The transformation of a solitary locust into a swarming animal.
A mass appearance of animals that does great damage.
The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.

gewusst: A large swarm of locusts can eat as much in a day as tens of thousands of people.
Swarms of the desert locust have already crossed the Atlantic from Africa as far as the Caribbean.

teile.einleitung: Albrecht von Haller was a scholar from Bern in the 18th century. He was a doctor, a naturalist and a poet all at once, and is regarded as one of the most important scientists of his time. His poem “The Alps” made the Swiss mountains known throughout Europe.
wichtigste: Albrecht von Haller lived from 1708 to 1777 and came from Bern.
He wrote his famous poem “The Alps” in 1729.
For many years he taught at the newly founded University of Göttingen.
He ascribed irritability to the muscle fibres.
For him, sensibility was the ability to feel stimuli through nerves.
He is often regarded as the founder of experimental physiology.
He was shown on the 500 franc note of the sixth series.

abschnitte.text: Haller was born in 1708 in **Bern**. Even as a young man he travelled through the Swiss mountains. In 1729 he wrote the long poem **“The Alps”**. In it he praises the simple, honest life of the mountain people and contrasts it with the luxury of the towns. The poem was read all over Europe and helped to make the Alps seen no longer merely as dangerous, but as beautiful and admirable.

Haller studied medicine and became a doctor. In 1736 he received a professorship at the **newly founded University of Göttingen**. There he taught anatomy, surgery and botany for many years. He built up a botanical garden and researched tirelessly. Later he returned to Bern and took on offices in the administration of the city and republic of Bern. He died in Bern in 1777.

Haller is often regarded as the **founder of experimental physiology**, that is, the study of how the body works, investigated through experiments. He distinguished two properties of tissues. He ascribed **irritability** to the **muscle fibres**: they contract when you stimulate them. For him **sensibility** was the **ability to feel stimuli through nerves**. His great textbook on the physiology of man was a standard work for a long time.

Haller was also a great **botanist**. In an extensive collected work he described the **plants of Switzerland**. For this he collected on many journeys and had plants sent to him from all parts of the country. He also wrote novels and countless book reviews, and corresponded with scholars all over Europe. That is why he is often called a **polymath**.

Switzerland honoured Haller on the **500 franc note** of the **sixth banknote series**. This series was in circulation from the 1970s and was later replaced by new notes. Even today, streets and buildings in Bern bear his name.

gewusst: Haller is said to have written poems and made his own dictionaries even as a child.
In the course of his life he wrote thousands of book reviews for a Göttingen scholarly journal.

teile.einleitung: Warning colouration is a striking colouring with which an animal shows its enemies: watch out, I am poisonous, able to defend myself or taste bad. Instead of hiding, these animals deliberately stand out.
wichtigste: Warning colours often consist of red, yellow, orange, black or white.
Animals with warning colouration are mostly poisonous, sting or taste bad.
Predators learn after a bad experience to avoid such animals.
Some butterflies have bright colours to warn enemies that they taste bad.
Well-known examples are wasps, ladybirds and fire salamanders.
Some harmless animals copy the warning colours of other animals, which is called mimicry.
The technical term for warning colouration is aposematism.

abschnitte.text: Many animals are coloured brown or green so that they cannot be seen. Animals with **warning colouration** do the opposite and are as striking as a road sign. Their colours mean to birds, lizards or mammals: leave me alone. Typical are strong **contrasts** such as yellow and black or red and black.

A young bird does not at first know which prey is dangerous. If it once pecks a bitter beetle or is stung by a wasp, it remembers the colours. After that it avoids all animals that look similar. The more striking the colour, the faster the enemy **learns** the warning.

The **burnet moths** are small butterflies and moths with red spots that carry poisonous substances in their bodies. The monarch butterfly in America takes in poison from milkweeds as a caterpillar. The black and yellow **fire salamander** gives off a poison from glands in its skin. In South America the brightly coloured poison dart frogs are especially poisonous.

Some harmless animals wear the same colours as dangerous animals. Many **hoverflies** are striped yellow and black like wasps, but cannot sting at all. This copying is called **mimicry** and protects the animals even though they are harmless themselves. There are also groups of several species able to defend themselves that resemble each other, so that enemies learn the warning even faster.

In Switzerland too you can watch warning colours well. The **ladybird** gives off a bitter yellow fluid from its legs when in danger. The red and black firebug, wasps, hornets and bumblebees are strikingly coloured. Fire salamanders are seen mainly in damp woods in rainy weather.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for warning colouration, that is, warning by striking colours.
A harmless animal copies the appearance of a dangerous animal.
Colouring with which an animal blends in with its surroundings and is hard to see.
An animal that hunts and eats other animals.

gewusst: People also use warning colours: danger signs and barriers are often yellow and black or red and white.
The skunk warns with its black and white fur of its foul-smelling spray.
Some burnet moths contain substances from which hydrogen cyanide can form.

teile.einleitung: The dwarf lanternshark is one of the smallest sharks in the world and grows only about as long as a hand. It lives in the dark deep sea of the Caribbean off the coast of Colombia. Its belly can glow, like a small lantern in the darkness.
wichtigste: The dwarf lanternshark is one of the smallest known sharks.
It grows about 16 to 20 centimetres long, so about as long as a hand.
It weighs only about 150 grams.
It lives in the deep sea of the Caribbean off Colombia.
Light organs on its belly produce a faint light.
It gives birth to live young.
Very little is known about its life.

abschnitte.text: The dwarf lanternshark, scientifically *Etmopterus perryi*, grows at most about 20 centimetres long. A fully grown animal therefore fits on an adult's hand. By comparison, the **whale shark**, the biggest fish in the world, can grow over twelve metres long. The dwarf lanternshark has a slim, dark body, large eyes and two dorsal fins with spines.

It is known only from a few sea areas in the **Caribbean** off the north coast of Colombia. There it lives at depths of about 200 to 600 metres. At this depth hardly any sunlight arrives, and it is cool. Because the place is so hard to reach, only a few specimens have been caught so far.

The dwarf lanternshark belongs to the family of **lanternsharks**, which can produce light of their own. In the skin of its belly sit many tiny **light organs**. Their faint light matches the little light from above. In this way the shark casts no dark shadow and is hard to spot for predators below it. This camouflage is called counter-illumination.

What exactly the dwarf lanternshark eats has been little studied. Experts suspect that it hunts small crustaceans, squid and small fish, like its relatives. Like other lanternsharks, it does not lay eggs in the water, but gives birth to **live young**. The eggs develop in the body of the mother.

The dwarf lanternshark was scientifically described in 1985. Its Latin name honours the marine researcher Perry Gilbert. Because the deep sea is hardly explored, researchers are still discovering new species there. How many dwarf lanternsharks there are and how old they grow is not known so far.

begriffe.erklaerung: The dark, cold part of the sea below about 200 metres.
A part of the body with which an animal can produce light itself.
The ability of living things to glow by themselves.
A camouflage in which an animal uses its light to make its own shadow disappear.

gewusst: A dwarf lanternshark weighs about as much as a bar of chocolate and a half besides.
The pygmy spiny dogfish is also among the smallest sharks and grows hardly bigger than the dwarf lanternshark.

teile.einleitung: The wild boar is the wild ancestor of our domestic pig and also lives in Swiss forests. It is strong and clever and has an excellent nose. Because it is mostly out and about at night, you rarely see it, but you often find its tracks.
wichtigste: The male is called a boar, the female a sow, and the young piglets.
A boar can weigh over 150 kilograms.
With its snout it roots in the ground for food.
Wild boars are active mainly at dusk and at night.
They wallow in mud to cool down and get rid of parasites.
The mating season is called the rut.
Wild boars can swim very well.

abschnitte.text: The wild boar has a dense, dark brown to black bristly coat. The head is wedge-shaped and ends in a strong **snout**. A fully grown boar can weigh over 150 kilograms, and sows are lighter. Boars have long canine teeth that are called **tusks**. The piglets have light stripes along the body, which camouflage them in the forest.

Wild boars live in forests, often near fields and water. Originally they occur in Europe, Asia and North Africa. In Switzerland they live mainly on the Central Plateau, in the Jura and in Ticino, and their numbers have increased. They are mostly active at dusk and at night and hide in thickets by day.

Wild boars are **omnivores**. With the snout they find and root their food out of the ground. In the forest they especially like to eat acorns, beechnuts, roots and worms. They also eat mushrooms, mice and carrion. On fields they like to help themselves to maize and potatoes, which causes damage to farmers.

Wild boars live in family groups called **sounders**, led by an experienced sow. Adult boars mostly live alone. The mating season is called the **rut** and falls mainly in late autumn and winter. A sow usually has about 4 to 6 piglets at once. With raised bristles on the back, wild boars show excitement or threat.

Wild boars like to roll in a muddy puddle, the **wallow**. This cools them, protects them from insects and sun and helps against parasites. Afterwards they rub themselves on trees. They are useful for the forest, because they loosen the soil and spread seeds. They can also swim very well and even cross rivers and lakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: An adult male wild pig.
A female wild pig.
A young wild pig with striped fur.
A muddy spot in which wild boars roll.
A group of wild boars.

gewusst: The nose of a wild boar is so good that it can smell food under the snow.
A sow with piglets can attack if you get too close to her, which is why you keep your distance.

teile.einleitung: A hydroelectric power station makes electricity from the force of flowing or falling water. In Switzerland hydropower is the most important source of electricity, but power stations also cause problems for fish and other water animals.
wichtigste: Hydroelectric power stations turn the energy of water into electricity with turbines.
Switzerland gets about 55 to 60 per cent of its electricity from hydropower (as of about 2024).
There are run-of-river power stations on rivers and storage power stations with reservoirs in the mountains.
Dams and weirs block the way upstream for fish.
For fish migrating downstream, turbines are dangerous, because they can get into them and be injured.
Fish ladders and protective screens help the animals to get past power stations.
Hydropower is regarded as a renewable energy, but it changes habitats in rivers.

abschnitte.text: The water flows through pipes or channels to a **turbine**, a large paddle wheel. The turbine turns and drives a **generator**, which makes electricity. The more water flows and the further it falls, the more energy is produced. After that the water flows back into the river.

**Run-of-river power stations** stand on rivers such as the Rhine, Aare or Rhone and use the constantly flowing water. **Storage power stations** collect water in reservoirs in the Alps and let it plunge into the valley through long pressure pipes when needed. Pumped storage power stations pump water back up when there is a surplus of electricity. The Grande Dixence dam in the Valais, at 285 metres, is the highest gravity dam in the world.

Many fish migrate upstream and downstream in the course of their lives, such as trout, grayling, nase and eels. Weirs and dams are often impassable **obstacles** for them. When fish swim downstream, they can get into the turbines and be badly injured. Especially affected are eels, which swim as far as the sea to spawn.

With **fish ladders**, fish can get round a power station by way of many small pools. Fine screens and bypass channels lead fish migrating downstream past the turbines. Power stations also have to leave enough **residual water** in the riverbed so that it does not dry out. The fast rise and fall of the water level below storage power stations, called hydropeaking, is also to be reduced.

Thanks to its mountains, glaciers and plentiful precipitation, Switzerland has very good conditions for hydropower. Across the country there are about 700 larger hydroelectric power stations and many small plants besides. The Water Protection Act requires power stations to become more fish-friendly by about 2030. In the past even the **salmon** swam up the Rhine as far as Switzerland, but the many weirs helped to make it die out here.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large paddle wheel that is turned by flowing water.
A machine that turns a turning movement into electric current.
A structure of many small steps or pools by which fish get past an obstacle.
The amount of water that has to stay in the natural riverbed below a power station.

gewusst: Centuries ago, people already used water wheels to drive mills and sawmills.
At some fish ladders, experts count with cameras how many fish swim up.
An eel from Switzerland swims to spawn as far as the Sargasso Sea in the Atlantic.

teile.einleitung: Turritopsis dohrnii is a tiny jellyfish that has become famous as the “immortal jellyfish”. It can change back into a younger stage and so, in a way, begin its life afresh. This makes it especially long-lived and fascinates researchers all over the world.
wichtigste: Turritopsis dohrnii is called the immortal jellyfish.
The fully grown jellyfish is only about 4 to 5 millimetres in size.
Under stress, injury or in old age, it can turn back into a polyp.
New, young jellyfish arise again from this polyp.
Originally the species comes from the Mediterranean.
It is not completely immortal, because it can be eaten or die of disease.
Researchers hope to learn more about ageing from it.

abschnitte.titel: What kind of animal is it?
abschnitte.text: Turritopsis dohrnii belongs to the **cnidarians**, like all jellyfish, corals and sea anemones. More exactly, it counts as a hydrozoan. The adult jellyfish is transparent, bell-shaped and smaller than a fingernail. It is named after the German zoologist Anton Dohrn, who founded a famous marine research station in Naples.

Normally a **polyp** that stays fixed in place grows from a larva and buds off small jellyfish. These grow up, reproduce and in most species die afterwards. Turritopsis dohrnii, however, can reverse this path. If it is injured, starves or grows old, it sinks to the bottom and turns back into a polyp.

In the change back, its **cells** change their job, and cells of the jellyfish become cells of the polyp. This process is called **transdifferentiation**. Later many genetically identical jellyfish can arise from the new polyp. This ability was discovered in the 1990s by researchers in Italy.

Originally the species lives in the **Mediterranean**, for example off the Italian coast. By now very similar Turritopsis jellyfish are found in many seas of the world. They probably travelled along in the ballast water of ships. Because they are so small, swimmers hardly notice them.

The jellyfish is an exciting model for **research into ageing**. Scientists study its genes in order to understand how cells stay young or renew themselves. One day this could help in medicine, for example in the healing of tissue. For people, however, there is no way of making themselves young again like this jellyfish.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals with stinging cells that includes jellyfish, corals and sea anemones.
The form of a cnidarian that stays fixed in place and looks like a small tube.
A cell changes its job and becomes a different kind of cell.
The sequence of life stages of a living thing.

gewusst: In theory a Turritopsis jellyfish could repeat its life cycle as often as it likes.
In the laboratory, a jellyfish has been seen to change back several times in a row.
The immortal jellyfish is about as big as a lentil.

teile.einleitung: The cuckooflower is a pale lilac spring flower of damp meadows. Because it blooms when the cuckoo calls, it is also called lady's smock or cuckoo flower. For butterflies such as the orange tip, it is an important food plant.
wichtigste: The cuckooflower has pale lilac to white flowers.
It blooms from about April to June.
It is also called the lady's smock.
It grows in damp meadows and on stream banks.
It belongs to the crucifers.
It is a food plant for the caterpillars of the orange tip.
The German name comes from the froth of the froghopper on its stems.

abschnitte.text: The cuckooflower grows to about 15 to 50 centimetres tall. Its flowers have four **petals** and are pale lilac, pink or white. The leaves are pinnate, and the lower ones form a rosette on the ground. It belongs to the **crucifer** family, like rapeseed and mustard.

The plant loves damp soils. You find it in wet meadows, on stream banks, in floodplain woods and along ditches. In Switzerland it is widespread from the lowlands up into the mountains. In spring, whole meadows can shimmer lilac.

The cuckooflower blooms from about April to June, when the **cuckoo** returns from Africa and calls. That is where it gets its second name. On the stems you often find small balls of froth, called cuckoo spit. In it hides the larva of the **froghopper**, which makes the froth for protection.

For the **orange tip**, the cuckooflower is very important. The female lays her eggs on the flowers, and the caterpillars eat the seed pods. You can recognise the males of the butterfly by the orange wing tips. Bees and other insects also visit the flowers for the nectar.

The young leaves taste sharp like cress and can be eaten in small amounts in salad. If a meadow is drained or mown and fertilised very often, the plant disappears. That is why it is an **indicator plant** for damp, near-natural meadows. In 2006 the cuckooflower was Flower of the Year in Germany.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant family with four petals arranged in the shape of a cross.
A small insect whose larva hides in froth.
A plant that shows what the soil is like, for example damp or rich in nutrients.
A white butterfly in which the males have orange wing tips.

gewusst: The cuckooflower can also multiply by tiny plantlets that grow on the leaves.
The froth of the cuckoo spit blobs has nothing to do with the cuckoo.

teile.einleitung: Andreas Vesalius was a doctor from Brussels and is regarded as the founder of modern anatomy. He examined the human body himself, instead of just believing old books. His famous main work was printed in Basel in 1543.
wichtigste: Andreas Vesalius was born in Brussels in 1514 and died in 1564.
As a young professor he taught anatomy and surgery in Padua.
What was new was that he dissected the bodies himself in his teaching.
He corrected many mistakes made by the ancient doctor Galen.
In 1543 his main work “De humani corporis fabrica” appeared in Basel.
A skeleton that he prepared himself has survived in Basel to this day.
He became personal physician to Emperor Charles V.

abschnitte.text: For more than a thousand years in Europe, the teachings of the Greek doctor **Galen** were thought to be correct. Galen lived in Rome in the 2nd century. But he had mainly **dissected** animals such as monkeys and pigs, that is, cut them up and examined them. So his descriptions of humans contained many mistakes. In lessons, a professor usually read aloud from Galen’s books while an assistant opened up the body.

**Andreas Vesalius** studied in Paris, among other places, and in 1537 became a professor in **Padua** in Italy. There he taught anatomy and surgery. What was new was that he **dissected the bodies himself** and showed the students directly what he saw. In this way he discovered that Galen had been wrong on many points. He trusted his own observation more than the old texts.

In 1543 Vesalius published his main work, **“De humani corporis fabrica”**, which means roughly “On the Structure of the Human Body”. It was printed in **Basel** by the printer Johannes Oporinus. The work contains many beautifully made woodcuts of bones, muscles and organs. It is regarded as one of the most important books in the history of medicine.

During his stay in Basel, Vesalius prepared the skeleton of an executed man. He gave it to the university. This **human skeleton** can still be seen today in the **Anatomical Museum in Basel**. It is regarded as the oldest surviving anatomical specimen in the world.

After his success, Vesalius became **personal physician to Emperor Charles V**. Later he also served the emperor’s son, King Philip II of Spain. In 1564 he went on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. On the journey back he fell ill and died on the Greek island of Zakynthos.

gewusst: When Vesalius published the “Fabrica”, he was only about 28 years old.
In the same year, 1543, the famous book by Copernicus appeared, saying that the Earth goes round the Sun.

teile.einleitung: The Roman snail is the largest land snail in central Europe and carries a beautiful, striped shell on its back. It crawls slowly on a single broad foot and is out and about above all after rain.
wichtigste: The Roman snail is a large land snail with a shell of about 3 to 5 centimetres.
Its shell is usually brownish yellow with stripes and grows along with the snail.
Its eyes sit at the tip of the long tentacles.
It moves very slowly on a single broad foot.
It is a hermaphrodite, and after mating both partners can lay eggs.
It lays about 40 to 60 eggs per clutch.
It cannot hear, but it feels vibrations.

abschnitte.text: The round **shell** is usually brownish yellow with darker stripes. It grows along with the snail as new layers of lime are always built on at the edge. Old snails therefore have more whorls than young ones. On its head it carries four **tentacles**: the eyes sit on the two long ones, and the two short ones are used for smelling and feeling.

The Roman snail lives in open woods, hedges, gardens and meadows, preferably on soil containing lime. It needs the lime for its shell. It is especially active in damp weather, for example after rain, and at night. In dry weather it withdraws into its shell so as not to dry out.

It eats mainly plants, and likes wilted leaves too. For this it has a **radula**, a rasping tongue with thousands of tiny teeth. It crawls on a single broad **foot** that contracts in waves. So that it glides well, it gives off slime, which also protects it from sharp edges.

Roman snails are **hermaphrodites**, so each animal is male and female at the same time. Before mating, two snails perform a long ritual in which they rear up and touch each other. In doing so, they push a **love dart** made of lime into each other's body. After that, both partners can lay about 40 to 60 eggs in a hole in the earth, from which tiny snails hatch after a few weeks.

In autumn the Roman snail digs itself into the ground and goes into **winter rest**. It seals its shell with a firm lid of lime and comes out again only in spring. In France, snails are regarded as a delicacy and are eaten as escargots. Because wild populations used to be heavily collected, collecting them is banned or restricted in many European countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that is male and female at the same time.
A tongue with many small teeth, with which snails rasp off their food.
A small needle of lime that snails prick into each other during the mating ritual.
A resting time in winter in which an animal is hardly active.

gewusst: Very rarely there are Roman snails whose shell is coiled to the left instead of to the right, and they are called king snails.
A Roman snail can crawl over a razor blade without hurting itself, because the slime protects it.
Roman snails can live for several years.

teile.einleitung: Acetylcholine is an important messenger substance of the nervous system. It passes signals from nerves to muscles, between nerve cells and from the vagus nerve to the heart. Acetylcholine was the first messenger substance ever discovered.
wichtigste: Acetylcholine is made by the enzyme choline acetyltransferase.
It is broken down in the synaptic cleft by acetylcholinesterase.
In 1921 Otto Loewi proved chemical signal transmission with the “vagus substance”.
Muscarinic receptors are named after the poison of the fly agaric.
Acetylcholine from the vagus nerve lowers the heart rate.
The amount from a single vesicle is called a quantum.
If a poison blocks the breakdown, acetylcholine builds up.

abschnitte.text: For a long time it was unclear whether nerves pass on their signals electrically or chemically. The pharmacologist **Otto Loewi** carried out a famous experiment with two frog hearts in 1921. He stimulated the vagus nerve of the first heart, which then beat more slowly. Then he gave the fluid from this heart to the second heart, and this too became slower. A substance must have carried the signal, and Loewi called it **“Vagusstoff”**, the vagus substance. Later it turned out that it was acetylcholine. In 1936 Loewi received the Nobel Prize together with Henry Dale.

In the nerve ending, the enzyme **choline acetyltransferase** puts acetylcholine together from **choline** and an acetyl group. The finished acetylcholine is stored in tiny bubbles, the **vesicles**. The amount from a single vesicle is called **a quantum**. When a nerve signal arrives, many vesicles are emptied into the **synaptic cleft**. There **acetylcholinesterase** breaks the substance down again in fractions of a second, so that the signal stays short.

Acetylcholine acts through two groups of **receptors**. The **nicotinic** receptors also react to nicotine, and they sit, for example, at the **motor end plate**, where nerves control the skeletal muscles. The **muscarinic** receptors are named after **muscarine**, a poison of the **fly agaric**. Through them acetylcholine acts, among other places, on the heart: released by the vagus nerve, it makes the **heart rate fall**.

Some insect poisons and the **nerve agents** block acetylcholinesterase. Then **acetylcholine builds up** and excites muscles and organs continuously, which is life-threatening. In a small, controlled amount, medicine uses the same principle. In the disease **myasthenia gravis**, there are too few working receptors at the end plate. **Cholinesterase inhibitors** such as pyridostigmine make sure that acetylcholine **acts longer in the cleft**, and so improve muscle strength.

gewusst: The idea for his decisive experiment is said to have come to Otto Loewi in a dream, as he later told it himself.
Acetylcholinesterase is among the fastest enzymes known.

teile.einleitung: An antibiotic is a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from multiplying. Since the 20th century, antibiotics have saved millions of lives. But they do not help against viruses, for example in a cold.
wichtigste: Antibiotics work against bacteria, not against viruses.
Colds are mostly caused by viruses, so antibiotics usually do not help there.
The first known antibiotic is penicillin.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.
In Switzerland, antibiotics are only available with a doctor’s prescription.
Using them too often makes bacteria become resistant.
You should take an antibiotic exactly as the doctor says.

abschnitte.text: The word **antibiotic** means roughly “against life”, meaning the life of bacteria. Some antibiotics kill bacteria directly, others stop their growth. Many antibiotics originally come from fungi or bacteria, which use them to defend themselves against competitors. Today many active substances are made or altered in the laboratory.

In 1928 the Scottish researcher **Alexander Fleming** noticed something special in London. A mould had grown on a dish of bacteria, and around the mould the bacteria were dying. The mould made a substance that Fleming called **penicillin**. From the 1940s, penicillin was made in large quantities and used as a medicine.

Bacteria are built differently from the cells of our body. Many of them, for example, have a firm **cell wall**, which human cells do not have. Penicillin disturbs the building of this cell wall, so that the bacteria burst. Other antibiotics block the making of proteins in the bacteria.

Viruses are not independent living things with their own metabolism: they multiply inside our cells. So antibiotics have nothing to attack in them. Colds, coughs and flu are mostly caused by viruses. Against some viruses, vaccinations or special antiviral medicines help instead.

If antibiotics are taken too often or wrongly, tough bacteria sometimes survive. These bacteria are called **resistant**, because the medicine no longer works against them. Resistant germs are a big problem in hospitals all over the world. Switzerland therefore has a national strategy against antibiotic resistance, which is abbreviated to StAR.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny single-celled living things; some of them can cause diseases.
A very small germ that can only multiply inside other cells.
When a medicine no longer works against a germ.
The first known antibiotic, obtained from a mould.

gewusst: Fleming discovered penicillin rather by chance, because a dish of bacteria had gone mouldy while he was away.
In 1945 Alexander Fleming received the Nobel Prize in Medicine together with two other researchers.
Antibiotics are also used in animal farming, which can contribute to resistance developing.

teile.einleitung: A nightmare is a scary, bad dream. Often you wake up from it with a pounding heart or feeling afraid. Almost all children have nightmares sometimes, and that is quite normal.
wichtigste: A nightmare is a scary, bad dream.
Many children sometimes have nightmares, which is normal.
A monster from a nightmare is not real, it is only dreamt.
If you have worries, you often dream badly more often.
A scary film in the evening can trigger nightmares.
Breathing calmly and deeply helps to calm you down.
The German word “Alb” comes from a night spirit in old legends.

abschnitte.text: Every night you dream, even if you often no longer remember it in the morning. In a dream your brain processes what you have experienced, seen and felt. Sometimes dreams are funny or strange. But sometimes they become scary, and you are afraid in the dream. Then it is called a **nightmare**. Often you wake up from it and for the first moment do not know whether it was real.

A **monster** from a nightmare is **not real**. It is only **dreamt**, and it cannot do anything to you. Even if the dream felt completely real, everything was only in your head. **Many children** sometimes have nightmares, which is **quite normal**. Adults too dream badly now and then.

If you have **worries**, for example about a test, a quarrel or a change in the family, you often dream badly more often. A **scary film** or an exciting story in the evening can also trigger nightmares. That is why it is good to do something calm before sleeping, for example to read a nice book or listen to music. It also helps to talk about worries before you go to sleep.

When you wake up after a nightmare, you may **go to Mum or Dad** or to another person you trust. **Breathing calmly and deeply** helps so that the heart beats more slowly again. A small light, a cuddly toy or a sip of water can also calm you. Some children paint the dream the next day and invent a new, good ending for it.

The German word **“Alb”** comes from a **night spirit in old legends**. In the past people believed that such a spirit sat on the chest of sleepers at night and gave them heavy, bad dreams. That is why people said you were “pressed” by the Alb. Today we know that nightmares arise in your own brain and no spirits are involved.

gewusst: Most vivid dreams happen in the second half of the night.
In many children nightmares become rarer the older they get.

teile.einleitung: Obesity is the technical term for severe overweight, in which the body stores a great deal of fat. It is regarded as a chronic disease that raises the risk of further diseases. The causes are many, and nobody is simply to blame.
wichtigste: The WHO speaks of obesity from a BMI of 30, and of class III from 40.
A lot of fat in the abdomen around the organs is especially unfavourable.
A common consequence is type 2 diabetes mellitus.
The fatty tissue reports the size of the reserves to the brain with the hormone leptin.
Severe overweight promotes osteoarthritis, especially in the knees.
Obstructive sleep apnoea occurs more often.
In severe obesity, bariatric surgery can help.

abschnitte.text: The **body mass index**, **BMI** for short, is often used. You divide the body weight in kilograms by the height in metres squared. The World Health Organization, the **WHO**, speaks in adults of obesity from a BMI of 30. It distinguishes three classes, and **class III** begins **from a BMI of 40**. In children and young people, comparison is made with curves for others of the same age, because they are still growing.

Not only the amount, but also the place of the fat is important. **A lot of fat in the abdomen around the organs** is regarded as especially unfavourable. This belly fat is very active and gives off substances that promote inflammation, for example. That is why the **waist circumference** is often also measured. Fatty tissue is not just a store, however: it makes the hormone **leptin**, which reports to the brain how large the fat reserves are.

A common consequence is **type 2 diabetes mellitus**, in which the blood sugar is too high. The high weight also strains the joints and promotes **osteoarthritis**, especially in the knees. In sleep there can be pauses in breathing, **obstructive sleep apnoea**. If abdominal obesity, high blood pressure, unfavourable blood fats and insulin resistance occur together, people speak of the **metabolic syndrome**. It raises the risk of cardiovascular diseases.

Obesity arises when the body takes in more energy than it uses over a long time. Behind it, however, lie many influences: **genes**, diet, little exercise, too little sleep, stress, some medicines and the surroundings in which you live. That is why it is not fair to mock people for their weight. Respect and support are important.

Treatment usually includes a change of **diet**, more **exercise** in everyday life and counselling, often over a long time. In children the whole family is involved. There are now also medicines that affect the feeling of hunger. In severe obesity, **bariatric surgery** can help, which creates a **gastric bypass**, for example. After that, lifelong medical follow-up is needed.

gewusst: The hormone leptin was discovered only in 1994.
The BMI was already described in the 19th century by the Belgian researcher Adolphe Quetelet.

teile.einleitung: Ursus is the scientific name of a genus of bears. It includes, for example, the brown bear, the polar bear and the American black bear. The word Ursus is Latin and simply means bear.
wichtigste: Ursus is a genus of the bear family (Ursidae).
The brown bear and the polar bear both belong to the genus Ursus.
Other species are the American black bear and the Asiatic black bear.
Ursus is the Latin word for bear.
The polar bear and the Kodiak bear, a subspecies of the brown bear, are the largest land predators.
Brown bears and polar bears are so closely related that they can have young together.
In Switzerland, single brown bears from Italy occasionally roam about.

abschnitte.text: In biology every species gets a two-part **scientific name**. The first part names the **genus**, the second the species. The brown bear is called Ursus arctos, and the polar bear Ursus maritimus. This shows that both belong to the same genus. Ursus is Latin and means bear, and arctos is the Greek word for bear.

The genus Ursus is usually counted as having four species: the **brown bear**, the **polar bear**, the American black bear and the Asian black bear, also called the moon bear. Some researchers also count the sloth bear and the sun bear. The giant panda and the spectacled bear are bears too, but belong to other genera. The cave bear, which lived in the Ice Age also in Switzerland, is extinct.

The polar bear and the brown bear are closely related, and the polar bear developed a few hundred thousand years ago from ancestors like brown bears. That is why they can even have young together, and the crosses are sometimes called **cappuccino bears** or pizzlies. The polar bear lives in the Arctic and hunts seals on the sea ice. The brown bear lives in forests and mountains in Europe, Asia and North America and eats plants, berries, insects and meat.

Bears of the genus Ursus are big and strong, with a massive body, short tails and strong claws. They walk as **plantigrades**, that is, with the whole sole of the foot on the ground, as we humans do. Most are **omnivores**. Many spend the winter in a den in a winter rest, in which the body temperature drops only slightly.

The last brown bear in Switzerland was shot in 1904 in the Lower Engadine. Since 2005, single young bears have repeatedly wandered from Trentino in Italy into the Engadine and the Münstertal. The bear is the heraldic animal of Bern and Appenzell. In the **Bear Park** in Bern you can watch brown bears.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of very closely related species, for example Ursus.
An animal that walks on the whole sole of the foot.
An animal that eats both plants and meat.
A long sleep in winter in which the body cools down only a little.

gewusst: The constellation Great Bear is called Ursa Major in Latin.
The name Arctic comes from the Greek word arktos for bear, because the constellation stands in the north.
A polar bear has black skin under its white fur.

teile.einleitung: The amygdala is a small cluster of nerve cells deep in the brain. In English it is sometimes called the almond nucleus, because its shape reminds people of an almond. It is especially important for feelings such as fear and for spotting danger quickly.
wichtigste: Amygdala means almond; in German it is called Mandelkern.
Every person has two amygdalae, one in each half of the brain, in the temporal lobe.
It belongs to the limbic system.
It is closely linked to the feeling of fear.
In fear conditioning, it helps you learn what is dangerous.
In stress, it sets off the release of cortisol through a hormone axis.

abschnitte.text: The name **amygdala** comes from Greek and means **almond**. Every person has two of them, one deep in the left and one in the right **temporal lobe**. The amygdala is counted as part of the **limbic system**. This network in the brain is important for feelings, memory and drive.

The amygdala judges in a flash whether something is dangerous. The researcher **Joseph LeDoux** described a fast route: threatening signals travel straight from the **thalamus** to the amygdala, before the cerebral cortex has examined them closely. That is why, for example, you jump before you notice that the stick on the ground is not a snake. By a slower route, the first judgement is then checked more carefully.

In **fear conditioning**, a neutral signal, such as a tone, is linked with an unpleasant event. After that, the tone alone is enough to cause fear. This kind of learning depends especially on the amygdala. In stress, the amygdala indirectly sets off the release of the stress hormone **cortisol** through the **hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis**.

In monkeys, after both temporal lobes were removed together with the amygdala, researchers observed the **Klüver-Bucy syndrome**. Among other things, the animals no longer showed fear. In humans, the patient **“S. M.”** became well known. A rare inherited disease, **Urbach-Wiethe disease**, had destroyed both of her amygdalae. As a result she felt hardly any fear.

gewusst: The patient “S. M.” was hardly afraid even of snakes and spiders.
The amygdala reacts especially strongly to frightened faces, even when you see them only very briefly.

teile.einleitung: Muscles need energy to work. In very hard, fast effort, there is not enough oxygen to get all the energy. Then the muscles also get energy without oxygen, that is, anaerobically.
wichtigste: “Anaerobic” means “without oxygen”.
The energy for every muscle movement is supplied by the substance ATP.
Creatine phosphate lasts only a few seconds of top effort.
In anaerobic energy production with lactate formation, glucose is used.
In the process the muscles become acidic, which is why you cannot keep up a sprint pace for long.
In the 400 metres, anaerobic energy production plays a very big part.
Gentle jogging afterwards helps to clear the lactate faster.

abschnitte.text: Every muscle movement needs the energy substance **ATP**. But the muscle only has a small store of it. In calm, long effort, the body makes new ATP with the help of **oxygen**, which is called **aerobic**. In a sprint this is too slow. Then ways that work **without oxygen** step in, that is, **anaerobic** ones.

For the first seconds of a top effort, the muscle uses **creatine phosphate**. With it, it can make new ATP very quickly. But this store lasts only **a few seconds**, for example for a short sprint or a jump. After that, the body has to switch to other energy sources.

Next, the muscle splits **glucose**, or grape sugar, without oxygen. This produces **lactate**, the salt of lactic acid. This route supplies energy quickly, but only a little per sugar molecule. In addition, the muscles **become acidic**. They feel heavy and burn, and you have to slow down. That is why nobody can keep up a sprint pace for an hour.

Anaerobic energy production is especially important in efforts that are very hard and last less than one or two minutes. A typical example is the **400-metre race**. Above a certain level of effort, lactate builds up strongly in the blood. This changeover is called the **anaerobic threshold**. In a marathon, runners therefore stay well below it.

After a very hard effort, you keep breathing faster for a while, even though you are already resting. The body takes in extra oxygen to refill its stores. This extra need is called **oxygen debt**. The lactate is cleared again in the following minutes and partly used to produce energy. **Gentle jogging** helps this to happen faster.

gewusst: Lactate is not waste: the heart and liver can use it again.
A good sprinter only reaches top speed after about 50 to 60 metres.

teile.einleitung: Adenosine triphosphate, ATP for short, is the energy currency of all cells. Every movement, every thought and every heartbeat needs energy from ATP. The body therefore makes it anew without a break.
wichtigste: ATP is made of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
When it is split into ADP and phosphate, around 30 kJ per mole are released.
The ATP store in the muscle lasts only a few seconds at maximum effort.
Most ATP is made in the mitochondria.
The enzyme ATP synthase makes most of it there.
Anaerobic glycolysis yields a net 2 ATP per glucose.
An adult turns over about their own body mass of ATP per day.

abschnitte.text: An ATP molecule is made of three parts: the base **adenine**, the sugar **ribose** and a chain of **three phosphate groups**. Between the phosphate groups lies a lot of usable energy. When the last phosphate group is split off, **ADP** (adenosine diphosphate) and phosphate arise. Under standard conditions, around **30 kJ per mole** are released in the process. Cells use this energy for their work.

The muscle stores only a little ATP. At maximum effort, for example in a sprint, this store lasts **only a few seconds**. After that, ATP has to be made anew at once. First **creatine phosphate** helps, which quickly passes its phosphate group to ADP. The enzyme **myokinase** also steps in: it makes one ATP and one AMP from two ADP molecules. At the same time, the production of energy from sugar and fat gets going.

In **glycolysis**, grape sugar, that is, **glucose**, is broken down in the cell fluid. This is fast and needs no oxygen. **Anaerobic glycolysis**, however, yields only a net **2 ATP** per molecule of glucose. **Lactate** arises in the process. That is why you can keep up very intense effort only for a short time.

The cell gains much more ATP when enough oxygen is there. Then the nutrients are broken down completely in the **mitochondria**, which is why they are also called the power stations of the cell. In their inner membrane sits **ATP synthase**. This enzyme works like a tiny turbine: a stream of hydrogen ions makes a part turn, and ATP is made in the process. In this way, the **largest part** of the ATP in the body arises.

In the body there is only a little ATP present at any moment. Each molecule, however, is split and built up again very often. Adding everything together, an adult human turns over **about their own body mass** of ATP per day. In hard physical work it is clearly even more.

gewusst: For research on ATP synthase there was a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1997.
ATP synthase is one of the smallest rotary motors in nature.

teile.einleitung: The great white shark is one of the biggest predatory fish in the sea and probably the most famous shark in the world. It has a mighty body and sharp triangular teeth, and hunts mainly seals and large fish.
wichtigste: The great white shark is one of the biggest predatory fish in the seas.
A fully grown great white shark can grow to about 6 metres long.
Large animals weigh well over a tonne.
It lives in temperate and warm coastal seas all over the world.
Its triangular teeth have serrated edges and keep growing back.
It can keep parts of its body warmer than the surrounding water.
The great white shark is regarded as vulnerable and is protected in many countries.

abschnitte.text: The great white shark has a spindle-shaped, very powerful body. It is grey on top and white on the belly, which is where its name comes from. This colouring is a **camouflage**: from above it looks like the dark sea, and from below like the bright light. Females grow bigger than males and can reach about 6 metres in length.

In its mouth it has several rows of triangular **teeth** with serrated edges, like a saw knife. If a tooth breaks off, a new one moves up from the next row. It can smell tiny amounts of blood in the water. With special sense organs on its snout, the **ampullae of Lorenzini**, it can even feel the weak electric fields of prey animals.

Great white sharks live mainly near the coast in temperate seas. They are well known, for example, off South Africa, Australia, California and Mexico. They also occur, rarely, in the **Mediterranean**. Some animals make long journeys of thousands of kilometres across the oceans.

Young great white sharks eat mainly fish. Adults like to hunt **seals** and sea lions, but also eat dolphins, turtles and dead whales. They often attack from below, from the depths, and sometimes shoot right out of the water as they do so. People are not part of their prey, and accidents usually happen through mistaken identity.

abschnitte.titel: Raising young and danger of extinction
abschnitte.text: Great white sharks do not lay eggs: the young develop in the body of the mother and are born alive. Newborns are already over a metre long and independent at once. The animals become adult late and have few young, so their populations recover only slowly. Through fishing and hunting for fins and jaws, the great white shark is **vulnerable** and today is protected in many countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fish that hunts and eats other animals.
Sense organs of sharks with which they feel weak electric fields.
Camouflage colouring with a dark back and a light belly.
A fish whose skeleton is made of flexible cartilage instead of bone.

gewusst: Sharks have no bony skeleton but one made of cartilage, like our ear.
Great white sharks can probably live to about 70 years old.
The 1975 film “Jaws” gave many people an exaggerated fear of sharks.

teile.einleitung: Actin is a protein found in all body cells. In muscle it forms, together with myosin, the machinery with which muscles contract. In other cells actin is an important part of the inner framework.
wichtigste: F-actin arises through polymerisation of G-actin monomers.
An actin filament consists of two chains wound around each other like a screw.
ATP or ADP is bound to every G-actin.
At rest, tropomyosin covers the binding sites for myosin.
Troponin C binds the calcium ions.
Alpha-actinin anchors the filaments in the Z-disc, and nebulin measures their length.
Outside muscle, actin belongs to the cytoskeleton.

abschnitte.text: Actin exists in two forms. The ball-shaped **G-actin** is a single building block, a **monomer**. Many of them join together into long threads, the thread-shaped **F-actin**. This process is called **polymerisation**. A nucleotide, **ATP or ADP**, is bound to every G-actin molecule. An actin filament has the shape of **two chains wound around each other like a screw**, rather like two twisted strings of beads.

In the muscle fibres, thin **actin filaments** and thick **myosin filaments** lie in order next to each other. The little heads of myosin can bind to actin and pull on it. In doing so the filaments slide past each other, and the muscle shortens. The actin filaments are anchored in the **Z-disc**, by the protein **alpha-actinin**. In skeletal muscle the large protein **nebulin** serves as a kind of **measuring rod** that determines the length of the actin filaments.

At rest the muscle should not contract. The thread-shaped protein **tropomyosin** sees to this. It lies in the groove of the actin filament and **covers the binding sites for myosin**. On the tropomyosin sits the **troponin complex** with three subunits. When a nerve signal arrives, the amount of calcium in the cell rises. The subunit **troponin C binds the calcium ions**, the complex changes its shape and pushes the tropomyosin aside. Now myosin can bind to actin.

Actin is not found only in muscle. In all body cells it belongs to the **cytoskeleton**, the inner framework of the cell. There it forms fine threads that are called **microfilaments**. They give the cell shape and support and help it to move. White blood cells, for example, crawl with the help of actin to a site of inflammation. In cell division too, a ring of actin pinches the cell into two parts.

gewusst: Actin is among the most common proteins in many cells of the body.
Actin was discovered in 1942 in the laboratory of Albert Szent-Györgyi in Hungary.

teile.einleitung: The Valais Blackneck goat is a striking breed of goat from the Upper Valais: deep black at the front, snow white at the back. It is regarded as one of the oldest breeds of domestic goat and is perfectly adapted to life in the high mountains. With its long, shaggy coat and big horns, it is a true emblem of the Valais.
wichtigste: The Valais Blackneck goat comes from the canton of Valais and the neighbouring Piedmont in Italy.
The front half of the body is black, and the rear half is white.
It has a long, shaggy coat, and both sexes carry horns.
The horns of the bucks can grow up to 80 centimetres long.
It is regarded as one of the oldest breeds of domestic goat in the world.
In the 1970s there were only about 440 purebred animals left.
Today it is found mainly around Visp, Zermatt and Saas-Fee.

abschnitte.text: The Blackneck goat is easy to recognise: the front half of the body with head, neck and front legs is **black**, and the rear half is **white**. Its coat is long and shaggy and protects well against the cold. Bucks and nannies both carry horns, and the horns of the bucks grow up to 80 centimetres long. The nannies also have a forelock, which in other breeds usually only the bucks have.

The breed comes from the **Upper Valais** and is also kept in the neighbouring Piedmont in Italy. Especially many animals live around the Vispertal, Zermatt and Saas-Fee. Other names are glacier goat, Vispertal goat or saddle goat. It is a true high mountain breed and climbs surely over steep, stony slopes.

Bucks are 75 to 85 centimetres high at the withers and weigh 65 to 70 kilograms. The nannies are a little smaller and weigh 45 to 50 kilograms. The head is relatively short, and the ears stand out slightly. The animals are regarded as hardy and **undemanding**, which means they get by on poor food.

The Blackneck goat is a **dual-purpose breed** that supplies milk and meat. A nanny gives about 600 kilograms of milk a year. On average she has 1.7 kids a year. In summer the goats often graze on alpine pastures, where they eat grass and herbs that lie too steep for cows.

At the end of the 19th century the goat was very popular in the Valais. Later its coat and horns were no longer thought fashionable, and in the 1970s only about 440 purebred animals were left in Switzerland. Thanks to breeders and associations the numbers rose again, and in 1999 there were almost 1300 registered nannies. A rare colour variant, the **copper-neck goat**, is supported by the foundation ProSpecieRara.

The Blackneck goat belongs to the Valais like the Matterhorn. At shows and when the animals come down from the alp, the most beautiful animals are displayed and awarded prizes. Goats also like to test their strength playfully with their horns in order to fix the **pecking order** in the herd. Many tourists photograph the black and white goats in Zermatt, where in summer they are sometimes driven through the village.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of domestic animals of the same species with shared features.
The highest point on the back of an animal, between the neck and the back.
A breed kept for two purposes, for example milk and meat.
The order of who is in charge in a group of animals.

gewusst: Because of the sharp line between the colours, it looks as if the goat has put on a black coat.
In Zermatt there has long been a custom of goatherds leading their herd through the village to the pasture in summer.

teile.einleitung: The coat of arms of Australia is the official national coat of arms of the country. It is especially well known because two typically Australian animals hold the shield: the kangaroo and the emu.
wichtigste: The present coat of arms of Australia was introduced in 1912.
On the left a kangaroo holds the shield, and on the right an emu.
Both animals occur naturally only in Australia.
The shield shows the badges of the six Australian states.
Above the shield shines a star with seven points.
In the background are branches of the golden wattle, Australia's national flower.
Below it on a ribbon is the word “Australia”.

abschnitte.titel: Layout of the coat of arms
abschnitte.text: In the middle stands a shield that is divided into six fields. Each field shows the badge of a **state**, that is, New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania. A thick border around the shield stands for the unity of the country. Above the shield sits the **Commonwealth Star** with seven points, six for the states and one for the territories.

The kangaroo is a **marsupial** and carries its young in a pouch on its belly. The largest is the red kangaroo, which moves along by hopping on its strong hind legs. It can make leaps of several metres as it does so. The long tail helps it to keep its balance.

After the ostrich, the emu is the second largest bird in the world and can grow almost two metres tall. It cannot fly, but runs very fast. In the emu, the **male** sits on the eggs and looks after the striped chicks. Emus live in open landscapes almost everywhere on the Australian mainland.

The kangaroo and the emu were chosen because they are native only to Australia and make the country easy to recognise. It is often said that neither animal can walk backwards easily. They are therefore seen as a sign that a country looks **forwards**. Whether that really played a part in the choice is not firmly proven, however.

Australia became a federation in 1901 and got a first coat of arms in 1908. In 1912 it was replaced by the present version. The **golden wattle** in the background, strictly speaking, is not part of the actual coat of arms, but an artistic addition. The coat of arms appears today on documents, government buildings and coins.

begriffe.erklaerung: A picture with fixed signs that stands for a country, a town or a family.
Figures, usually animals, that stand to the left and right of a shield and hold it.
A mammal whose young is born very small and goes on growing in the mother's pouch.
A flower that is regarded as a sign of a whole country.

gewusst: Switzerland also has animals in coats of arms: the canton of Bern bears a bear, and the canton of Uri a bull's head.
An emu can run as fast as a car in a 50 km/h zone.
The coat of arms is shown on the Australian 50 cent coin.

teile.einleitung: An adrenaline auto-injector is an emergency medicine in the form of a pen. People with severe allergies always carry it with them. In an allergic shock it can save lives, and even lay people can use it easily.
wichtigste: You inject it into the outer side of the thigh.
In an emergency you may inject through the trousers.
At severe signs of allergy you use it at once.
Adrenaline narrows the blood vessels and widens the bronchi.
The emergency kit often also includes an antihistamine and cortisone.
You have to check the expiry date and the viewing window regularly.
The dose depends on body weight.

abschnitte.text: Some people react very strongly to insect stings, nuts or other foods. A particularly severe allergic reaction is called **anaphylaxis**, in the worst case an **anaphylactic shock**. In it the airways can swell, breathing becomes difficult, and the blood pressure drops. Then it has to be quick. That is why those affected always carry an **adrenaline auto-injector** with them, often two of them.

Adrenaline is a hormone that the body also makes itself. In anaphylaxis it **narrows the blood vessels**, so that the blood pressure rises again. At the same time it **widens the bronchi**, the air passages in the lungs, and breathing becomes easier. Swellings also go down. The effect sets in quickly, but does not last very long.

At severe signs of allergy you use the auto-injector **at once**, without hesitating for long. You take off the protective cap and press the pen firmly against the **outer side of the thigh**. In an emergency you may inject **through the trousers**. You hold the pen in place for a few seconds, as the instructions describe. After that you call the emergency number **144** at once, because the person has to go to hospital, even if they are feeling better.

In the **emergency kit** of a person with allergies there belong, besides the auto-injector, typically an **antihistamine** and **cortisone**. The antihistamine relieves, for example, itching and rash, and cortisone works against the inflammation, but more slowly. A written **emergency plan** is also helpful, so that teachers or friends know what to do.

You have to check the **expiry date** regularly and arrange a replacement in good time. Through a small **viewing window** you can see the liquid. If it is **discoloured or cloudy**, you must **replace** the auto-injector. It is kept at **room temperature**, not in a hot car and not in the fridge. The **dose** depends on **body weight**, which is why there are pens for children and for adults.

gewusst: There are practice pens without a needle and without medicine with which you can train the use.
