Adrenaline is also called epinephrine, which is why this name is on some pens.

teile.einleitung: Whales are huge mammals that spend their whole lives in the water. Although they look like fish, they breathe with lungs like us and have to come up to the surface to take in air. Whales include the blue whale, the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth.
wichtigste: Whales live in the sea, but breathe with lungs like us humans.
They are mammals, give birth to live young and nurse them with milk.
A distinction is made between baleen whales and toothed whales.
Dolphins and porpoises are also whales.
The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived.
Whales breathe through a blowhole on the head.
Their ancestors lived on land about 50 million years ago.

abschnitte.text: Whales form a group of sea mammals with about 90 species. They are not fish, but **mammals** like cows or humans. Their tail fin, the **fluke**, lies horizontally and moves up and down, while fish move their tail fin from side to side. Under the skin, a thick layer of fat, the blubber, protects against the cold.

Whales breathe through a **blowhole** on top of the head, which is a kind of nostril. When breathing out, they blow out a fountain of air and water droplets, the blow. Large whales can dive for a long time: the sperm whale stays under water for over an hour and dives over 2000 metres deep. So that they do not drown in their sleep, in many whales only one half of the brain rests at a time.

**Baleen whales** such as the blue whale, humpback whale and fin whale have no teeth, but plates of baleen made of horn in the mouth. With them they sieve huge amounts of small crustaceans such as krill out of the water. The blue whale grows to about 30 metres long and can weigh well over 100 tonnes. Humpback whales are famous for their long songs.

The **toothed whales** include the sperm whale, orca, dolphins and porpoises. They hunt fish and squid, and the orca even catches seals. Toothed whales find their prey by **echolocation**: they send out clicking sounds and listen for the echo. The sperm whale is the largest toothed whale and the animal with the heaviest brain.

Whales usually give birth to a single young one alive, often tail first. The mother nurses it with very fatty milk. Many whales live in groups called **pods**. Orcas and sperm whales live in close family groups that are led by older females.

The ancestors of whales lived on land about 50 million years ago and had four legs. Over millions of years they adapted to life in the water. Their closest living relatives on land today are the **hippopotamuses**. No whales live in Switzerland, but fossil remains of sea animals show that the Central Plateau was once covered by a sea.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal whose young are fed on their mother's milk.
Horny plates in the mouth of baleen whales that work like a sieve.
The breathing opening on top of a whale's head.
Finding the way by sound, whose echo reveals the position of things.

gewusst: Blue whales are among the loudest animals in the world, and their deep calls carry hundreds of kilometres.
The song of humpback whales can be heard under water for many kilometres.
A newborn blue whale drinks hundreds of litres of milk every day.

teile.einleitung: An action potential is a short electrical impulse with which nerve cells pass on signals. It lasts only about one millisecond. All perceptions, thoughts and movements are based on such impulses.
wichtigste: In a typical neuron it is triggered from a threshold of about minus 50 mV.
The inflow of sodium causes the depolarisation.
The outflow of potassium brings about the repolarisation.
Afterwards the membrane is briefly hyperpolarised.
The all-or-nothing principle applies.
Normally an action potential arises at the axon hillock.
The neuron encodes a stronger stimulus by a higher frequency.

abschnitte.text: At rest a nerve cell is negatively charged on the inside, and the **resting potential** is about minus 70 millivolts (mV). The reason is ions distributed differently inside and outside. When signals reach the cell, the voltage becomes less negative. If it rises above a **threshold**, in a typical neuron **about minus 50 mV**, an action potential is triggered. This normally happens at the **axon hillock**, where the long extension of the nerve cell begins.

First, voltage-gated **sodium channels** open. Positive sodium ions rush into the cell, and the voltage rises into the positive range. This phase is called **depolarisation**. Then the sodium channels close, and **potassium channels** open. Through the **outflow of potassium** the cell becomes negative again, which is the **repolarisation**. For a moment the membrane even becomes more negative than at rest, which is the **hyperpolarisation**. The sodium-potassium pump then restores the old distribution of ions.

An action potential is triggered either **completely or not at all**, which is called the **all-or-nothing principle**. All action potentials of a cell are equally high. A neuron therefore encodes a **stronger stimulus** **by a higher frequency**, that is, it sends more impulses per second. Directly after an action potential comes the **absolute refractory period**. Then no new one can be triggered, because the **sodium channels are inactivated**. In this way the signal travels on in only one direction.

The researchers **Alan Hodgkin** and **Andrew Huxley** explained the mechanism around 1950. They studied the **giant axon of the squid**, an especially thick nerve fibre into which fine measuring electrodes could be inserted. With their measurements they described how sodium and potassium currents produce the action potential. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1963.

Many nerve fibres are surrounded by a fatty sheath, the **myelin**. At regular intervals the sheath has small gaps, the **nodes of Ranvier**. The action potential jumps from gap to gap, which is called **saltatory conduction**. In this way signals reach speeds of over 100 metres per second.

gewusst: The giant axon of the squid is so thick that you can see it with the naked eye.
The fastest nerve fibres pass on signals faster than a car travels on the motorway.

teile.einleitung: Birds are vertebrates with feathers, wings and a beak that lay eggs. Most of them can fly, but some such as the ostrich or the penguin stay on the ground or in the water. There are about 11 000 species of bird on Earth, from the tiny hummingbird to the giant ostrich.
wichtigste: Birds are the only living animals with feathers.
All birds lay eggs with a hard shell of lime, and a well-known example is the hen.
Instead of teeth, birds have a beak made of horn.
Many bird bones are hollow and therefore light.
Birds are warm-blooded, and their body temperature is usually around 40 degrees.
Birds are descended from dinosaurs.
About 200 species of bird nest in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The most important feature of birds is their **feathers**. Feathers keep them warm, make flying possible and, with their colours, serve as camouflage or for display. The front legs have turned into **wings**. Birds have a beak without teeth and lay eggs, which they usually sit on in a nest. Their heart beats fast, and they have a high body temperature.

To fly, birds need a light body and strong **chest muscles**. Many bones are hollow and run through with air chambers. The wings are curved, so that lift is created in flight. Their special breathing system with **air sacs** supplies them well with oxygen even at great heights. Some birds such as swifts stay in the air without a break for months.

Birds developed more than 150 million years ago from small, feathered **dinosaurs**. A famous fossil is Archaeopteryx from southern Germany, a mixed creature with feathers, teeth and a long tail. That is why researchers say today that birds are living dinosaurs. The crocodiles are their closest living relatives among the other reptiles.

There are about 11 000 **species of bird** worldwide. The smallest is the bee hummingbird, a hummingbird from Cuba weighing about 2 grams. The largest is the African ostrich, which can grow over 2.5 metres tall. Penguins cannot fly, but are excellent swimmers. Many species are **migratory birds** that fly south in autumn.

About 200 species of bird nest in Switzerland, including the blackbird, great tit, golden eagle and bearded vulture. The **Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach** studies and protects the native birds. Many migratory birds such as swallows and storks spend the winter in Africa. About 40 per cent of the breeding bird species are on the Red List, mainly species of farmland.

The **domestic chicken** is the most common farm animal in the world and supplies eggs and meat. People also keep ducks, geese, turkeys and budgerigars. Birds pollinate flowers, spread seeds and eat insects. Birdwatching is a popular hobby that you can start in your own garden.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal with a backbone, for example a fish, bird or human.
The body keeps its temperature itself, however warm it is outside.
A bird that flies to another area at certain times of year.
A male's wooing of a female, for example with song or dance.

gewusst: There are many more chickens in the world than people.
A swift can fly for up to ten months at a stretch without landing.
The ostrich lays the largest egg of all living birds.

teile.einleitung: Ticks are small, blood-sucking arachnids that live in meadows, woods and gardens. In Switzerland they matter for health, because they can pass on diseases such as Lyme disease and the brain infection TBE. With a few simple rules you can protect yourself well.
wichtigste: Ticks can pass on diseases such as Lyme disease and TBE.
In Switzerland the castor bean tick is the most common tick.
Ticks sit on grasses and bushes, usually up to a height of about a metre and a half.
They are active mainly from March to November.
There is a vaccination against TBE, but not against Lyme disease.
A tick should be removed as quickly as possible with tweezers.
After spending time outdoors, you should check your body for ticks.

abschnitte.text: **Lyme disease** is caused by bacteria that live in ticks. A typical sign is the **migrating redness**, a red ring around the site of the sting that spreads from days to weeks after the sting. Anyone who notices something like this should go to the doctor, because Lyme disease can be treated well with antibiotics. The longer a tick sucks, the greater the danger of infection.

**TBE** is an inflammation of the meninges or the brain that is caused by a virus. Most of those infected notice nothing or have only flu-like symptoms, but in rare cases the disease becomes severe. Against TBE there is an effective **vaccination**. The Federal Office of Public Health recommends it for almost the whole of Switzerland except the cantons of Geneva and Ticino.

Ticks live in the undergrowth, at woodland edges, in tall grass and also in gardens. They become active as soon as it is about 7 degrees warm, which is why they are out and about from spring to autumn. They climb onto grasses and bushes and wait there until a person or animal brushes against them. They do not fall from trees, but often crawl upwards on the body before they sting.

Long trousers and closed shoes are good protection in the woods, and you can pull your socks over your trouser legs. On light-coloured clothing you can see ticks better. A **tick repellent** on skin or clothing keeps them away in addition. After the outing you check your whole body, especially behind the knees, armpits, hairline and groin.

You grip a tick with fine **tweezers** or a tick card as close to the skin as possible and pull it out slowly and straight. You should not use oil, glue or nail varnish. Afterwards you disinfect the spot and note the date. In the following weeks you watch the site of the sting and go to the doctor if there is redness or fever.

begriffe.erklaerung: A disease triggered by bacteria that ticks pass on.
A viral inflammation of the meninges or brain, against which you can be vaccinated.
A red, spreading ring on the skin after a tick sting.
Protection against a disease by means of a vaccine.

gewusst: Ticks actually sting rather than bite, even though people often speak of a tick bite.
A tick sting usually does not hurt, because its saliva contains a numbing substance.
With the app “Zecke” you can report tick stings in Switzerland and so help research.

teile.einleitung: In biology, a host is a living thing on or in which another living thing lives and feeds from it. Usually this guest is a parasite, for example a tick, a tapeworm or an aphid. Plants on which aphids live and from which they feed are called host plants.
wichtigste: A host is a living thing that offers another living thing food or living space.
The guest is often a parasite that harms the host.
Plants on which aphids live and feed are called host plants.
Some parasites need several hosts one after another.
A distinction is made between intermediate host and definitive host.
A host can be an animal, a plant or a human.
Many parasites are specialised on quite particular hosts.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the innkeeper, who entertains guests. In biology, the **host** is the living thing that carries an uninvited guest. This guest is called a **parasite**. It takes food from the host, but gives nothing back and can weaken it or make it ill.

Aphids pierce plants with their mouthparts and suck the sweet plant sap. These plants are called **host plants**. Many caterpillars also eat only particular plants, for example the caterpillar of the brimstone butterfly on the alder buckthorn. The mistletoe is a plant that itself lives on trees as a hemiparasite, and its host is then the tree.

Some parasites change host in the course of their life. In the **intermediate host** the young stages grow up, and in the **definitive host** they become adult and reproduce. In the fox tapeworm, mice are the intermediate host and the fox is the definitive host. Humans can catch it by accident and are then what is called a dead-end host.

Parasites that live on the outside of the host are called **ectoparasites**, for example ticks, fleas and lice. Parasites on the inside, such as worms, are called endoparasites. The castor bean tick uses over 300 different species of vertebrate as hosts, from the mouse to the roe deer. In doing so it can carry disease germs from one host to the next.

The cuckoo also uses hosts, but in a special way. The female lays her eggs in the nests of other birds, for example of reed warblers or robins. These **host birds** sit on the strange egg and feed the young cuckoo until it is grown. This is called **brood parasitism**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that lives at the expense of another.
A plant on which an animal lives and from which it feeds.
A host in which only the young form of a parasite develops.
A host in which the parasite becomes adult and reproduces.

gewusst: A good parasite usually does not kill its host, because otherwise it loses its home.
Some species of aphid switch every year back and forth between two different host plants.

teile.einleitung: Sighthounds are slim, long-legged dogs that are famous for their enormous speed. They hunt with their eyes instead of their nose. The greyhound is regarded as one of the fastest breeds of dog in the world.
wichtigste: Sighthounds are a group of dog breeds that were bred for speed.
The greyhound is regarded as one of the fastest dogs in the world.
It reaches about 70 km/h.
Sighthounds hunt by sight, not with the nose.
Well-known breeds are the greyhound, whippet, Afghan hound and saluki.
Sighthounds are mostly calm and sleep a lot.

abschnitte.text: Sighthounds are a group of **dog breeds** with a slim body, long legs and a narrow head. They have a deep chest with a large heart and large lungs. The back is flexible like a spring. Well-known breeds are the **greyhound**, whippet, Afghan hound, saluki and borzoi.

The greyhound is regarded as one of the fastest breeds of dog in the world. For a short time it can reach about 70 km/h, as fast as a car on a country road. In the gallop all four legs are in the air twice per bound. Over long distances, however, sighthounds do not have more stamina than other dogs, they are **sprinters**.

Sighthounds are also called **gazehounds**. They spot prey such as hares from a long way off with their eyes and chase it. Other hunting dogs, by contrast, follow the trail with their nose. That is why sighthounds often have to be kept on a lead outdoors, because when they see something, they run off.

Sighthounds are among the oldest types of dog. Even in pictures from ancient Egypt you can see dogs like sighthounds. The saluki has been kept for hunting in the Middle East for thousands of years. In Europe, nobles hunted with sighthounds. The Russian borzoi was bred by nobles for hunting wolves.

Today, coursing with dogs for hunting is banned in Switzerland and many countries. Sighthounds instead run after an artificial lure in **greyhound races** or in lure coursing. At home they are mostly gentle, calm and sleep a lot. Many former racing dogs from Ireland, England or Spain are placed with families.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dog that spots prey with its eyes and chases it.
A large, very fast breed of sighthound from Great Britain.
A dog sport in which sighthounds follow an artificial lure across a field.
A runner who is very fast over short distances.

gewusst: A greyhound reaches its top speed after only a few bounds.
The whippet is a kind of small greyhound and is regarded as especially nimble in proportion to its size.

teile.einleitung: We speak of antibiotic resistance when bacteria have become insensitive to an antibiotic. The medicine then no longer works. Resistant bacteria are seen worldwide as one of the great dangers to health.
wichtigste: Resistant bacteria become more common through selection when antibiotics are used.
Bacteria can swap resistance genes with one another by horizontal gene transfer.
In conjugation, plasmids are passed from cell to cell through a pilus.
The enzyme beta-lactamase splits penicillins and makes them ineffective.
A germ that is resistant to several classes of antibiotics is called multi-resistant.
The One Health approach looks at humans, animals and the environment together.
In 2015 the Federal Council adopted the Antibiotic Resistance Strategy, StAR for short.

abschnitte.text: Bacteria multiply very fast, and in the process random changes in their genetic material keep appearing. Some of these make a bacterium tougher against an antibiotic. If an antibiotic is now used, the sensitive bacteria die and the resistant ones survive. They keep multiplying and become more common. This evolutionary process is called **selection**.

Bacteria can also pass resistance on to each other. In **horizontal gene transfer**, genes are swapped between existing cells. One important form is **conjugation**: two bacteria join up through a fine projection, the **pilus**. A **plasmid** is passed across, a small ring of genetic material. In this way, resistance can even spread between different kinds of bacteria.

Bacteria have various tricks against antibiotics. Many make the enzyme **beta-lactamase**, which **splits** penicillins and so makes them ineffective. Others change the spot where the antibiotic attacks, or pump the drug back out. If a germ is resistant to **several classes of antibiotics**, it is called **multi-resistant**. A well-known example is MRSA, a particularly tough form of Staphylococcus aureus.

Antibiotics are used not only in people but also in animals. Resistant bacteria and residues also get into water and soil. The **One Health** approach therefore looks at **humans, animals and the environment together**. In Switzerland, the **Federal Council** adopted the national **Antibiotic Resistance Strategy**, or **StAR**, in 2015. Several federal offices work together in it.

You should only take antibiotics if a doctor prescribes them. It is important to follow the instructions exactly. Anyone who **stops or changes the dose without talking to a doctor** helps resistance to develop. Antibiotics do not help against viruses, so not against an ordinary cold either. Leftover medicines should be taken back to the pharmacy instead of being poured down the drain.

gewusst: Resistant bacteria have even been found in ice and in caves where antibiotics were never used.
Alexander Fleming already warned about resistance in his Nobel Prize speech in 1945.

teile.einleitung: World Bee Day is an international day of remembrance on 20 May. It reminds us how important bees and other pollinators are for nature and for people. On World Bee Day, people celebrate the protection and the importance of bees.
wichtigste: World Bee Day takes place every year on 20 May.
The United Nations decided on it in 2017.
It was first celebrated in 2018.
The idea came from Slovenia.
20 May is the birthday of the bee pioneer Anton Janša.
The day draws attention to the protection of bees.
Bees pollinate many of our crops.

abschnitte.text: **World Bee Day** is a day of action of the United Nations, or UN for short. The General Assembly decided on it in December 2017. Since 2018 it has been marked every year on 20 May. It is meant to show how important bees and other **pollinators** such as bumblebees, butterflies and flies are.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the idea come from?
abschnitte.text: The proposal came from **Slovenia**, a country with a long tradition of beekeeping. 20 May is the birthday of **Anton Janša**, who was born in 1734. He was a Slovenian beekeeper and is regarded as a pioneer of modern beekeeping. He was a teacher of beekeeping at the court in Vienna.

Bees carry pollen from flower to flower and so **pollinate** the plants. Only then do many plants produce fruit and seeds. Apples, cherries, strawberries and rapeseed depend strongly on pollinators. Without bees there would therefore be much less fruit and vegetables.

Many wild bees are endangered today. In Switzerland there are over 600 species of wild bee, and almost half are on the Red List. The reasons are a lack of flower meadows, pesticides and diseases. For honey bees, the **varroa mite** is a big problem.

On World Bee Day there are events by beekeeping clubs, schools and nature conservation organisations. Everyone can help by planting native flowers or letting a patch of meadow grow. A **wild bee hotel** offers nesting places. Anyone who buys honey from local beekeepers supports beekeeping.

begriffe.erklaerung: When pollen gets onto another flower so that seeds and fruit can form.
A person who keeps bees and collects honey.
All kinds of bee except the honey bee, most of which live alone.
A list of endangered animal and plant species.

gewusst: About three quarters of the world's most important crops benefit from pollinators.
In Slovenia, traditionally painted beehive panels are a famous folk art.

teile.einleitung: An antagonist is a muscle that works as the opposing partner of another muscle. Because muscles can only pull, every movement needs one muscle for the movement one way and one for the movement back. The best-known example is the biceps and triceps in the upper arm.
wichtigste: An antagonist is an opposing muscle.
Muscles can only pull, not push.
The muscle that mainly carries out a movement is called the agonist.
A synergist supports the main muscle.
When the agonist contracts, the antagonist relaxes and is stretched.
The stomach muscles are the opposing partners of the muscles that straighten the back.

abschnitte.text: A muscle works by **contracting** and so becoming shorter. Through the tendons, it then pulls on a bone. But a muscle cannot **push**. For a joint to return to its starting position, a second muscle is therefore needed on the other side. This **opposing partner** is called an **antagonist**.

The muscle that mainly carries out a movement is called the **agonist**, the “player”. The muscle that makes the opposite movement is the **antagonist**. Muscles that support the main muscle in its work are called **synergists**. Depending on the movement, the agonist and antagonist swap roles. While the agonist contracts, the **antagonist relaxes** and is **stretched**.

In the upper arm, the **biceps** is at the front and the **triceps** at the back. When you bend the elbow, the biceps contracts and the **triceps is stretched**. When you straighten the arm again, it is the other way round: the triceps works, and the biceps is stretched. There are similar pairs all over the body. In the trunk, for example, the **stomach muscles** are the opposing partners of the **muscles that straighten the back**.

In strength training you should always train **both the agonist and the antagonist**. That keeps the muscles in **balance**. If one muscle is much stronger than its opposing partner, this can lead to poor posture or injuries. Anyone who only trains the stomach muscles, for example, should also strengthen the back. Balanced muscles protect the joints.

gewusst: Even when you stand still, opposing muscles are constantly working a little, so that you do not fall over.
The word “antagonist” comes from Greek and means opponent.

teile.einleitung: Tringa sandpipers are a group of slim wading birds with long legs and a long bill. They probe along shores and in shallow water for small animals and can often be seen in Switzerland on migration.
wichtigste: The Tringa sandpipers are a genus of birds from the family of snipes and sandpipers.
They include, for example, the green sandpiper, the wood sandpiper, the redshank and the greenshank.
Their bill is usually long and slender.
They eat mainly insects, worms and small crustaceans.
They have long legs and wade through shallow water with them.
Most species are migratory birds that breed in the north and spend the winter in the south.
In Switzerland they are seen mainly in spring and autumn on migration.

abschnitte.text: Tringa sandpipers are medium-sized **wading birds** about 20 to 35 centimetres long. They have long, often coloured legs and a long, slender bill. Their plumage is mostly patterned in grey, brown and white, so that they are well camouflaged on the shore. When taking off, many species call loudly and shrilly.

The **redshank** has bright red legs and breeds on coasts and in wet meadows. The greenshank has greenish legs and a slightly upturned bill. The **green sandpiper** is dark above and has a white rump that is easy to see in flight. The wood sandpiper is daintier and is often seen on migration at Swiss waters.

Sandpipers look for their food in mud, puddles and shallow water. They eat mainly insects and their larvae, worms and small **crustaceans**. With the long bill they probe the soft ground or pick prey from the surface. Sometimes they also catch small fish or tadpoles.

Many sandpipers breed in the far north, for example in Scandinavia, Russia and Siberia. In autumn they fly as **migratory birds** as far as the Mediterranean or Africa. The green sandpiper has a special feature: it often breeds in old nests of other birds high up in trees. After hatching, the chicks jump from the nest to the ground.

In Switzerland, sandpipers rest mainly on flat shores of lakes, river mouths and sewage works. Good places to watch them are, for example, the **Fanel** on Lake Neuchâtel or the Bolle di Magadino on Lake Maggiore. For the birds, such **resting places** are important for taking on energy on the long journey. Because wetlands have become rare, they are under special protection.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird with long legs that looks for food in shallow water.
A group of closely related species in the classification of living things.
A bird that flies back and forth every year between its breeding ground and its winter quarters.
A place where migratory birds take a break and feed on the way.

gewusst: The insect pond skater and the bird sandpiper are not related at all, they only share the name in German.
Some sandpipers fly thousands of kilometres on their migration.
The chicks of many wading birds can run and look for food by themselves soon after hatching.

teile.einleitung: Water quality tells you how clean and healthy the water of a stream, river or lake is. Many animals such as whitefish or stonefly larvae can live only in good water, and so they reveal how a water body is doing.
wichtigste: For water quality, oxygen, temperature, nutrients and pollutants are important.
Cold water can take up more oxygen than warm water.
Whitefish are a sign of good water quality, because they need cool, oxygen-rich water.
Animals that reveal something about the state of the water are called bioindicators.
Stonefly larvae show clean water, while many water lice show rather polluted water.
Too much fertiliser in the water makes algae grow strongly and uses up oxygen.
In Switzerland, sewage works clean the waste water before it gets into rivers and lakes.

abschnitte.text: Water quality describes the state of a water body for animals, plants and people. What is measured is, for example, the **oxygen content**, the temperature and the acidity. It is also important how many nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen are in the water. Added to this are pollutants such as pesticides, remains of medicines or microplastics.

Some animals tolerate only clean water, while others also put up with pollution. Such animals are called **bioindicators**. Larvae of stoneflies, mayflies and caddis flies live only in clean, oxygen-rich water. Many water lice, leeches or red midge larvae, on the other hand, show that the water is polluted.

Fish use their gills to breathe the oxygen that is dissolved in the water. **Cold water** can take up more oxygen than warm water. That is why fish such as trout, grayling and whitefish suffer in hot summers, when rivers and lakes warm up strongly. In the heatwave summer of 2018, many grayling died in the Rhine near Schaffhausen.

If a lot of fertiliser or waste water gets into a lake, algae grow very strongly. When the algae die, bacteria use up a lot of oxygen on the lake bed as they break them down. This **over-fertilisation** was a big problem in many Swiss lakes in the 1960s and 1970s. Since 1986, phosphates in washing powders have been banned in Switzerland, and some lakes such as Lake Baldegg are even supplied with oxygen artificially.

Today almost every household in Switzerland is connected to a **sewage works**. For some years now, many large sewage works have been given an additional cleaning stage against micropollutants. Thanks to these measures, you can swim again without worry in most Swiss lakes and rivers. Even so, residues from farming, roads and households remain a challenge.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing whose presence reveals something about the environment.
Too many nutrients in the water, so that algae grow strongly.
A plant that cleans dirty waste water.
Tiny amounts of substances such as medicines or pesticides in the water.

gewusst: School classes can find out for themselves how clean a stream is with a sieve and an identification chart.
A litre of cold water contains clearly more dissolved oxygen than a litre of warm water.
A large part of Swiss drinking water comes from groundwater and springs and often needs hardly any treatment.

teile.einleitung: The pond skater is a bug that runs over the surface of ponds and streams without sinking. On its long, thin legs it glides lightning-fast across the water and hunts insects.
wichtigste: Pond skaters are insects from the group of true bugs and have six legs.
Their body is slim and elongated.
Fine hairs on the legs repel water, so they do not sink in.
They row with the middle legs and steer with the hind legs.
They use the short front legs to seize their prey.
With their piercing mouthparts they suck their prey dry.
Their young look like small adults, but without wings.

abschnitte.text: The common pond skater grows to about 1 centimetre long and is dark brown to black. Its body is slim and elongated, and the middle and hind legs are very long. The **front legs** are short and serve as grasping tools. Some pond skaters have wings and can fly, while others have only short wings or none at all.

Pond skaters make use of the **surface tension** of the water, a kind of thin skin on the surface. On their legs sit countless fine, water-repellent hairs. Their feet press only small dimples into the water without breaking through it. In sunshine you can therefore see round **shadows** on the bottom of the pond beneath a resting pond skater.

To move, pond skaters make strong **rowing strokes** with their middle legs. This makes them glide in jerks across the surface of the water. The hind legs are used mainly for steering, rather like a rudder. In this way they can change direction quickly and dodge enemies.

Pond skaters eat mainly insects that have fallen into the water and are struggling. They feel the waves from these **vibrations** with their legs. They grab the prey with the front legs and pierce it with their **piercing mouthparts**. Then they suck the prey dry.

Pond skaters often stay in groups on a pond. The females lay their eggs on plants in or at the water. Larvae hatch from the eggs and develop into adults over several moults, without a **pupal stage**. Adult pond skaters usually spend the winter hidden on land, for example under moss or leaves.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that makes the surface of water behave like a thin skin.
A property by which water runs off in beads and does not stick.
A pointed mouth tool with which bugs pierce and suck up fluid.
The young form of an animal, which still has to develop into the adult animal.

gewusst: If you put a few drops of washing-up liquid into the water, the surface loses its tension and a pond skater would sink.
Some relatives of the pond skater live on the open sea and are the only insects at home there.
Pond skaters communicate by making small waves on the water with their legs.

teile.einleitung: The whale shark is the largest fish in the world and can grow as long as a city bus. Despite its size, it is a peaceful giant that filters only tiny living things such as plankton out of the water. It lives in warm seas around the globe and is badly endangered today.
wichtigste: The whale shark is the largest living fish in the world.
The longest reliably documented body length is about 18.8 metres.
It filters tiny living things such as plankton out of the water.
It belongs to the cartilaginous fish and to the order of carpet sharks.
Its family Rhincodontidae contains only a single genus.
Andrew Smith first described it scientifically in 1828.
Every whale shark has its own pattern of light spots.

abschnitte.text: The whale shark is a **shark** and so a fish, not a mammal. It belongs to the class of **cartilaginous fish**, whose skeleton is made of cartilage instead of bone. It gets its name from its size and because it filters its food out of the water in a similar way to baleen whales. In classification it counts in the order of carpet sharks and in the family Rhincodontidae, which contains only a single genus.

The whale shark has a broad, flat head with a huge mouth right at the front. Its dark grey to bluish back is covered with light spots and stripes that form a **pattern** of its own in every animal. Most adult whale sharks grow to about 10 to 12 metres long. The greatest reliably documented length is about 18.8 metres.

The whale shark eats mainly **plankton**, that is, tiny crustaceans, fish eggs, jellyfish and small fish. It swims with its mouth open or sucks in large amounts of water. Sieve-like **gill rakers** hold the food back, and the water flows out again through the gill slits. Although it has thousands of tiny teeth, it hardly needs them for eating.

Whale sharks live in all the tropical and warm seas of the world. They often migrate long distances and sometimes dive very deep. At certain times of year they meet at places with a lot of food, for example at **Ningaloo Reef** in Western Australia, off Mexico or the Philippines. There divers swim with the harmless giants.

The whale shark was first described scientifically in 1828 by the doctor and zoologist **Andrew Smith**. It was based on an animal that had been harpooned in Table Bay near Cape Town in South Africa. The genus name Rhincodon probably means “rasp tooth”. The full scientific name is Rhincodon typus.

Whale sharks give birth to live young that first develop from eggs inside the mother. A female caught in 1995 carried around 300 **embryos** inside her. Because whale sharks grow slowly and become adult late, their populations recover only slowly. Through fishing, bycatch and collisions with ships, the whale shark is regarded today as **endangered**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fish such as sharks and rays whose skeleton is made of flexible cartilage.
Tiny living things that float in the water and drift with the current.
An animal that sieves its food out of the water.
A sieve at the gills that holds back food.

gewusst: You can recognise every whale shark by its pattern of spots, rather as people are recognised by their fingerprints.
A whale shark usually swims along comfortably at only about five kilometres an hour, so about walking pace.

teile.einleitung: Acne is a very common skin condition with blackheads and spots. It occurs mainly in the teenage years, on the face, the back and the chest. Acne is not contagious and has nothing to do with a lack of cleanliness.
wichtigste: Acne is a skin condition with blackheads and spots.
It occurs most often in the teenage years.
The sebaceous glands play the main role.
The technical term for a blackhead is comedo.
The bacterium Cutibacterium acnes is involved in the inflamed spot.
You should not squeeze spots, or scars can form.
Severe acne is treated by a dermatologist.

abschnitte.text: In the skin there are many small **sebaceous glands**. They make **sebum**, a fat that keeps the skin supple. In the **teenage years** hormones change the skin, and the sebaceous glands often make clearly more sebum. At the same time the opening of the gland becomes more horny and gets blocked. The sebum builds up, and a **blackhead** forms. Inherited traits also play a part in whether someone gets severe acne.

The technical term for a blackhead is **comedo**. Closed blackheads are small white bumps under the skin. In open blackheads the tip is **dark**. This is not dirt: the **contents turn dark in the air**. That is why scrubbing especially hard does not help either. Washing too vigorously can even irritate the skin.

In the blocked opening of the sebaceous gland the bacterium **Cutibacterium acnes** multiplies. It actually lives on every skin, but finds especially much food in the dammed-up sebum. The immune system reacts, and a red, inflamed **spot** forms, sometimes with pus. You should not **squeeze** spots: the **inflammation can spread**, and **scars** can be left behind.

For mild acne, gentle cleansing and special creams or gels from the pharmacy are often enough. It also helps not to touch the skin constantly with your fingers. **Severe acne** belongs with a **dermatologist**, that is, a specialist in skin diseases. There are effective medicines to apply and to take by mouth. Patience is important, because a treatment often works only after a few weeks.

**Severe, untreated acne** can leave permanent **scars**. Many teenagers also suffer from how they look and feel unsure. That is why it is worth having severe acne treated early. In most people the acne becomes clearly milder after the teenage years or disappears completely.

gewusst: Acne is one of the most common skin diseases of all, and the great majority of teenagers have at least a few spots.
The bacterium Cutibacterium acnes used to be called Propionibacterium acnes.

teile.einleitung: An allergy is an overreaction of the immune system to substances that are actually harmless, such as pollen, house dust or peanuts. The body wrongly thinks these substances are dangerous and fights back fiercely. Allergies are very common, including among children in Switzerland.
wichtigste: An allergy is an exaggerated defence reaction of the immune system against harmless substances.
Substances that cause an allergy are called allergens.
Common allergens are pollen, house dust mites, animal hair, nuts, milk and insect venom.
Typical symptoms are sneezing, itchy eyes, a skin rash or difficulty breathing.
Hay fever is the best-known allergy and happens mainly in spring and summer.
A very strong allergic reaction is called anaphylactic shock and is an emergency.
Allergies can be identified with tests at the doctor’s and eased with medicines.

abschnitte.text: Our **immune system** protects us from germs such as bacteria and viruses. In an allergy it makes a mistake and fights harmless substances. These substances are called **allergens**. The first time the body meets an allergen, it remembers it, and the next time there is a reaction.

Allergies to the **pollen** of birches, hazels or grasses are very common. The droppings of house dust mites, cat hair or moulds also often cause allergies. Among foods, peanuts, hazelnuts, cow’s milk, eggs and fish are well-known triggers. Some people also react to bee or wasp stings.

In many allergies the body makes special antibodies called **IgE**. They sit on defence cells known as mast cells. When the allergen meets these cells, they release the messenger substance **histamine**. Histamine makes the nose run, the eyes water and the skin itch.

Most allergic reactions are annoying, but not dangerous. But there is also **anaphylaxis**, a strong reaction in the whole body. The airways can swell up and blood pressure can fall sharply. People with severe allergies therefore often carry an **adrenaline auto-injector**, a kind of emergency syringe.

The most effective thing is to avoid the allergen, for example by not eating certain foods. **Antihistamines** are medicines that block the effect of histamine. In **desensitisation**, you are given small amounts of the allergen over several years so that the body gets used to it. In Switzerland, the pollen warning service of MeteoSwiss gives information about the current pollen count.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that causes an allergy in some people, for example pollen.
A messenger substance in the body that causes itching, swelling and a runny nose.
An allergy to pollen that causes sneezing and watering eyes.
A very strong, life-threatening allergic reaction in the whole body.

gewusst: About one in five people in Switzerland suffers from hay fever.
The hazel often flowers as early as January or February, so the pollen season sometimes starts in the middle of winter.
The word allergy comes from Greek and means roughly “other reaction”.

teile.einleitung: The white stork is a large black and white bird with red legs and a red bill. It builds huge nests on roofs and poles, often spends the winter in Africa and once died out in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The white stork has white plumage with black wing feathers, as well as red legs and a red bill.
It breeds in Switzerland and often spends the winter in Africa.
Instead of calling, it clatters loudly with its bill.
Storks use their nest again every year and build it up further.
A very old stork nest can weigh over 100 kilograms.
In Switzerland the white stork had died out by about 1950 and was reintroduced at Altreu.
A white stork can live to about 20 years old.

abschnitte.text: The white stork is about 80 to 100 centimetres tall and has a wingspan of around 2 metres. Its plumage is white, and only the large **flight feathers** are black. Legs and bill are bright red. It is clearly different from the rarer **black stork**, which has black plumage and lives hidden in the forest.

The white stork strides slowly over meadows, fields and wetlands and looks for food. It eats mice, frogs, earthworms, insects and small fish. When it rests, it often stands on **one leg**. Because it has hardly any voice, it communicates by loud **clattering** of its bill.

Storks build their nests on roofs, chimneys, church towers, poles or tall trees. Stork pairs often return every year to the same **eyrie** and build it up further with branches, grass and earth. In time a nest can weigh over 100 kilograms. The female usually lays three to five eggs, which both parents sit on in turn.

In August the storks leave Europe and fly south. Because they like to glide on warm, rising air in **soaring flight**, they avoid long stretches over open sea. They therefore take a western route over Spain and Gibraltar or an eastern route over the **Bosporus** and Israel. On the way they find their bearings by landscapes, by the sun and by their experience, and many Swiss storks today already spend the winter in Spain.

In the past, storks bred in many Swiss villages, but by about 1950 the white stork had died out here. The ornithologist Max Bloesch founded a stork station in **Altreu** in the canton of Solothurn in 1948 and brought in storks from North Africa. With release programmes and protection measures, the stork returned. Today several hundred pairs breed in Switzerland again, and Altreu is known as a stork village.

begriffe.erklaerung: A loud noise that a stork makes by rapidly knocking its bill together.
The large nest of storks or birds of prey.
Flying without a wingbeat on warm, rising air.
Animals that have lived in captivity are set free in the wild.

gewusst: According to an old legend, the stork brings the babies.
Many storks wear a ring on the leg so that researchers can follow their route.
Young storks fly south in their first autumn without their parents.

teile.einleitung: Whaling means hunting whales in order to use their fat, their meat and other parts. Over centuries so many whales were killed that some species such as the blue whale almost died out. Today commercial whaling is greatly restricted by an international ban.
wichtigste: People have hunted whales for thousands of years.
In the past many blue whales were hunted for their fat and meat.
From whale fat people obtained train oil, which was used as lamp oil and for soap and margarine.
In the 20th century, factory ships killed more whales than ever before.
The International Whaling Commission was founded in 1946.
Since 1986 an international ban on commercial whaling has been in force.
Some countries such as Japan, Norway and Iceland still go on hunting whales.

abschnitte.text: Even in the Stone Age people hunted whales on the coasts, as old rock pictures show. Peoples of the Arctic such as the **Inuit** used almost everything from a whale: meat and fat to eat, bones for tools and hides for boats. In the Middle Ages the **Basques** in northern Spain became well-known whalers. Later whalers from the Netherlands, England and America sailed on all the seas.

The most important product was **train oil**, an oil from the fat of whales. Lamps burned with it in streets and houses, and it was made into soap and lubricant. The baleen of baleen whales, the **whalebone**, was flexible and was used for corsets and umbrellas. The meat was also eaten.

Around 1870 the Norwegian Svend Foyn developed a **harpoon gun** with an exploding tip. Together with fast steamships, it was now possible to hunt large, fast whales such as the blue whale as well. In the 20th century, huge **factory ships** processed the whales right on the open sea. In the 20th century alone, well over 300 000 blue whales were killed.

Through the hunting, the populations of many whale species collapsed dramatically. Of the blue whale only a tiny fraction was left, and it was close to extinction. In 1946 several states founded the **International Whaling Commission**, IWC for short. Since 1966 the blue whale has been protected worldwide.

In 1982 the IWC decided on a **moratorium**, that is, a pause on commercial whaling, which applied from 1986. Today blue whales and other whales are protected worldwide by this international ban on whaling. Only a small hunt is still allowed for some indigenous peoples who have always lived on whales. Switzerland is also a member of the IWC and works for the protection of whales.

Norway and Iceland go on hunting whales despite the ban, mainly minke whales and fin whales. Japan left the IWC in 2019 and has since hunted commercially again in its own waters. Many whale species are recovering slowly, but dangers such as ship collisions, fishing nets and noise in the sea remain. In many countries today, **whale watching** brings in more money than hunting did in the past.

begriffe.erklaerung: Oil obtained from the fat of whales or fish.
A throwing spear or missile with barbs for catching large sea animals.
An agreed stop or pause on something.
Trips by boat to watch whales in the wild.

gewusst: Before there was paraffin and electricity, many street lamps in Europe burned whale oil.
One blue whale supplied as much oil as several dozen smaller whales put together.

teile.einleitung: Hibernation is a deep sleep lasting months with which some animals survive the cold winter. Their body almost switches to low power. Hedgehogs, marmots, dormice and bats are true hibernators.
wichtigste: In hibernation the body temperature falls sharply.
In the hedgehog it falls from about 35 to around 5 degrees.
Heartbeat and breathing become very slow.
The animals live on their fat reserves.
True hibernators are the hedgehog, marmot, dormouse and bats.
In between, the animals wake up briefly.
Disturbances can be deadly for hibernators.

abschnitte.text: In **hibernation** an animal runs its body almost completely down. The body temperature falls sharply, often to only a few degrees above the surroundings. Heartbeat and breathing become very slow, and the **metabolism** needs hardly any energy. In this way the animal can get by for months without food on its fat reserves.

The **hedgehog** hibernates from about November to March. Its body temperature falls from about 35 degrees to around 5 degrees. Its heart then beats only about 5 to 10 times per minute instead of almost 200 times. It sleeps in a nest of leaves, for example under hedges or in piles of leaves. In autumn a hedgehog needs enough weight to survive the winter.

The **Alpine marmot** sleeps for up to six months of the year. The family spends the winter close together in a burrow that they line with hay and seal. The body temperature falls to about 3 to 5 degrees. Every few weeks the animals wake up briefly and warm themselves up. Marmots are common in the Swiss Alps.

The **edible dormouse** gets its German name Siebenschläfer, meaning seven sleeper, because it sleeps for about seven months. Bats spend the winter in caves, tunnels or attics and hang there upside down. The hazel dormouse and the ground squirrel are also hibernators. Cold-blooded animals such as frogs and lizards, by contrast, fall into **cold torpor**.

Every waking costs a lot of energy. If an animal is woken too often, its fat does not last until spring. That is why you should leave piles of leaves lying in the garden and not disturb bat roosts. A hedgehog that you find in winter should not simply be taken into the house, but you should ask a hedgehog rescue centre.

begriffe.erklaerung: A deep sleep in winter with a sharply lowered body temperature.
All the processes in the body that use up and convert energy.
The stiff state of cold-blooded animals in the cold.
Animals whose body temperature depends on the surroundings.

gewusst: A hedgehog loses up to a third of its weight in hibernation.
In hibernation, marmots sometimes breathe only a few times a minute.

teile.einleitung: The tawny owl is a medium-sized owl with a round head and big dark eyes. It is the most common owl in Switzerland and lives in woods, parks and even in villages and towns. Its call “hooo, hu hu-hooo” can be heard on many nights, but the well-camouflaged bird itself is seldom seen.
wichtigste: The tawny owl is active mainly at night and at dusk.
It lives in woods, parks and also in settlements.
A fully grown tawny owl usually weighs between 400 and 700 grams, and females are heavier than males.
There is a grey and a reddish brown plumage variety.
Its very big eyes see excellently in twilight.
Tawny owl pairs usually stay together for life.
The eggs are incubated for about 28 to 30 days.

abschnitte.text: The tawny owl grows to about 40 centimetres tall and has a round head without **ear tufts**. Its plumage is either grey or reddish brown and patterned with dark streaks, so it is perfectly camouflaged against tree bark. The females are usually heavier than the males. A fully grown bird usually weighs between 400 and 700 grams.

The tawny owl lives in deciduous and mixed woods, in parks, cemeteries and gardens with old trees. It is found in almost all of Europe and is also widespread in Switzerland. Especially important are old deciduous trees with natural **tree holes**, in which it nests and hides by day. But it also accepts nest boxes, barns or church towers.

The tawny owl hunts at night and at dusk from a perch. Its eyes are very big and can see excellently in twilight, and its hearing is so fine that it can hear a mouse under the leaves. Thanks to soft feathers with serrated edges, it flies almost **silently**. It eats mainly mice, but also small birds, frogs, beetles and earthworms, and it coughs up indigestible remains as **pellets**.

The male calls a long drawn-out “hooo, hu hu-hooo”, and the female often answers with a sharp “ku-wit”. Many people recognise only this call, without ever spotting the well-camouflaged bird. A tawny owl pair defends a **territory**, which usually covers a few hectares of forest or built-up area. The pairs often stay together there all their lives.

Tawny owls nest very early in the year, often in February or March. The female usually lays two to four white eggs and sits on them for about 28 to 30 days, while the male brings food. The young leave the hole before they can really fly and then sit on twigs as **branchers**. Such young birds are not abandoned, because the parents go on feeding them.

A wild tawny owl usually lives to be about 5 to 10 years old, and some much older. Dangers are road traffic and the lack of old trees with holes. In Switzerland the tawny owl is not regarded as threatened. Anyone who puts up nest boxes and leaves old trees standing helps it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird of prey of the night with big eyes that point forwards.
A lump of hair and bones that an owl coughs up.
A young bird that has left the nest but cannot really fly yet.
An area that an animal defends against others of its species.

gewusst: A tawny owl can turn its head very far, about three quarters of a full turn.
The well-known owl hoot “hoo-hoo” in films mostly comes from the tawny owl.
Tawny owls defend their nest very bravely and even attack people who come too close.

teile.einleitung: The tundra is a treeless cold steppe in the far north of the Earth, where there are long, icy winters and only short summers. Mainly mosses, lichens, grasses and low shrubs grow here. Typical inhabitants are reindeer, Arctic foxes and ptarmigan.
wichtigste: The tundra is a treeless cold steppe in cold regions.
It lies mainly in the north of Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia and Siberia.
Deep down the ground is frozen all year round, which is called permafrost.
Trees cannot grow here because of the cold and the short summer.
Reindeer travel in large herds through the tundra and eat lichens.
In summer many plants bloom and countless mosquitoes swarm out.
Because of global warming, the permafrost is thawing in many places.

abschnitte.text: The **Arctic tundra** lies north of the great coniferous forests, for example in Alaska, northern Canada, Greenland, northern Scandinavia and Siberia. High in the mountains there are also landscapes like the tundra, which are called **alpine tundra**. In the Alps this is the zone above the tree line. The word tundra comes from Finnish or Sámi and means roughly treeless hill.

In winter it often gets to minus 30 degrees in the tundra, and for months it is almost always dark. The summer lasts only about two months, but then the sun sometimes shines round the clock. Below the surface lies the **permafrost**, a soil that stays frozen permanently. In summer only the top layer thaws, which is why many pools and bogs form.

In the tundra grow **lichens**, mosses, grasses, sedges and dwarf shrubs such as the dwarf birch. The plants stay small and grow close to the ground, where it is warmer and less windy. Many bloom very quickly and brightly in the short summer. Reindeer lichen is one of the most important sources of food for animals.

The best-known animal is the **reindeer**, called caribou in North America, which migrates in huge herds. Other inhabitants are Arctic foxes, lemmings, snowy owls, musk oxen and ptarmigan. Many have a thick coat or plumage and turn white in winter. In summer millions of migratory birds come to breed, because there are then many insects.

In the tundra live peoples such as the **Sámi** in Scandinavia, the Inuit in Canada and Greenland and the Nenets in Siberia. Some of them traditionally keep reindeer. The Arctic is warming faster than the rest of the Earth. When the permafrost thaws, greenhouse gases escape, and houses and roads can sink.

begriffe.erklaerung: Ground that has been frozen without a break for at least two years.
A partnership of a fungus and an alga that also grows in barren places.
The line above or north of which no trees grow any more.
Open land without trees in a very cold climate.

gewusst: Dwarf willows in the tundra are often only a few centimetres tall, although they are many years old.
Well-preserved mammoths have already been found in the permafrost of Siberia.
Reindeer are the only deer in which the females also carry antlers.

teile.einleitung: Toucans are tropical birds from Central and South America that you can recognise at once by their huge, colourful bill. They form the family Ramphastidae and belong to the order of woodpecker-like birds. Their bill is amazingly light and even helps them to control their body temperature.
wichtigste: Toucans form the bird family Ramphastidae in the order of woodpecker-like birds (Piciformes).
The family includes about 40 species in mostly five genera.
The closest relatives of the toucans are the toucan barbets of the genus Semnornis.
The toco toucan (Ramphastos toco) is the largest species, about 55 to 63 centimetres long and 0.5 to 0.9 kilograms in weight.
Its bill is on average about 20 centimetres long in the male.
Inside, the bill is made of airy bone foam under a thin keratin sheath and is therefore light.
In 2009, researchers showed in the journal Science that the bill works as a heat exchanger.

abschnitte.text: Toucans have a **huge bill**, which in some species makes up almost a third of the body length. It is often coloured bright yellow, orange, red, green or black. The plumage is mostly black or green with colourful patches on the throat and rump. Like woodpeckers, toucans have two toes pointing forwards and two backwards, which they use to cling well to branches. The largest species, the **toco toucan**, grows to about 55 to 63 centimetres long.

Although the bill is so big, it is very light. Inside it is made of an airy **bone foam** with many small hollow spaces. On the outside lies a thin sheath of **keratin**, the same substance as our fingernails. This horny layer is built up from overlapping little plates, like roof tiles. Engineers study this structure in order to develop light and stable materials.

abschnitte.titel: The bill as an air conditioner
abschnitte.text: In 2009 researchers showed in the journal **Science** that the bill of the toco toucan works as a **heat exchanger**. When it gets hot, more blood flows through the blood vessels in the bill, and heat is given off. When it gets cool, the blood flow is reduced. In this way the bird can regulate its body temperature cleverly, rather like an elephant with its ears.

Toucans live in forests from Mexico to northern Argentina, many in **tropical rainforest**. The toco toucan is also found in more open landscapes, for example in the Pantanal in Brazil. Toucans eat mainly fruit, but also insects, lizards and the eggs and young of other birds. With the long bill they reach fruit on thin twigs that would not bear their weight. Because they pass out seeds, they help to spread the forest.

Toucans often live in pairs or in small groups and call loudly and harshly. They nest in **tree holes**, for example in old woodpecker holes. The female usually lays 2 to 4 white eggs, and both parents sit on them and feed the young. To sleep, toucans tuck their bill and tail under their plumage and become a small ball of feathers.

Toucans belong to the order of **woodpecker-like birds**, which also includes our woodpeckers. Their closest relatives are the **toucan barbets** of the genus Semnornis. The family includes about 40 species, in five genera under the classification most used today, among them the large toucans (Ramphastos) and the aracaris. Some species are threatened by the felling of rainforests and by the illegal animal trade. In Switzerland you can see toucans only in zoos.

begriffe.erklaerung: A horny substance that hair, nails and feathers are also made of.
Something that passes heat from one place to another.
A bird order that includes woodpeckers, barbets and toucans.
A group of very closely related species.

gewusst: The bill of the toco toucan is almost as long as the rest of its body without the tail.
Toucans sometimes toss fruit into the air with their bill and catch it again.
Young toucans hatch naked and still have a very small bill.

teile.einleitung: Poaching is the forbidden hunting, catching or killing of wild animals. It threatens many species all over the world, such as rhinos, elephants and tigers. The fight against poaching is one of the great tasks in nature conservation.
wichtigste: Poaching is illegal hunting of wild animals.
Rhinos are often hunted for their horn.
That rhino horn helps against illnesses has not been proved.
Elephants are poached for their ivory.
The Washington Convention on endangered species, CITES, regulates trade in endangered species.
Wardens and rangers protect the animals.
There is poaching in Switzerland too.

abschnitte.text: **Poaching** means that someone hunts, catches or kills wild animals without permission. This can happen in protected areas, at the wrong time or with protected species. The people who do it are called **poachers**. Often a lot of money is involved, because body parts of rare animals are sold at high prices.

Rhinos are unfortunately often hunted for their horn. The horn is made of **keratin**, the same material as our fingernails. Some people believe it helps against illnesses, but that has not been proved. Elephants are killed for their tusks of **ivory**. Tigers, pangolins and gorillas are also threatened.

Because of poaching, some species have almost died out. The northern white rhino, for example, has only two living females left. If large animals are missing, the whole **ecosystem** is thrown into confusion. Elephants, for example, spread seeds and keep landscapes open.

abschnitte.titel: What is being done about it
abschnitte.text: Since 1973 there has been the **Washington Convention on endangered species**, CITES for short, which regulates trade in endangered species. Its secretariat is in Geneva. In protected areas, **rangers** patrol, sometimes with tracker dogs and drones. In some countries, rhinos have had their horns sawn off so that poachers no longer kill them.

There is poaching in Switzerland too, for example when red deer, chamois or ibex are shot without a permit. Protected animals such as the wolf, lynx or birds of prey are also sometimes killed illegally. The cantons' **game wardens** supervise hunting. Anyone who poaches is punished. In the past, poachers in the mountains were sometimes even seen as folk heroes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who illegally hunts wild animals.
A material from the tusks of elephants.
An international agreement that regulates trade in endangered animals and plants.
A warden who looks after animals in a protected area.

gewusst: Rhino horn is chemically almost the same as hair and fingernails.
Anyone who brings souvenirs made from protected animals into Switzerland commits an offence, and customs seizes them.

teile.einleitung: The Achilles tendon is a thick, firm band at the back of your lower leg. It connects the calf muscle to the heel. Without it you could neither stand on tiptoe nor run or jump properly.
wichtigste: The Achilles tendon lies at the back above the heel.
It connects the calf muscle to the heel bone.
It is the strongest tendon of the human body.
It is named after the Greek hero Achilles.
According to the legend, Achilles could be wounded only at the heel.
A weak spot is therefore called an Achilles heel.
When jumping, the tendon has to withstand especially much.

abschnitte.text: If you reach to the back of your lower leg, just **above the heel**, you feel a hard cord. That is the **Achilles tendon**. A tendon connects a muscle to a bone. The Achilles tendon connects the **calf muscle** to the **heel bone**. When the calf contracts, the tendon pulls on the heel, and your foot stretches downwards. This is how you can stand on tiptoe.

The Achilles tendon is the **strongest tendon** in your body. It also has to withstand a lot: with every step, when running and above all **when jumping**, forces act on it that amount to a multiple of your body weight. The tendon is a little elastic, like a strong spring. It stores energy on landing and gives it back on take-off.

The tendon gets its name from **Achilles**, a hero from the Greek legends. His mother dipped him as a baby into a magic river so that he became invulnerable. In doing so she held him by the **heel**, and exactly this spot was not touched by the water. In the battle for the city of Troy, an arrow finally hit him in the heel. That is why a weak spot is still called an **Achilles heel** today.

Anyone who does a lot of sport should **warm up** well before it really gets going. Sudden, very heavy strain can harm the tendon, and in the worst case it can even tear. Good shoes and training that is built up slowly help. If the heel hurts during sport, a rest is important, and if the pain continues, a doctor should take a look.

gewusst: Kangaroos also have strong tendons in their hind legs, which store energy like springs when they hop.
The expression “Achilles heel” is also used for weaknesses that have nothing to do with the foot.

teile.einleitung: Cells constantly have to take in and give off substances. Often they have to move these substances against a concentration gradient, that is, to where there is already a lot of them. This needs energy and is called active transport.
wichtigste: Active transport works against a concentration gradient, diffusion does not.
Secondary active transport uses an ion gradient built up beforehand.
In symport two substances are moved in the same direction.
In antiport two substances go in opposite directions.
SGLT1 takes up glucose together with sodium in the small intestine.
Proton pump inhibitors block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase in the stomach.
ABC transporters can pump medicines out of cells.

abschnitte.text: Substances spread out evenly by themselves, moving from places of high concentration to places of low concentration. This is called **diffusion**, and it needs no energy. **Active transport**, on the other hand, works **against a concentration gradient**, rather as if you carried a ball up a slope. For this, special **transport proteins** in the cell membrane are needed, and energy is required.

In **primary active transport**, a pump uses the energy from **ATP** directly. The best-known example is the **sodium-potassium pump**. It pumps sodium out of the cell and potassium in. A **secondary active transport**, on the other hand, uses an **ion gradient built up beforehand**. Sodium flows back into the cell and takes another substance along with it, rather like a water wheel driven by flowing water.

If two substances are moved at the same time **in the same direction**, this is called **symport**. An example is **SGLT1** in the small intestine: this transporter takes up **glucose together with sodium ions** from food. If two substances are moved **in opposite directions**, it is called **antiport**. A third term is **uniport**, in which only a single substance is moved.

In the **parietal cells** of the stomach lining, the **H⁺/K⁺-ATPase** pumps acid into the stomach. **Proton pump inhibitors** block this pump and so lower the stomach acid, for example in heartburn. The **ABC transporters** are a large family of ATP-driven pumps. Some of them can move medicines back out of cells. In this way cancer cells or bacteria become **resistant** to medicines.

Some substances are too large for transport proteins. Then the **cell membrane** folds inwards and encloses the substance in a little bubble. This is called **endocytosis**. If tiny droplets of liquid are taken up in this way, it is called **pinocytosis**, which means “cell drinking”. If cells eat whole particles or bacteria, it is called **phagocytosis**. The reverse way out is called **exocytosis**.

gewusst: The sodium-potassium pump uses up a large part of the energy that the body turns over at rest.
The Danish researcher Jens Christian Skou received the Nobel Prize in 1997 for discovering the sodium-potassium pump.

teile.einleitung: Feeding birds means that people offer wild birds extra food, mostly in winter in a bird table or feeder. This gives pleasure, because you can watch tits, finches and robins from close up. For it to really help the birds, however, you should follow a few rules.
wichtigste: Feeding birds takes place mainly in winter, when frost and snow make food scarce.
You should not scatter food straight on the ground, because it quickly gets dirty and wet.
If a lot of food is offered in winter, more great tits survive.
Seed eaters like sunflower seeds, while soft food eaters prefer oat flakes, raisins and apples.
Bread, salted foods and leftovers are unsuitable for birds.
Feeding places have to be kept clean so that diseases do not spread.
A natural garden with berry bushes helps the birds most.

abschnitte.text: In **feeding birds**, people offer wild birds extra food. In Switzerland this happens mainly in **winter**, when the ground is frozen or covered with snow. At the bird table you can watch great tits, blue tits, chaffinches, blackbirds and robins. For many children it is a great introduction to the study of birds.

Birds with strong beaks such as finches and sparrows are **seed eaters** and like sunflower seeds. Blackbirds and robins are **soft food eaters** and prefer oat flakes, raisins, fruit and fat food. Fat balls contain fat with seeds, and you should buy them without a plastic net. Bread, salty food and food scraps harm the birds.

You should not scatter food straight on the ground, because it quickly gets dirty and wet. Germs and mould can form in it. Better are **feeding silos**, where the birds do not walk around in the food. You should clean bird tables regularly with hot water.

The feeding place should stand where **cats** cannot sneak up, for example free-standing on a post. A bush a few metres away offers the birds cover. Panes of glass nearby can be dangerous, because birds fly into them. Stickers or patterns on the window help against this.

Studies show that more great tits survive the winter when a lot of food is offered. However, it is mainly common species that benefit from this, and rare birds hardly do. Experts such as the **Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach** therefore recommend supporting birds above all through a natural garden. Native shrubs such as elder, rowan and hawthorn supply berries and insects all year round.

begriffe.erklaerung: A food dispenser from which only a little food slides down and which stays clean.
A bird that eats mainly seeds and grains.
A bird that prefers insects, berries and soft food.
A ball of fat and seeds that you hang up for birds.

gewusst: A great tit weighs only about 18 grams and in winter has to eat almost a third of its weight every day.
At the bird table there is a pecking order, and bigger birds often drive off smaller ones.
Every year in January, many people count the birds in their garden for research.

teile.einleitung: The wild camel is a two-humped camel that lives wild in the deserts of Central Asia. It looks very like the Bactrian camel, but is a species of its own. Today it is one of the rarest large mammals in the world.
wichtigste: The wild camel is the wild-living relative of the Bactrian camel.
It has two humps.
It lives in the Gobi Desert in China and Mongolia.
According to the Red List it is critically endangered.
Only about 1,000 animals are left.
Its kidneys get rid of salt well, so it can tolerate salt water.
Wolves can be dangerous to wild camels.

abschnitte.text: The wild camel has two humps like the **Bactrian camel**. The humps, however, are smaller and more pointed, and the body is slimmer. The fur is sandy brown, and in winter thick and woolly. Studies of its genes show that the wild camel is a **species** of its own and not simply a Bactrian camel gone wild. Its ancestors separated a very long time ago.

Wild camels live in the **Gobi Desert** in north-west China and in south-west Mongolia. There it is over 40 degrees hot in summer and far below minus 20 degrees cold in winter. There is hardly any fresh water. Important areas are the Lop Nur desert in China and a large protected area in Mongolia.

The wild camel can drink water that is saltier than sea water. Its **kidneys**, which get rid of salt well, make this possible. In the hump it stores fat as an energy reserve, not water. It eats shrubs, grasses and thorny plants and can go a long time without drinking.

Wild camels live in small groups, often with a stallion and several mares. They are very shy and flee from people even at a great distance. After a pregnancy of about 13 months, a mare has one young one. Natural enemies are mainly **wolves**.

According to the IUCN **Red List**, the wild camel is critically endangered. It is estimated that only about 1,000 animals are still alive (as of about the 2020s). The dangers are poaching, mining, droughts and mixing with domestic camels. In China and Mongolia there are protected areas and a breeding programme.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tamed camel with two humps from Central Asia.
A large, cold desert in China and Mongolia.
A group of living things that can reproduce with one another.
A fat store on the back of camels.

gewusst: The Lop Nur area, where wild camels live, was once a test site for atomic weapons.
Wild camels are much shyer than domestic camels and run away even when they see a person kilometres off.

teile.einleitung: Goat's milk is the milk of domestic goats. It has been drunk for thousands of years and made into cheese, yoghurt and butter. Some people tolerate it better than cow's milk, because its fat droplets are smaller.
wichtigste: Goat's milk comes from domestic goats.
Its fat droplets are smaller than in cow's milk, so some people tolerate it better.
It is very white, because it contains hardly any yellow beta-carotene.
Goat's milk contains about as much milk sugar as cow's milk.
In lactose intolerance it is therefore usually not a solution.
A good dairy goat gives several hundred litres of milk in a year.
From goat's milk, people make cheese, yoghurt, soap and cosmetics.

abschnitte.text: **Goat's milk** is the milk that a nanny goat produces after the birth of her kids. As with cows, part of it is milked, while the kids drink the rest or get replacement milk. The milk is white, slightly sweetish and tastes only mild when fresh. If it stands for longer or is stored near a billy goat, it can take on a stronger **goaty taste**.

Goat's milk contains about as much protein, fat and **milk sugar** as cow's milk. Its **fat droplets**, however, are smaller and spread better, which is why it creams more slowly. The proteins too are put together a little differently. This makes it easier to digest for some people, but a true milk allergy usually does not go away because of it.

Because goat's milk contains almost as much **lactose** as cow's milk, it hardly helps in lactose intolerance. For babies, pure goat's milk is not suitable, but there is special baby food based on goat's milk. Raw milk should be boiled before drinking, to kill disease germs. Anyone who is unsure had best ask a doctor or nutrition adviser.

The best-known dairy goat in the world is the **Saanen goat** from the Bernese Oberland. A good Saanen goat can give about 800 litres of milk a year or more. Toggenburg and Chamois Coloured goats are also good dairy goats. In Switzerland, a lot of goat's milk is made into cheese, especially on alps and small farms.

From goat's milk people make cheese, yoghurt, quark and butter. **Soap** and skin creams with goat's milk are also popular. In many countries of Africa, Asia and the Mediterranean, goat's milk is very important. Goats are popular there because they find enough food even on barren pastures.

begriffe.erklaerung: Milk sugar, which is in almost every milk.
You do not tolerate milk sugar well and get a stomach ache.
Milk that has not been heated.
Fat rises to the top in milk and forms cream.

gewusst: Goat's butter is almost white instead of yellow.
In the past the goat was called the poor man's cow, because it needs little space and food and still gives milk.

teile.einleitung: In aerobic energy production, cells use oxygen to gain energy from sugar and fat. In this way the body can work for a long time, for example when hiking, cycling or running a marathon. The word “aerobic” means “with air”.
wichtigste: For this the muscle cells absolutely need oxygen.
Aerobic energy production takes place in the mitochondria.
Carbon dioxide and water are produced as waste.
In long, easy efforts the body uses more and more fat.
In a marathon the body gains its energy almost only aerobically.
The muscles get their energy directly from ATP.
The greatest amount of oxygen per minute is called maximal oxygen uptake.

abschnitte.text: Muscles need energy for every movement. They get it directly from the molecule **ATP**. Because the store of ATP is small, it has to be made anew all the time. In **aerobic energy production** this happens with **oxygen**. The cells break down **carbohydrates** such as glucose and **fats** completely. This yields far more ATP than breaking them down without oxygen.

abschnitte.titel: The power stations of the cell
abschnitte.text: Aerobic energy production takes place in the **mitochondria**. These are tiny parts of the cells that are often called the **power stations of the cell**. Muscle cells that need a lot of endurance have especially many of them. **Carbon dioxide and water** are produced as waste. The carbon dioxide travels with the blood to the lungs and is breathed out.

In long efforts at a medium pace, for example in a **marathon**, the body gains its energy **almost only aerobically**. The longer and easier you move, the more it uses **fat** as a source of energy.
