Fat is a huge store, but it is broken down more slowly than sugar. In short, very hard efforts such as a sprint, the oxygen is not enough, and the body then also gains energy without oxygen.

In endurance sport you breathe **faster and deeper** to **take in more oxygen**. The heart also beats faster and pumps more blood to the muscles. The greatest amount of oxygen that the body can take in per minute is called **maximal oxygen uptake**. It is an important measure of endurance. Regular training makes it larger, and the muscles build more mitochondria.

gewusst: Top cross-country skiers are among the people with the highest measured oxygen uptake.
Fat reserves hold so much energy that they would be enough for many marathons.

teile.einleitung: Amylase is an enzyme that breaks starch down into smaller sugar building blocks. It is found in our saliva and in the juice of the pancreas. Thanks to it, the digestion of bread, rice or potatoes begins in the mouth.
wichtigste: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical processes.
Alpha-amylase starts splitting starch already in the mouth.
It splits the alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds of starch.
This mainly produces the double sugar maltose.
Salivary amylase used to be called ptyalin.
The pancreas also makes alpha-amylase.
In the acidic stomach, salivary amylase soon stops working.

abschnitte.text: If you chew a piece of bread for a long time, you notice that it slowly tastes a little sweet. This is because of the **alpha-amylase** in saliva. It breaks the **starch** in the bread down into smaller sugars. Salivary amylase used to be called **ptyalin**. Because you usually do not keep bread in your mouth for long, only part of the starch is split here.

Starch consists of long chains of grape sugar, that is, **glucose**. The building blocks are joined by so-called **alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds**. Amylase cuts these bonds open. This mainly produces the double sugar **maltose**, also called malt sugar. Other enzymes in the small intestine then break the maltose down into single glucose units. To keep its stable shape, alpha-amylase needs **calcium**.

The **stomach** is very acidic. The low **pH** soon makes salivary amylase useless. So the digestion of starch only carries on in the **small intestine**. There the **pancreas** releases its own alpha-amylase. Only the single sugar units can be taken up into the blood by the body.

With **iodine solution** you can show that starch is present: it turns blue-black. If you mix starch solution with a little saliva and keep testing with iodine, the blue colour gets weaker. In the end it disappears completely. This shows that the amylase has **broken down the starch**. This experiment is often done in biology lessons.

Normally only a little amylase is found in the blood. If the value is strongly raised, it is a typical sign of **acute pancreatitis**, an inflammation of the pancreas. Doctors therefore often measure the value in the laboratory when someone has severe stomach pain. An inflammation of the salivary glands can also raise it.

gewusst: Amylase is also used in industry, for example in brewing beer and in baking.
People whose ancestors ate a lot of starch often have more copies of the gene for salivary amylase.

teile.einleitung: Tarantulas are large, very hairy spiders that live in warm countries all around the world. They include the goliath birdeater, the heaviest spider in the world. Although many people are afraid of them, they are mostly harmless to us.
wichtigste: Tarantulas form the family Theraphosidae and belong to the large group Mygalomorphae.
According to the World Spider Catalog there are about 1100 to 1200 species.
The goliath birdeater is regarded as the heaviest spider in the world and weighs up to about 175 grams.
Its legs can reach a span of up to about 30 centimetres.
Tarantulas have eight eyes, but still see rather poorly.
They breathe with two pairs of book lungs.
The German name, Vogelspinne or “bird spider”, probably goes back to the naturalist Maria Sibylla Merian.

abschnitte.text: Tarantulas have a strong, densely hairy body and eight long legs. Their **chelicerae**, that is, their biting claws, lie parallel to the long axis of the body and strike from top to bottom. The eight eyes sit close together on a small mound, but the spider relies mainly on fine tactile hairs. For breathing it has two pairs of **book lungs**, and most species have four spinnerets, that is, two pairs.

Tarantulas live in the tropics and subtropics of America, Africa, Asia and Australia. Many species dig burrows in the ground or hide under stones and roots. Others live in trees and build silk tubes there between leaves. The **goliath birdeater** lives in the rainforests in the north of South America.

Tarantulas do not build catching webs, but are **ambush hunters**. They wait at night in front of their hiding place until a prey animal comes past, and then grab it in a flash. Mostly they eat insects such as grasshoppers and cockroaches. Large species sometimes also catch frogs, lizards or mice, but birds only rarely. They paralyse the prey with their venom, and then it is turned liquid with digestive juice.

Many American tarantulas have **urticating hairs** on the abdomen, which they can flick off with their hind legs. These hairs itch badly on the skin and irritate the eyes and nose of attackers. The bite of most species is for people about as painful as a wasp sting. It becomes dangerous at most for people with an allergy.

The male transfers his sperm to the female with the palps on his head. Afterwards he often has to flee quickly so that he is not eaten. The female spins a **cocoon** in which, depending on the species, a few dozen to over a thousand eggs lie. Females of many species can live to over 20 years old, while males mostly live only a few years.

The artist **Maria Sibylla Merian** travelled to Suriname in South America and drew insects and spiders there. In her famous copperplate engraving of 1705, a large spider is eating a hummingbird. For a long time many people doubted the picture, but today we know that such cases occur very rarely. In 1758 Carl Linnaeus described a tarantula as Aranea avicularia, and today it is called Avicularia avicularia.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of primitive spiders whose biting claws strike downwards.
A breathing organ made of many thin leaves lying on top of each other like the pages of a book.
Fine barbed hairs that the spider flicks at enemies for defence.
The spider sheds its old skin that has become too small, in order to grow.

gewusst: At a moult, a tarantula can even partly regrow lost legs.
The shed skin of a tarantula looks like a second, complete spider.
Tarantulas are among the most popular terrarium animals, in Switzerland too.

teile.einleitung: In complete metamorphosis, an insect develops in four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult animal. The larva looks quite different from the finished insect, like a caterpillar and a butterfly. Experts call this amazing development holometaboly.
wichtigste: Complete metamorphosis has four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult insect.
A dung beetle, for example, develops from the egg through larva and pupa to the beetle.
In the pupa, the body of the larva is completely rebuilt.
Beetles, butterflies, flies, mosquitoes, bees, wasps, ants and fleas go through a complete metamorphosis.
Grasshoppers, dragonflies and bugs, on the other hand, have an incomplete metamorphosis without a pupa.
Larva and adult animal often eat quite different food.
The great majority of all insect species develop with complete metamorphosis.

abschnitte.text: Complete metamorphosis, also called **holometaboly**, is a form of development in insects. A larva hatches from the egg, which eats and grows. After that it changes into a **pupa**, which mostly lies still. From the pupa the adult insect finally hatches, which is called the imago.

The larva is an eating machine and grows fast. Because its skin does not grow with it, it has to moult several times. Larvae have names of their own depending on the animal group: in butterflies they are called **caterpillars**, in flies maggots and in the cockchafer grubs. A cockchafer grub lives three to four years in the soil before it turns into a pupa.

From the outside nothing seems to happen in the pupa, but inside almost the whole body is rebuilt. From small groups of cells, the **imaginal discs**, the wings, legs and eyes of the adult animal arise. This is controlled by hormones. Butterflies form a mummy-like pupa, flies a barrel-shaped pupa and beetles a free pupa, in which you can already see the legs and antennae.

In the garden you can watch the metamorphosis well. The caterpillar of the peacock butterfly eats nettles, turns into a pupa and becomes a colourful butterfly. A maggot in the compost becomes a fly. The **dung beetle** also goes through egg, larva, pupa and beetle, with the larva living in the ground on dung that the parents have buried.

In **incomplete metamorphosis** there is no pupal stage. The young of grasshoppers, bugs or dragonflies already resemble the adults, but do not yet have finished wings. They moult several times and become adult step by step. In complete metamorphosis, on the other hand, the larva and the adult often have no similarity at all.

Because the larva and the adult animal live differently, they do not compete for food. The caterpillar eats leaves, and the butterfly drinks nectar. In this way each stage of life can be specialised for one job: the larva for growing, the adult for breeding and spreading. This strategy is very successful, which is why the majority of all insect species belong to this group.

begriffe.erklaerung: The young stage of an insect that comes after the egg and looks quite different from the adult.
The resting stage in which the larva rebuilds itself into the finished insect.
The finished, adult insect.
The technical word for complete metamorphosis.

gewusst: In some insects the adult animal lives only a few hours or days, while the larva grows for years.
The naturalist Maria Sibylla Merian showed as early as about 1700 that caterpillars and butterflies belong together.

teile.einleitung: Web-building spiders are eight-legged animals that make silk threads and often use them to build artful webs. They live almost everywhere in the world, from the home to the high mountains, and eat huge numbers of insects.
wichtigste: Web-building spiders are not insects but arachnids.
A spider has eight legs, while an insect has six.
More than 50,000 species of spider are known worldwide.
All spiders can make spider silk, but not all build webs.
Their body is made of two parts: the front part and the abdomen.
Almost all spiders have venom fangs, but the species in Switzerland are harmless to people.
Spiders have no antennae and no wings.

abschnitte.text: The body of a spider is made of the **front part** with the head and legs and the roundish **abdomen**. On the front part sit eight legs, two palps and the jaws with venom glands. Most spiders have eight eyes, but many see only poorly with them. At the end of the abdomen are the **spinnerets**, from which the silk comes.

Spider silk is very thin, but in relation to its weight it is stronger than steel. The **garden spider** builds a round orb web with sticky catching threads. The house spider weaves a dense funnel web in corners. Spiders also use silk for egg cocoons, as a safety line and for wrapping up their prey.

Many spiders hunt without a web. **Jumping spiders** have big eyes, creep up and leap on their prey. Wolf spiders run about on the ground, and crab spiders lie in wait, well camouflaged, in flowers. All spiders kill their prey with venom and turn it liquid with digestive juice before they suck it up.

The male has to approach the female carefully so that she does not take him for prey. The female lays her eggs in a **cocoon** of silk. Female wolf spiders carry the cocoon with them and later the young on their backs. Young spiders often let the wind carry them on a thread, which is called **ballooning**.

In Switzerland there live almost 1,000 species of spider, from tiny money spiders to the large water spider. You often see garden spiders, daddy-long-legs spiders on the ceiling and the zebra jumping spider on house walls. The **wasp spider** with its yellow and black stripes has become more common because of warmer summers. There are no dangerous spiders here, and only the bite of the yellow sac spider can hurt like a wasp sting.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal group with eight legs that includes spiders, scorpions, harvestmen and mites.
Small tubes on the abdomen from which the spider silk comes.
A covering of silk in which spider eggs are protected.
The journey of young spiders on a silk thread that is carried by the wind.

gewusst: The water spider lives under water in an air bell of silk that it builds itself.
The floating threads of young spiders in autumn gave the German “Altweibersommer”, an Indian summer, its name.
Harvestmen look like spiders but belong to a different group of arachnids.

teile.einleitung: The Valais Blacknose sheep is a breed of sheep from the Upper Valais with white wool and a black face. With its black nose, black ears and curled horns, it looks almost like a cuddly toy. It is perfectly adapted to life in the steep mountains of the Valais.
wichtigste: The Valais Blacknose sheep is a Swiss breed of sheep with a black face and white wool.
You can recognise it at once by its black nose and black ears.
It is kept mainly in the Upper Valais.
Rams and ewes carry curled horns.
The whole body is covered with long, thick wool, including the face and legs.
The breeding association in the Upper Valais was founded in 1948.
The sheep also graze on very steep, stony mountain slopes.

abschnitte.text: The Valais Blacknose sheep has white wool and a black face with a black nose and black ears. It also often has black **patches** on the knees and feet. Rams and female sheep, which are called **ewes**, carry horns twisted into a spiral. The wool covers the whole body, even the face and the legs, so that the animals look especially fluffy.

The breed comes from the **Upper Valais** and is still mainly kept there today. It probably descends from the old copper sheep and other native landrace sheep. The first signs of such sheep in the Valais go back several hundred years. The animals are hardy and cope well with the harsh mountain climate.

A ram weighs on average 80 to 100 kilograms, and a female 70 to 80 kilograms. The wool is coarse and long-fibred and often over ten centimetres long. A ram supplies about 3.5 to 4.5 kilograms of wool a year. Underneath lies a fine **undercoat**, which protects well against the cold.

In 1884 the Valais government wanted to make sheep breeding uniform, and English Southdown sheep were crossed in. But these crosses were less hardy and their wool too short, so they were given up again. Between 1930 and 1960 the breed was pushed back by the White Alpine sheep. In 1948 breeders founded the **Upper Valais Blacknose Sheep Breeding Association**, and in 1962 the breed was officially recognised.

In the past the sheep supplied mountain farming families with wool, meat, leather and sometimes milk. Today it is mostly kept as a **hobby** or as a sideline. It is regarded as a good mother and supplies tasty meat. In summer the flocks graze on alpine pastures and keep steep slopes free of scrub there.

Because of its funny looks, the Blacknose sheep is often called one of the cutest sheep in the world. By now animals are also bred in Great Britain and other countries. In the Valais the most beautiful animals are given prizes at **sheep shows**. For many people in the Valais, the Blacknose sheep is a piece of home and tradition.

begriffe.erklaerung: A female sheep, also called a mother sheep.
A male sheep.
A society of breeders that looks after a breed and sets rules for breeding.
Fine, dense hairs under the longer coat that keep especially warm.

gewusst: The lambs of the Blacknose sheep already have a black face too.
Blacknose sheep can graze on slopes that would be far too steep for cows.

teile.einleitung: Ruminants are plant eaters that chew their food twice. They include cows, sheep, goats, deer and giraffes. Their special stomach with four chambers helps them to digest tough grass.
wichtigste: Ruminants bring their food back up and chew it again.
Cattle, sheep and goats have four stomach chambers, which people also call four stomachs.
In the rumen, micro-organisms help to break down cellulose.
In the upper jaw they have no incisors at the front, but a dental pad.
Cows eat and ruminate for many hours a day.
Llamas and camels also chew the cud, but have only three stomach chambers.

abschnitte.text: Ruminants are **even-toed ungulates** that first swallow their food quickly and later chew it again. They include cattle, sheep, goats, deer, antelopes and giraffes. Bison and the African buffalo are also ruminants. Llamas and camels also chew the cud, but belong to a group of their own, the camelids.

When eating, the grass is only roughly chewed and swallowed. It lands in the **rumen**, the first and biggest stomach chamber. Later the animal brings small balls of food back up into the mouth and chews them thoroughly, which is **rumination**. That is why you often see cows, sheep and goats chewing even when they are not eating at that moment.

The stomach has four chambers: the rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. In the rumen live billions of **micro-organisms** such as bacteria. They break down the tough **cellulose** in plants, which the animal could not digest alone. The rumen of a cow holds over 100 litres. Only in the abomasum is the food digested with gastric juice, as in us.

Cows, sheep and goats have incisors at the front of the lower jaw, but none in the upper jaw. There sits a hard **dental pad**. With the tongue and lips they tear off the grass. At the back they have broad molars that grind the food like millstones.

Ruminants can turn grass into milk and meat, which people cannot do. This is important in Switzerland, because much of the land is grassland and alpine pasture. A cow eats and ruminates for many hours every day. In digestion, however, **methane** is produced, a greenhouse gas.

begriffe.erklaerung: The first and biggest stomach chamber, in which micro-organisms pre-digest the food.
A firm building material of plants that is hard to digest.
Hoofed animals with two toes on each foot, for example the cow and the pig.
A hard pad in the upper jaw of ruminants in place of incisors.

gewusst: A cow makes over 30,000 chewing movements a day.
A calf cannot yet ruminate right after birth, and the milk flows through a groove directly into the abomasum.

teile.einleitung: Teeth are hard structures in the mouth of vertebrates with which they grip, bite off and break up food. What an animal's teeth look like tells you a lot about what it eats. Young mammals such as puppies first get milk teeth, which are later replaced by permanent teeth.
wichtigste: Teeth are used to grip, bite and break up food.
The first teeth of young mammals are called milk teeth.
A puppy has about 28 milk teeth, and an adult dog 42 teeth.
A child has 20 milk teeth, and an adult usually 32 teeth.
Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the body.
There are incisors, canines and molars.
Sharks can grow new teeth all their lives.

abschnitte.text: The visible part is called the **crown**, and the part in the jaw is called the root. On the outside, the **enamel** protects it, the hardest substance in the body. Below it lies the dentine, and right inside is the pulp with nerves and blood vessels. That is why it hurts when a hole reaches the nerve.

Many mammals first get small **milk teeth**. A puppy has about 28 of them, which at around four to seven months are replaced by 42 permanent teeth. In children, the 20 milk teeth fall out from about the age of six. Later, usually 32 **permanent teeth** grow, although the wisdom teeth often come late or not at all.

Predators such as lions and wolves have long **canines** for holding on to prey and sharp carnassial teeth for cutting meat. Plant eaters such as cows and horses have broad, flat molars for grinding grass. Humans eat both and therefore have a mixed set of teeth. Birds have no teeth, and use their bill and their muscular gizzard instead.

The tusks of the elephant are huge incisors made of **ivory**. The long tusk of the narwhal is also a tooth. In rodents such as beavers and mice, the incisors keep growing all their lives and are worn down by gnawing. Sharks have a **revolving set of teeth**, in which replacement teeth are already waiting behind every tooth.

Bacteria in the mouth turn sugar into acid, which attacks the enamel and causes **tooth decay**. That is why you should brush your teeth twice a day with toothpaste containing fluoride. In Switzerland, many schools have visits from the school dental service, which show how to brush properly. Dogs and cats can also get tooth problems, which is why the vet also checks their teeth.

begriffe.erklaerung: The first teeth of a young mammal.
A very hard protective layer on the outside of the tooth.
All the teeth of an animal or a human together.
A hole in the tooth, caused by acid from bacteria.
A sharp molar in predators for cutting meat.

gewusst: A shark can lose and replace thousands of teeth in the course of its life.
Snails have a rasping tongue with thousands of tiny teeth.
You can roughly read off the age of a horse from its teeth.

teile.einleitung: Bird migration is the name for the regular journeys that many birds make between their breeding areas and their winter areas. Every autumn millions of birds leave Switzerland and fly south, and in spring they come back. Some cover thousands of kilometres and cross mountains, seas and the Sahara.
wichtigste: Many birds migrate south in autumn because they find too little food here in winter.
Many European migratory birds fly over the Sahara on the way to Africa.
Migratory birds find their way partly by the Earth's magnetic field.
Wild geese often fly in a V formation, because in this way they can save energy.
The lead bird at the front changes regularly in the V formation.
Large flocks of wild geese often rest on big lakes such as Lake Constance.
Many small songbirds migrate at night and rest by day.

abschnitte.text: In winter there are hardly any insects here, and snow covers the ground. Birds such as the barn swallow or the swift then find too little **food**. That is why they fly to warmer regions where there is enough to eat. In spring they come back, because here long days and many insects offer good conditions for raising the young.

**Long-distance migrants** such as the white stork, cuckoo and barn swallow spend the winter in Africa south of the Sahara. Short-distance migrants such as the black redstart fly only as far as the Mediterranean region. **Resident birds** such as the house sparrow or the great tit stay with us all year round. In some species only some animals leave, and they are called partial migrants.

On the way to Africa many birds have to cross the Mediterranean and the **Sahara**. Small songbirds eat their way to a thick layer of fat beforehand, which serves them as fuel. Large soaring birds such as the white stork avoid the open sea and fly over the Strait of Gibraltar or the Bosporus. The Alps are also an obstacle, which is why many birds cross over passes such as the Col de Bretolet.

Migratory birds have a built-in **compass**. They can sense the Earth's magnetic field and steer by the position of the sun. Birds that migrate at night also find their way by the stars. In addition there are landmarks such as coasts, rivers and mountains, which experienced birds recognise.

Large birds such as geese and cranes often fly in a **V formation**. Each bird uses the air swirls of the bird in front of it and so needs less effort. The lead bird at the tip has the hardest time, which is why the animals take turns regularly. In autumn and winter many wild geese rest on big lakes such as Lake Constance.

The Arctic tern flies every year from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back, which is tens of thousands of kilometres. Bar-tailed godwits fly without a break over 11 000 kilometres from Alaska to New Zealand. Researchers attach tiny **geolocators** to birds in order to follow their journeys. In Switzerland the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach has been studying bird migration since 1924.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that travels back and forth every year between its breeding area and its winter area.
A bird that stays in the same area all year round.
A place where migratory birds feed and rest on the way.
The restlessness of migratory birds when the time to fly away comes, even in a cage.

gewusst: A young cuckoo finds its way to Africa alone, although it has never met its parents.
The swift stays in the air for months and even sleeps in flight.
In autumn on clear nights, hundreds of thousands of birds cross over Switzerland without our noticing.

teile.einleitung: Leaf insects are insects that look like green leaves. They live in the tropics of Asia and are so well camouflaged that enemies hardly notice them among real leaves. Even their movements copy a leaf in the wind.
wichtigste: Leaf insects belong to the insect order of stick and leaf insects (Phasmatodea).
The name Phasmatodea goes back to the Greek word for ghost or apparition.
The genus name Phyllium comes from the Greek “phyllon” for leaf.
There are about 120 described species in about 13 genera.
About half of the species have been described only since 2016.
The researcher Carl Brunner von Wattenwyl, born in Bern, set up the family Phylliidae in 1893.
A fossil about 47 million years old from the Messel Pit shows that they once lived in Europe too.

abschnitte.text: The body of a leaf insect is flat and broad like a leaf. Even leaf veins and small brown spots that look like places where something has nibbled are copied. The legs also have flat, leaf-like flaps. This kind of camouflage is called **mimesis**.

Leaf insects belong to the **stick and leaf insects**, Phasmatodea in science, which also include the stick insects. The name goes back to the Greek word for ghost or apparition. They form the superfamily Phyllioidea and the family **Phylliidae**. This family was set up in 1893 by the insect researcher Carl Brunner von Wattenwyl, who was born in Bern.

Leaf insects live in the tropics and subtropics of South and South East Asia, for example in India, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines. Some species are also found on New Guinea and in the north of Australia. They live in trees and bushes and eat leaves. Today about 120 species are known in about 13 genera, and about half of them have been described only since 2016.

Leaf insects move very slowly. As they walk they **sway** back and forth, as if a leaf were being moved by the wind. They are active mainly at night and sit motionless among the leaves by day. That way birds and lizards easily overlook them.

The females are bigger and broader and usually cannot fly. The males are slimmer and have long wings with which they can fly. The females simply let their eggs fall to the ground, and the eggs look like **plant seeds**. In some species, females can even have young without males, which is called **parthenogenesis**.

In the **Messel Pit** near Darmstadt, the fossil Eophyllium messelensis was found. It is about 47 million years old and an early relative of today's leaf insects. The find shows that their range used to be much bigger and reached as far as Europe. It also suggests that leaf camouflage and swaying behaviour probably existed millions of years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: Camouflage in which an animal copies a lifeless object such as a leaf or a twig.
An insect order with stick insects and leaf insects.
Petrified remains or traces of a living thing from earlier times.
Breeding without males, from unfertilised eggs.

gewusst: Sometimes leaf insects nibble at each other, because they take each other for real leaves.
Leaf insects are also kept in terrariums and are often fed bramble leaves there.

teile.einleitung: A gelding is a male horse that has been neutered and so cannot father foals. Geldings are regarded as calm, even-tempered and good to handle. That is why many riding horses, sport horses and leisure horses are geldings.
wichtigste: A neutered male horse is called a gelding.
A male horse that is not neutered is called a stallion, and a female a mare.
In neutering, the testicles, which make the hormone testosterone, are removed.
Geldings are usually calmer and less aggressive than stallions.
A vet carries out the neutering under anaesthetic.
Geldings can live in mixed herds with mares.
The German name Wallach comes from Wallachia, a region in present-day Romania.

abschnitte.text: A gelding is a **neutered** stallion. In horses, a distinction is made between the stallion as the male animal, the **mare** as the female animal and the foal as the young animal. A gelding looks like a stallion, but can no longer have young. The same thing exists in other animals: a neutered bull, for example, is called an ox.

In neutering, a **vet** removes the testicles of the stallion. This is done under anaesthetic so that the animal feels no pain. Many stallions are neutered at the age of about one to two years. After that the body makes hardly any **testosterone**, the hormone that often makes stallions wild and keen to fight.

Stallions can be very spirited, especially when mares are nearby. They often fight with other stallions and are hard for beginners to ride. Geldings are usually **even-tempered** and easy to get on with. They can stand in the field with mares and other geldings without problems.

abschnitte.titel: Geldings in sport and everyday life
abschnitte.text: Many successful show-jumping, dressage and racehorses are geldings. In riding schools and among leisure riders, geldings are especially popular because they are reliable. In Switzerland too, many **Franches-Montagnes horses** are ridden or driven as geldings. Only the best stallions with good qualities are kept for breeding.

The German word Wallach goes back to **Wallachia**, a historic region in present-day Romania. From there, many neutered horses used to come to central Europe. They were therefore called Wallachian horses, Wallache for short. Even the riding peoples of the steppes neutered horses in order to tame them more easily.

begriffe.erklaerung: A male horse that is not neutered.
A female horse.
An operation in which the sex glands are removed so that an animal can no longer father young.
A male hormone that influences behaviour and body build.

gewusst: Geldings often live longer than stallions, because they fight less and injure themselves less.
A stallion in which one testicle has not moved properly into the scrotum is called a rig.

teile.einleitung: The loggerhead sea turtle is a large sea turtle with a strikingly broad head. With its especially strong beak it cracks mussels, snails and crabs with ease. It travels through all the warm seas and lays its eggs on sandy beaches, including on the Mediterranean.
wichtigste: The loggerhead is one of the seven species of sea turtle.
Its scientific name is Caretta caretta.
It has a big head and an especially strong beak for cracking mussels.
Its shell is reddish brown and can grow to about a metre long.
It lives in warm and temperate seas all over the world, including the Mediterranean.
The females lay their eggs at night on sandy beaches.
Plastic waste, fishing nets and built-up beaches endanger the species.

abschnitte.text: The loggerhead has a heart-shaped, **reddish brown shell** that usually grows 70 to 100 centimetres long. Adult animals often weigh around 100 kilograms, and some more. Striking is its very **broad head** with strong jaw muscles. Instead of teeth it has a hard horny beak. Its legs have turned into flippers, with which it swims elegantly.

The species lives in tropical and temperate seas, in the Atlantic, the Pacific, the Indian Ocean and in the **Mediterranean**. Young turtles drift for years in the open ocean, often among mats of seaweed. Adults like to stay near the coast. They cover huge distances, and some cross whole oceans.

The loggerhead eats mainly **hard-shelled animals** such as mussels, snails, crabs and sea urchins. With its strong beak it crushes the shells with ease. It also eats jellyfish. Sadly it sometimes mistakes drifting plastic bags for jellyfish and swallows them.

To lay eggs, the females often return to the beach where they themselves hatched. At night they dig a pit in the sand and lay about 100 eggs in it. How warm the sand is decides the **sex** of the young: when it is warm, more females hatch. After about two months the young crawl to the sea at night and find their way by the bright horizon. Well-known **nesting beaches** are in Florida, Greece, Turkey and Cyprus.

Many turtles get caught in **fishing nets** or on long lines and drown. The lights of hotels on beaches lead newly hatched young away from the sea. Plastic waste and the building up of beaches are also big problems. In many countries nesting beaches are therefore guarded and nests marked. Holidaymakers can help by avoiding beaches at night and leaving no rubbish behind.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hard casing of bone that protects the turtle's body.
A hard mouth without teeth, such as turtles and birds have.
A beach where sea turtles bury their eggs.
Animals that end up in fishing nets unintentionally.

gewusst: The loggerhead can stay under water for several hours when it is resting.
Young sea turtles find their way by the Earth's magnetic field, like a compass.
Only a very small share of the young that hatch grow up.

teile.einleitung: Adrenaline is a hormone that your body releases in dangerous situations. It raises the heart rate and readiness for energy, so that you can fight or flee. That is why people speak of the fight-or-flight response.
wichtigste: Adrenaline is a stress hormone.
It is made mainly in the adrenal medulla.
In danger it raises the heart rate and readiness for energy.
This reaction is called the fight-or-flight response.
Adrenaline acts within seconds.
In medicine it helps in severe allergic reactions and in cardiac arrest.
In 1901 adrenaline became the first hormone to be made in pure form.

abschnitte.text: Adrenaline is a **hormone**, that is, a messenger substance that is distributed through the body by the blood. It is made mainly in the adrenal medulla, the inner part of the **adrenal glands**. These small glands sit like caps on top of the kidneys. The name comes from the Latin ad renes, which means “near the kidneys”.

When you are startled, for example because a dog suddenly barks, the body releases adrenaline within seconds. Your heart beats faster and more strongly, and the blood pressure rises. The airways widen so that more oxygen gets into the lungs. The liver releases sugar into the blood so that the **muscles** at once have plenty of energy.

The pupils become bigger, and you are wide awake and alert. Digestion, on the other hand, is slowed, because it is not important at the moment of danger. Many people feel a pounding heart, shaky hands or a queasy feeling in the belly. This reaction comes from primeval times, when our ancestors had to flee from predators or defend themselves.

Not only real danger but also excitement triggers a **rush of adrenaline**. This happens in an exam, before a performance, on a roller coaster or on a bungee jump. In Switzerland, brave people jump, for example, from the 220 metre high Verzasca dam in Ticino. Some people seek this tingle on purpose, and are jokingly called adrenaline junkies.

In a severe allergic reaction, **anaphylaxis**, adrenaline can save lives. People with a strong allergy, for example to bee stings or nuts, therefore often carry an adrenaline auto-injector. In an emergency this pen is pressed against the thigh. In cardiac arrest too, rescuers give adrenaline during resuscitation.

In 1901 the Japanese chemist **Jokichi Takamine** succeeded in making adrenaline in pure form, and it was the first hormone obtained in this way. In English it is often called epinephrine. Short stress is quite normal and even helpful, because it makes us capable of performing. Constant stress, on the other hand, can make you ill, which is why breaks, sleep and exercise are important.

begriffe.erklaerung: A messenger substance that distributes messages in the body through the blood.
A small gland on top of each kidney that makes hormones such as adrenaline.
The number of heartbeats per minute.
A very strong, dangerous allergic reaction of the whole body.

gewusst: Adrenaline acts so fast that you are already reacting before you have really noticed what is going on.
Animals have adrenaline too, which is why a frightened cat makes its fur bristle.
Under adrenaline, people sometimes hardly feel pain, for example after an accident.

teile.einleitung: Animals are living things that feed on other living things and can mostly move by themselves. From the tiny water flea to the blue whale, over 30 metres long, there is a huge variety. Researchers have so far described well over a million animal species, and every year new ones are added.
wichtigste: Animals are living things that get their food from other living things.
A distinction is made between vertebrates with a backbone and invertebrates without a backbone.
Vertebrates include mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.
The dolphin is a mammal, although it lives in the sea.
Insects are the group of animals richest in species on Earth.
Bees pollinate many plants that supply us with food.
Many animal species are endangered today because of humans.

abschnitte.text: Animals are made of many cells and, unlike plants, cannot make food from sunlight. They eat plants, other animals or both. Most animals can move and have sense organs. The science that studies animals is called **zoology**.

**Vertebrates** have an inner skeleton with a backbone. Mammals such as cows, bats and dolphins suckle their young with milk and breathe with lungs. That is why a dolphin has to come to the surface of the water again and again to breathe. Birds have feathers, reptiles a scaly skin, amphibians such as frogs live on land and in water, and fish breathe with gills.

More than nine in ten animal species are **invertebrates**, which have no backbone. They include insects, spiders, snails, mussels, worms, jellyfish and crabs. Insects alone, with over a million described species, make up the largest part of all animal species. Many invertebrates have a hard outer skeleton or a shell.

Animals are very important for us humans. Bees and other insects **pollinate** many plants, for example apple trees, cherry trees and rapeseed, which supply us with food. Farm animals such as cows, pigs and hens give milk, meat and eggs. Dogs, cats and rabbits live with us as pets.

In Switzerland live typical mountain animals such as the ibex, chamois, marmot and mountain hare. The **ibex** had been wiped out here and was released again from 1911, with animals from Italy. Since 1991, lammergeiers have been reintroduced in the Swiss National Park and elsewhere. The wolf, lynx and beaver have also returned in recent decades.

Many animal species are threatened because their habitats are disappearing, the climate is changing or they are hunted. In **Red Lists**, experts record how seriously a species is endangered. Nature reserves, hedges and flowering meadows help to protect animals. Children can help too, for example with an insect hotel or a wild corner in the garden.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal with a backbone made of bone or cartilage.
An animal without a backbone, for example an insect or a snail.
An animal whose young drink milk from the mother.
Pollen is carried from one flower to another so that fruit can form.

gewusst: The blue whale is the biggest animal that has ever lived on Earth.
Scientists suspect that many millions of animal species have not been discovered at all yet.
A bee colony can have several tens of thousands of bees in summer.

teile.einleitung: Mindfulness means being quite deliberately in the moment, without judging what you experience. You notice what you are seeing, hearing, feeling or thinking right now. You can practise mindfulness, rather like an instrument or a sport.
wichtigste: Mindfulness means being consciously in the moment, without judging.
The roots lie in Buddhist meditation.
Jon Kabat-Zinn developed the MBSR programme in 1979.
In simple exercises you often pay attention to your own breath.
In the body scan you travel in your mind through the whole body.
If your thoughts wander, you notice it and return in a friendly way.
According to studies, many people who practise feel less stress.

abschnitte.text: Often our thoughts are somewhere else: on yesterday's quarrel or tomorrow's exam. **Mindfulness** means having your attention **in the present moment**. What matters here is **not to judge**. You simply note: “I am tired” or “I hear a bird”, without finding it good or bad straight away. That sounds simple, but takes practice.

The roots of mindfulness exercises lie in **Buddhist meditation**, which has been practised for a very long time. The American medical professor **Jon Kabat-Zinn** developed a programme from it without religious content in 1979. It is called “mindfulness-based stress reduction”, abbreviated **MBSR** after the English name. Since then, mindfulness has been offered in hospitals, schools and companies all over the world.

In a simple exercise you direct your attention to **your own breath**: how does the air feel at the nose, how does the belly rise and fall? In the **body scan** you travel slowly in your mind through the whole body, from the toes to the head. Surely your thoughts will wander as you do this. That is quite normal. You **notice it** and return **in a friendly way** to the breath or to the body, without getting annoyed.

You can also practise mindfulness in the middle of everyday life. One example is **eating an apple mindfully**: what does it look like, what does it smell like, what does the first bite sound like, what does it taste like? You can also be completely in the moment when brushing your teeth, walking or showering. A few calm breaths before an exam are also a small mindfulness exercise.

Many studies have examined how mindfulness exercises work. People who practise regularly often report **less perceived stress** and can concentrate better. Experts also stress, however, that mindfulness is not a miracle cure. For serious worries or illnesses, it does not replace help from professionals.

gewusst: A well-known exercise is the raisin exercise: you eat a single raisin very slowly and with all your senses.
Even a few minutes of practice a day can be enough to train mindfulness.

teile.einleitung: An adjuvant is an auxiliary substance that is in some vaccines. It strengthens the reaction of the immune system to the vaccination. In this way a vaccine works better or you need less of it.
wichtigste: The word comes from the Latin “adiuvare”, to help.
An adjuvant strengthens the immune response to the antigen.
The most commonly used for almost 100 years have been aluminium salts.
Live vaccines usually need no adjuvant.
With an adjuvant you need less antigen per dose.
The adjuvant MF59 is based on the natural substance squalene.
Redness and pain at the injection site occur more often.

abschnitte.text: A vaccine contains an **antigen**, that is, a part or a weakened form of a disease germ. The immune system learns from it to recognise the germ. Some antigens, however, trigger only a weak reaction on their own. Then an **adjuvant** helps. The word comes from the Latin **“adiuvare”**, which means **to help**. The adjuvant itself does not protect against a disease, it makes the immune response to the antigen stronger and longer lasting.

The most commonly used adjuvants are **aluminium salts**. They have been used in vaccines for almost **100 years**. A newer adjuvant is **MF59**, which is in some flu vaccines. It is an emulsion, that is, a fine mixture of oil droplets and water. The basis is the natural substance **squalene**, which also occurs in the human body and is made as a precursor of cholesterol.

Adjuvants wake up mainly the **innate immune defence**, the body's quick first line of defence. They attract defence cells to the injection site and help them to take up the antigen and pass it on. Modern adjuvants such as **monophosphoryl lipid A** act in a targeted way through **Toll-like receptors**. These are sensors with which defence cells recognise typical components of disease germs. After that, the immune system builds up a targeted protection.

**Live vaccines** contain weakened but still multiplying germs. They trigger a strong reaction on their own and therefore usually need **no adjuvant**. Adjuvants are important mainly in vaccines made from single components of germs. A further advantage: with an adjuvant you need **less antigen per dose**. That is important when vaccines are scarce, for example in a **flu pandemic**.

Because an adjuvant stimulates the immune system in a targeted way, **redness, swelling and pain at the injection site** occur more often with adjuvanted vaccines. Tiredness or a slight fever can also occur. These reactions are usually harmless and fade after one to two days. In Switzerland the authority **Swissmedic** checks vaccines before they are approved.

gewusst: The strengthening effect of aluminium salts was discovered in the 1920s.
Squalene was first obtained from shark liver oil, which is where its name comes from.

teile.einleitung: The budgerigar is a small, colourful parrot from Australia. It is one of the most popular pet birds in the world. Budgerigars are sociable, curious and very chatty.
wichtigste: The budgerigar belongs to the parrots.
It grows to about 18 centimetres.
Wild budgerigars are green with a yellow head and wavy stripes.
It eats seeds, but also likes fruit and vegetables.
Chocolate is poisonous to budgerigars.
A female usually lays about 4 to 8 eggs.
Budgerigars should never be kept alone.

abschnitte.text: A fully grown budgerigar is about 18 centimetres long, including the long tail. It weighs only about 30 to 40 grams. Wild birds are green with a yellow face, and the back has black **wavy lines**, which is where the name comes from. Bred budgerigars also come in blue, white, yellow or violet. On the bill sits the **cere**, which is usually blue in males and brownish in females.

Budgerigars come from the dry interior of **Australia**. There they live in flocks that sometimes number thousands of birds. In great drought they fly long distances to waterholes. They are **nomads** and move to where it has rained and grasses carry seeds.

In nature, budgerigars eat mainly grass seeds. With the strong, curved **bill** they crack the seeds and also climb with it. As pets they get seed food, plus fresh fruit, vegetables and herbs. Twigs or toys to nibble keep the bill busy. Chocolate, avocado and salty foods, on the other hand, are dangerous or poisonous.

Budgerigars breed in tree hollows, for example in eucalyptus trees. The female usually lays about 4 to 8 eggs and sits on them for around 18 days. The young leave the hollow after about four to five weeks. Pairs often greet each other by gently touching bills. To sleep they usually stand on one leg and tuck their head into their **plumage**.

Budgerigars are **flock birds** and need at least one companion of their own kind. They need a large cage or an aviary and free flight every day. In Switzerland, the Animal Welfare Act requires that sociable birds are not kept alone. Well-cared-for budgerigars can live to 10 years or older. If a budgerigar dozes quietly on one leg, it usually feels well and safe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of birds with a curved bill and gripping feet, which also includes macaws and cockatoos.
The bare skin above the bill, the colour of which often shows males and females apart.
A large group of birds that fly and live together.
A large bird enclosure in which birds can fly.

gewusst: Some budgerigars learn to repeat dozens of words.
Budgerigars can see UV light, so their plumage shines even more colourfully to them than to us.
In Australia they are called “budgerigar”, or “budgie” for short.

teile.einleitung: An anxiety disorder is a mental illness in which fear is much stronger or more frequent than the situation explains. It is one of the most common mental illnesses. Anxiety disorders can usually be treated well.
wichtigste: In an anxiety disorder, the fear is stronger than the real danger and limits everyday life.
A panic disorder shows itself in repeated, unexpected panic attacks.
In social phobia, people mainly fear being judged by others.
In generalised anxiety disorder, people worry constantly about many areas of life.
The sympathetic nervous system causes a racing heart and sweating.
Avoidance makes the fear stronger in the long run.
For specific phobias, exposure therapy is seen as especially effective.

abschnitte.text: Fear is a normal and useful feeling. We speak of an **anxiety disorder** when the fear is much stronger than the situation explains, and when it lasts a long time. People with it suffer from it and are limited in everyday life. Physical signs such as a racing heart, trembling and sweating are also typical. These are triggered by the **sympathetic nervous system**, a part of the nervous system that prepares the body for fight or flight.

In a **panic disorder**, there are repeated **unexpected panic attacks**. Very strong fear suddenly appears, often with difficulty breathing and a pounding heart. Afterwards many people already fear the next attack. In **agoraphobia**, people are afraid of places from which **escape seems difficult** or where no help would be at hand, such as crowded trains or crowds of people.

In **social phobia**, the main thing is the fear of **being judged by others**. People with it fear, for example, making fools of themselves when speaking in front of the class. In **generalised anxiety disorder**, people **worry constantly** about many areas of life such as health, family or school. In **specific phobias**, the fear is of one particular thing. One example is **claustrophobia**, the fear of narrow, closed spaces.

Many people with fear keep away from the situation they dread. In the short term this feels like a relief. In the long term, though, the fear gets stronger. Someone who always avoids it never finds out that the **feared danger does not happen**. So the brain does not learn that the situation is actually harmless.

Anxiety disorders can usually be treated well, mainly with **psychotherapy**. For specific phobias, **exposure therapy** is especially effective. In it, you face the dreaded situation step by step with the support of a professional. Sometimes medicines are also used. In Switzerland, children and young people can, for example, get advice anonymously on **147** from Pro Juventute.

gewusst: The word “phobia” comes from the Greek word for fear.
Anxiety disorders often begin in childhood or youth.

teile.einleitung: Dwarf hamsters are small hamsters that are clearly smaller than the well-known golden hamster. They come from the cold steppes and semi-deserts of Central Asia and are popular pets today. With their cheek pouches they can carry a surprising amount of food.
wichtigste: Dwarf hamsters are much smaller than golden hamsters.
Well-known species are the Djungarian, the Campbell's and the Roborovski dwarf hamster.
They come from steppes and semi-deserts in Central Asia, Mongolia and China.
Dwarf hamsters are active mainly at dusk and at night.
In their cheek pouches they carry food into their burrow.
They usually live only about two to three years.
For small children they are not well suited as animals to stroke.

abschnitte.text: Dwarf hamsters, depending on the species, are only about 5 to 10 centimetres long and weigh 20 to 50 grams. The smallest is the **Roborovski dwarf hamster**, which is hardly bigger than a walnut. Their tail is very short and can hardly be seen in the fur. The Djungarian dwarf hamster has a dark stripe on its back and can turn almost white in winter.

In nature, dwarf hamsters live in **steppes** and semi-deserts in Kazakhstan, Mongolia, Siberia and the north of China. There the winters are very cold and the summers dry. They dig underground burrows with several tunnels and chambers. In them they sleep, raise their young and store supplies.

Dwarf hamsters eat mainly seeds, grains and herbs. Added to this are insects, which give them important protein. With their **cheek pouches** they collect food and bring it to their storeroom. As pets they get a special seed mixture and now and then some fresh vegetables.

Dwarf hamsters are **crepuscular** and sleep through most of the day. At night in nature they often cover long distances. A female carries her young for only about three weeks and usually has four to eight young. The young are born naked and blind and are independent after about three to four weeks.

A dwarf hamster needs a large enclosure with plenty of deep bedding in which it can dig. A sand bath helps it to care for its fur. A large running wheel with a closed running surface prevents injuries to the paws. Because dwarf hamsters sleep by day and are easily startled, they are animals more for watching than for cuddling.

begriffe.erklaerung: Stretchy pockets in the cheeks in which hamsters carry food.
A wide, dry grassland almost without trees.
An animal that is awake mainly in the evening and early morning.
Soft material such as shavings or hay that covers the floor of an enclosure.

gewusst: A dwarf hamster can run several kilometres in its running wheel in one night.
The Djungarian dwarf hamster changes its fur colour in winter so that it is camouflaged in the snow.

teile.einleitung: The anaerobic threshold is a term from sports medicine. It describes how hard you can work without lactate in the blood piling up more and more. Athletes use it to plan their endurance training.
wichtigste: The anaerobic threshold is the highest effort at which blood lactate stays constant.
This effort is also called the maximal lactate steady state.
Following Mader, a fixed value of 4 mmol/l is often used.
Well above the threshold, lactate keeps rising.
Well-trained people can keep up an effort at the threshold for about 30 to 60 minutes.
Endurance training moves the threshold to a higher performance.

abschnitte.text: In any effort, the muscles make some **lactate**, and the body also breaks it down again. As long as the two are in balance, the lactate level in the blood stays the same. The **anaerobic threshold** is the highest effort at which this is still just possible. Experts speak of the **maximal lactate steady state**. “Steady state” means a constant condition.

The lactate level is measured with a drop of blood, usually from the earlobe. At rest it is about 1 to 2 millimoles per litre. The sports scientist **Mader** suggested using a fixed value of **4 mmol/l** as the anaerobic threshold. This rule is simple and is therefore used a lot. In some people, however, the real threshold is a little higher or lower.

If you increase the effort **well above the threshold**, lactate **keeps rising**. The muscles become acidic, and you soon have to stop or slow down. **Breathing** then also rises **disproportionately**, that is, much more than the performance. The threshold that is found from this change with a **breath gas analysis** is called the **ventilatory threshold**.

At the threshold, a well-trained person can keep going for about **30 to 60 minutes**. The **Conconi test** tries to find the threshold without blood samples, from a bend in the heart rate curve. This method is, however, seen as inaccurate. With targeted **endurance training**, the threshold moves to a higher performance. You can then run or cycle faster without lactate rising.

gewusst: The term “anaerobic” is actually misleading, because even at the threshold the muscles work mainly with oxygen.
Many top athletes have their threshold measured several times a year in order to adjust their training.

teile.einleitung: A dwarf rabbit is an especially small breed of rabbit that often weighs only about a kilogram. Dwarf rabbits are among the most popular pets in Switzerland. They are curious and playful, but need a lot of space, company and the right care.
wichtigste: Dwarf rabbits are especially small breeds of rabbit.
They usually weigh about 1 to 1.5 kilograms.
Well-known breeds are the colour dwarf and the dwarf lop with floppy ears.
All domestic rabbits descend from the European wild rabbit.
Rabbits are not rodents but lagomorphs.
Their teeth keep growing all their lives.
Rabbits always need the company of others of their kind.

abschnitte.text: Dwarf rabbits have a round head, a compact body and short ears. The **colour dwarf** usually weighs about one to one and a half kilograms and comes in many coat colours. The **dwarf lop** has long floppy ears, and a lionhead rabbit has a mane around its head. All these breeds were bred by people.

All domestic rabbits descend from the **European wild rabbit**, which originally lived on the Iberian Peninsula. The Romans already kept rabbits in enclosures, and later monks bred them further in monasteries. Dwarf rabbits arose mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries through deliberate breeding of small animals. Although rabbits look like rodents, they belong to the order of lagomorphs.

Rabbits are pure plant eaters and need mainly **hay** and fresh grass. Herbs, leafy vegetables such as lettuce and now and then a piece of carrot go with it. Because their teeth keep growing, they have to chew a lot so that the teeth wear down. Bread, sweets or a lot of dry food make rabbits ill.

In nature, rabbits live in groups and dig burrows. In danger they thump on the ground with their hind legs to warn others. When they feel at ease, they make funny leaps in the air. A female carries her young for only about a month and has several young, which are born naked and blind.

In Switzerland the **Animal Welfare Ordinance** requires that rabbits must have contact with others of their kind. A small cage is not enough, and they need a large enclosure with a hiding place and raised spots. Daily exercise for running and hopping is important. Well-cared-for dwarf rabbits can live to eight to twelve years old.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal group with hares, rabbits and pikas that looks like rodents.
A group of domestic animals with the same features that was bred by people.
A breed of dwarf rabbit with long floppy ears.
An animal of the same species.

gewusst: Rabbits eat part of their own droppings to get even more nutrients out of the food.
Rabbits can see almost all the way round without turning their head.

teile.einleitung: A white tiger is a tiger with white fur and black stripes. It is not a species of its own, but a Bengal tiger with a rare change in its genes.
wichtigste: The fur of the white tiger is white with black or dark brown stripes.
White tigers are not a species or subspecies of their own.
The white colour arises through a rare change in the genes.
White tigers are not albinos, because they have stripes and usually blue eyes.
In the wild, white tigers are extremely rare, and today they live almost only in zoos.
Many white tigers in zoos descend from a single animal called Mohan.
Tigers are the biggest cats in the world and are seriously endangered.

abschnitte.text: White tigers have creamy white fur with dark stripes. Their eyes are usually **blue**, and the nose is pink. They are often somewhat bigger and heavier than normally coloured Bengal tigers. As with all tigers, the stripe pattern is unique to each animal.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the white colour come from?
abschnitte.text: The white colour arises through a **mutation**, that is, a change in a gene. In normal tigers this gene provides the reddish orange colour. A tiger is white only if it has inherited the changed gene from both parents. Because the black stripes remain, it is not an **albino**.

White tigers were seen now and then in India a long time ago. In 1951 a young white tiger, who was given the name **Mohan**, was caught in the area of Rewa. He was bred with his offspring, and many white tigers in zoos around the world descend from him. In the wild, no white tiger has been reliably seen for decades.

To get white tigers, closely related animals were often bred together. This **inbreeding** often leads to illnesses, squinting or deformities. Many scientifically run zoos therefore no longer breed white tigers today. They concentrate on protecting the true subspecies.

The tiger is the biggest cat in the world and lives in Asia. The **Bengal tiger** occurs mainly in India, Bangladesh and Nepal. Poaching and the destruction of forests have put tigers under great threat. Thanks to protected areas, however, populations in India have risen again in recent years.

begriffe.erklaerung: A change in the genes that can alter, for example, the colour of the fur.
An animal without pigment, with white skin or fur and usually red eyes.
Breeding of closely related animals, which can make illnesses more likely.
A subspecies of tiger that lives mainly in India; also called the royal Bengal tiger.

gewusst: A tiger's skin is also striped under the fur.
There are also very rare, almost entirely white tigers in which the stripes can hardly be seen.
With its pale fur, a white tiger would be easier for prey animals to see in the jungle.

teile.einleitung: The green sandpiper is a slender wading bird that lives by streams, pools and in boggy woods. Unusual for a wader is that it does not nest on the ground, but in old nests of other birds high up in trees. Its chicks therefore have to make a brave leap down right after hatching.
wichtigste: The green sandpiper is a wading bird of the sandpiper and snipe family.
It often nests in old nests of other birds in trees, for example of thrushes.
After hatching, the chicks have to jump from the tree nest to the ground.
It breeds in the boggy woods of northern Europe and Asia.
In Switzerland you see it on migration and sometimes in winter.
It eats water insects, small crustaceans and small fish.
Typical is its constant bobbing of the tail.

abschnitte.text: The green sandpiper is 21 to 24 centimetres long and weighs about 50 to 80 grams. It has a long, dark bill and a dark brown upper side with fine light speckles. In flight the bright **white rump** is striking, which makes a strong contrast with the dark underside of the wings. When standing it bobs its rear end constantly.

The green sandpiper breeds in the northern coniferous forests of Eurasia, from Scandinavia to eastern Siberia. There it lives in **swamp woods**, bogs and on the wooded banks of lakes and streams. In central Europe it breeds, for example, in Poland and in the east of Germany. In Switzerland it does not breed, but it is a regular migrant visitor and occasionally a winter visitor.

Unlike almost all other waders, the green sandpiper does not build a nest on the ground. It uses old **nests** of thrushes, wood pigeons, crows or jays that lie in trees. The female usually lays four eggs, which both parents sit on for about 22 to 24 days. The male sits mainly at night.

The chicks are **nidifugous**, which means they can walk soon after hatching. But because the nest is often several metres up, they have to jump down. Thanks to their light weight and their downy plumage, they usually land unhurt on the soft forest floor. Afterwards the parents lead them to watering places, where they look for food themselves.

The green sandpiper looks for its food in shallow water and on the bank. It eats water insects and their larvae, small crustaceans, worms and sometimes small fish. It probes in the mud with its long bill. It is often looking for food at **dusk**.

The green sandpiper is a **migratory bird**. From June onwards the first birds leave their breeding areas in Scandinavia. They spend the winter in western Europe, in the Mediterranean region, in Africa and in southern Asia. On the way they also rest at small waters, ditches and sewage ponds, which is why you can watch them well in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long-legged bird that looks for food in shallow water.
A young bird that can already walk and leave the nest soon after hatching.
The lower back of a bird right above the tail.
A wet wood in which the ground is often under water.

gewusst: The green sandpiper is one of the very few waders that nest in trees.
The parent birds carry the eggshells away at once after hatching, so that enemies do not find the nest.

teile.einleitung: Wallabies are small to medium-sized relatives of the kangaroos that live in Australia and on New Guinea. Like all kangaroos, they hop on their strong hind legs and carry their young in a pouch. The name wallaby is used for many different species that are smaller than the big giant kangaroos.
wichtigste: Wallaby is the name for smaller species from the kangaroo family.
Wallabies are not a scientific group of their own, and the name describes mainly their size.
They live in Australia, Tasmania and on New Guinea.
They are marsupials, and the young one grows up in the mother's pouch.
Wallabies eat grasses, leaves and herbs.
They move along by hopping on their hind legs.
Wallabies can be seen in many zoos and wildlife parks, also in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Wallabies belong to the family of **kangaroos**. The name wallaby is usually used for species that are smaller than the big giant kangaroos. So it is not a strictly scientific term, but a name based on size. Among the best-known species is the **Bennett's wallaby**, also called the red-necked wallaby.

Depending on the species, wallabies weigh from only a few kilograms to about 20 kilograms. Their fur is mostly grey, brown or reddish, and some species have pretty stripes on the face. The hind legs are long and strong, and the front legs rather short. The long, muscular **tail** serves for balance when hopping and as a support when sitting.

Wallabies live in Australia, on Tasmania and on New Guinea. Depending on the species, you find them in forests, bushland, swamps or stony areas. The **rock wallabies** climb skilfully over rocks and cliffs. Some Bennett's wallabies were also released in New Zealand and Great Britain and live wild there today.

Wallabies are **plant eaters** and eat grasses, herbs, leaves and ferns. Like cows, they chew their food thoroughly and digest it with the help of bacteria. Most species are active at dusk and at night. In danger some thump on the ground with their hind legs to warn others.

Wallabies are **marsupials**. After a short gestation the young one is born tiny, naked and blind. It crawls at once into the mother's pouch, attaches itself to a teat and goes on growing there for many months. A young kangaroo is called a **joey** in English.

Some species of wallaby are common, while others have become rare and are endangered. Introduced animals such as foxes and cats hunt them, and their habitat is lost to farming and fires. In Australia there are protected areas and programmes to save rare species. In Swiss zoos and wildlife parks you can often watch wallabies from close up.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mammal whose young are born very small and go on growing in a pouch.
A family of Australian marsupials that hop on their hind legs.
The English word for a young kangaroo or wallaby.
An animal that feeds only on plants.

gewusst: White wallabies live on Bruny Island near Tasmania.
A newborn wallaby is hardly bigger than a bean.

teile.einleitung: A puppy is a young dog. Puppies are born blind and helpless and then grow very fast. In the first months they learn almost everything they need for their dog life.
wichtigste: A baby dog is called a puppy.
A female dog usually has several puppies, often 4 to 8.
Pregnancy lasts about 63 days, that is, around two months.
Newborn puppies have their eyes closed.
The eyes open after about two weeks.
Puppies at first drink only their mother's milk.
The imprinting phase is very important for later behaviour.

abschnitte.text: Young dogs are called puppies until they are about six months to a year old. The young of wolves and foxes are also called this. The female dog carries the young in her belly for about 63 days. Then she gives birth to a **litter**, usually several puppies, often 4 to 8. Large breeds often have more young than small ones.

Newborn puppies are blind and deaf. Their eyes are at first closed and open after about two weeks. Shortly after, they also begin to hear. They drink **their mother's milk** and sleep almost the whole day. The mother keeps them warm and licks them clean.

From about three weeks, the puppies crawl about and play with their siblings. In rough-and-tumble they learn how hard they may bite. The time from about the third to the twelfth week is called the **imprinting phase** or socialisation phase. What a puppy gets to know now, people, noises or other animals, will not frighten it later.

At about three to four weeks, puppies get their **milk teeth**. Then they already eat soft food as well. At about four to seven months the permanent teeth grow, which is why puppies like to chew on everything. Small breeds of dog are fully grown at about a year, while large ones need up to two years.

A puppy should leave its mother at the earliest at about eight to ten weeks. In Switzerland every dog must be marked with a **microchip** and registered in the Amicus database. Puppies need plenty of sleep, regular food and patience in training. In a puppy playgroup they learn to get along with other dogs.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the young that a mother gives birth to at once.
An important learning time in the first weeks of life that shapes later behaviour.
The first teeth of a young animal, which are later replaced by permanent teeth.
The time in which the young grow in the mother's belly.

gewusst: Puppies sleep up to 20 hours a day.
Dalmatian puppies are born all white, and the spots appear only later.

teile.einleitung: Buzz pollination is a special trick with which bumblebees and other bees pollinate flowers. They hold on to the flower and make their flight muscles vibrate quickly, so that the pollen is shaken out. Without this trick, tomatoes, blueberries and potatoes would be pollinated much less well.
wichtigste: In buzz pollination, bees shake the flower so that pollen falls out.
In German it is called Vibrationsbestäubung, or vibration pollination.
Some flowers, such as those of tomatoes, release the pollen only through small openings.
Bumblebees are especially good at it, but honey bees cannot do it.
The vibration comes from the flight muscles, without the wings beating.
About six to eight per cent of flowering plants depend on this method.
In greenhouses, bumblebee colonies are therefore used to pollinate tomatoes.

abschnitte.text: In **buzz pollination**, a bumblebee lands on a flower and holds on with its mouthparts. Then it tenses its **flight muscles** very quickly without beating its wings. The whole flower vibrates, and the pollen trickles out as if from a salt shaker. You often hear a loud buzzing as it does so.

In some plants the pollen sits in **anthers** that have only tiny holes at the tip. These are called poricidal anthers. The pollen comes out only if the flower is shaken hard. Examples are tomatoes, potatoes, aubergines, blueberries and cranberries.

Bumblebees are masters of buzz pollination, and many **wild bees** such as carpenter bees also manage it. The honey bee, on the other hand, cannot. The vibration is so strong that the flower experiences many times the acceleration of gravity. Wind cannot shake the pollen out as well either.

In the past, gardeners had to pollinate tomato flowers in the greenhouse laboriously by hand or with shaking devices. Since the end of the 1980s, bred **bumblebee colonies** in cardboard boxes have been used for this. That saves a lot of work and leads to nicer fruit. In Switzerland too, many tomato growers work with bumblebees.

Buzz pollination shows how closely plants and **pollinators** work together. Without bumblebees and wild bees, many plants would produce fewer fruits and seeds. Wild bees need flowering meadows and nesting places for this. Protecting bumblebees is therefore important for our food too.

begriffe.erklaerung: Passing pollen on to a flower so that fruit can form.
Fine flower dust containing the male cells of the plant.
The part of the flower in which the pollen is made.
A bee that is not kept by people, for example a bumblebee.

gewusst: When shaking, the bumblebee vibrates so fast that the note sounds higher than its normal flight buzz.
When shaking tomato flowers, bumblebees leave brown bite marks, by which gardeners can tell they have visited.
Blueberries in Swiss gardens, too, are pollinated especially well when bumblebees shake their flowers.

teile.einleitung: Alexander Fleming was a Scottish doctor and bacteria researcher. In 1928 in London he discovered penicillin, one of the first antibiotics. This discovery has since saved countless lives.
wichtigste: Alexander Fleming was born in Scotland in 1881 and died in London in 1955.
He worked at St Mary’s Hospital in London.
In 1928 he discovered by chance that a mould kills bacteria.
He called the active substance penicillin, after the mould Penicillium.
Howard Florey and Ernst Chain made penicillin usable as a medicine in Oxford around 1940.
In 1945 Fleming, Florey and Chain together received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.
Penicillin works against bacteria, but not against viruses.

abschnitte.text: Alexander Fleming grew up on a farm in Scotland and later moved to London. There he studied medicine and did research at **St Mary’s Hospital**. In the First World War he saw how many wounded soldiers died of wound infections. From then on he searched for substances that fight **bacteria**. As early as 1922 he found **lysozyme**, a substance in tears and saliva that attacks some bacteria.

In the summer of 1928 Fleming went on holiday and left some dishes of bacteria standing in the laboratory. When he came back, a **mould** had grown on one dish. Around the mould, the bacteria had died. Fleming realised that the fungus gives off a substance that kills bacteria. He called it **penicillin**, after the fungus genus **Penicillium**.

Fleming did not manage to make the active substance in pure form and in large amounts. It was only around 1940 that **Howard Florey** and **Ernst Chain** at the University of Oxford managed it. They showed that penicillin can cure serious infections in animals and people. In the Second World War the drug was then made in large quantities. In 1945 Fleming, Florey and Chain together received the **Nobel Prize in Medicine**.

Penicillin is one of the **antibiotics**. These medicines kill bacteria or slow their growth. Penicillin attacks the **cell wall** of bacteria. Viruses do not have a cell wall like that, so antibiotics do not help against flu or an ordinary cold. In Switzerland, antibiotics are only available with a doctor’s prescription.

Fleming himself warned against taking penicillin wrongly or in too small amounts. Then tough bacteria survive and multiply. They are called **resistant**, because the medicine no longer works on them. So you should only take antibiotics if a doctor prescribes them, and follow the instructions exactly.

gewusst: In Fleming’s old laboratory at St Mary’s Hospital in London there is now a small museum.
Later Fleming said that he had not invented penicillin: nature had made it, and he had only found it.

teile.einleitung: Zooplankton are tiny animals that float in the water and are carried about by the current. They include, for example, water fleas, copepods and the larvae of fish and mussels. Although you can hardly see them, they are the main food of many fish, such as the whitefish in Swiss lakes.
wichtigste: Zooplankton are small animals that drift in the water and can hardly swim against the current.
Most are smaller than a millimetre up to a few millimetres.
Many species feed on phytoplankton, that is, tiny algae.
Adult whitefish eat mainly tiny crustaceans from the zooplankton.
Krill in the sea is the main food of blue whales.
Many plankton animals rise to the surface at night and sink into the depths by day.
Without zooplankton, the food chains in lakes and seas would collapse.

abschnitte.text: The word **plankton** comes from Greek and means “the drifting”. Plant plankton made of algae is called phytoplankton, and animal plankton is called zooplankton. Zooplankton includes very different animals, for example small crustaceans, rotifers, small jellyfish and arrow worms. Some animals stay in the plankton their whole life, and others only as larvae.

In lakes and ponds, **water fleas** are common, which belong to the crustaceans and row through the water in hops. **Copepods**, which swim with their long antennae, are also very numerous. In the sea, krill is famous, small shrimp-like crustaceans a few centimetres long. Added to these are the larvae of fish, crabs, starfish and mussels.

Zooplankton stands in the **food chain** between the algae and the larger animals. The small crustaceans filter algae out of the water and are in turn eaten by fish. In Swiss lakes such as Lake Lucerne or Lake Neuchâtel, adult whitefish feed mainly on such crustaceans. In the Southern Ocean, blue whales, penguins and seals eat large amounts of krill.

Many plankton animals travel up and down every day, which is called **vertical migration**. By day they stay in the dark depths, where fish see them less well. At night they rise to the surface to eat algae there. Because this happens in all seas, this daily migration is regarded as the greatest animal migration on Earth.

Researchers regularly measure in Swiss lakes how much plankton there is. Since the lakes have become cleaner and contain fewer nutrients, there is also less plankton and therefore less food for fish. A new problem is the introduced **quagga mussel**, which filters huge amounts of plankton out of the water, for example in Lake Constance and Lake Geneva. Fishers notice this in smaller catches.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny algae that float in the water and make food with sunlight.
Small crustaceans in the sea that live in huge swarms.
A series of living things in which each is eaten by the next.
A young animal that still looks quite different from the adult animal.

gewusst: Copepods are probably among the most common many-celled animals on Earth.
A blue whale can eat several tonnes of krill in a day.
Water fleas are bred as live fish food for aquariums.

teile.einleitung: The tick is a small arachnid that feeds on the blood of other animals. In Switzerland the castor bean tick (Ixodes ricinus) is the most common species of tick. Its life runs in several stages, and for each stage it needs a blood meal.
wichtigste: Ticks belong to the arachnids, and within them to the group of mites.
The most common tick in Switzerland is the castor bean tick, Ixodes ricinus.
The castor bean tick belongs to the family of hard ticks.
Its species name ricinus comes from the castor oil plant, whose seeds resemble a tick swollen with blood.
