After the egg come larva, nymph and adult.
The larva has six legs, while the nymph and the adult have eight.
In its whole life a castor bean tick normally needs three blood meals.

abschnitte.text: Ticks belong to the class of **arachnids**, just like spiders and scorpions. Within the arachnids they count as **mites**. Worldwide there are several hundred species of tick. The **castor bean tick** belongs to the family of hard ticks, which carry a hard shield on the back.

A female castor bean tick that has not fed is only about three to four millimetres in size and reddish brown with a dark shield. After sucking blood it swells greatly and becomes grey, round and bean-shaped. In this way it looks like the seeds of the castor oil plant, which is where the name **ricinus** comes from. With a special sense organ on the front legs, Haller's organ, the tick feels the warmth and breath of a host.

From the egg hatches a tiny **larva** with only six legs. After its first blood meal it moults into a **nymph** with eight legs. After a second meal this becomes the adult, and the female needs a third, large blood meal before she lays eggs. The whole development usually takes about three years.

The castor bean tick is not fussy: over 300 species of vertebrate have been recorded as hosts. Larvae suck mainly on **small mammals** such as mice, while nymphs and adults also suck on birds, roe deer, dogs and humans. The tick climbs onto grasses and bushes and waits there with its front legs stretched out. If an animal brushes past, it holds on, but it does not drop from trees.

A female swollen with blood drops off the host and lays about 2,000 to 3,000 eggs on the ground. After that she dies. The males hardly suck any blood and die after mating. Because only a few of the many offspring find a host, so many **eggs** are needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal group with eight legs, which includes spiders, scorpions and mites.
Mostly tiny arachnids, to which ticks also belong.
The young stage of the tick between larva and adult.
An animal on which the tick sucks blood.

gewusst: A tick can get by for months without food.
A female castor bean tick can increase her weight many times over while sucking.

teile.einleitung: The little penguin is the smallest penguin in the world and grows only about 35 to 40 centimetres tall. It lives on the coasts of New Zealand and in the south of Australia. Because of its blue-grey plumage, it is also called the “little blue penguin”.
wichtigste: The little penguin is the smallest penguin in the world.
It is about 35 to 40 centimetres tall and weighs about a kilogram.
Its back is blue-grey, and the belly white.
It lives in New Zealand and in the south of Australia.
It is the only species of penguin that breeds on the Australian mainland.
It eats small fish, squid and crustaceans.
The birds come ashore only at dusk.

abschnitte.text: The little penguin, scientifically *Eudyptula minor*, is about 35 to 40 centimetres tall. It weighs about a kilogram, so about as much as a carton of milk. Back and head are **blue-grey**, and chest and belly are white. Like all penguins, it cannot fly, but it uses its wings as strong flippers.

The main range lies in **New Zealand**, where the bird is called kororā in Māori. There are breeding colonies on many coasts of the North and South Islands. In Australia it breeds on the south coast and on Tasmania. It is the only penguin that breeds on the Australian mainland.

Little penguins hunt in the sea for small **shoaling fish** such as sardines and anchovies. They also eat squid and small crustaceans. By day they are out at sea and dive again and again for prey. Only when it gets dark do they return to land.

Little penguins breed in **burrows**, between rocks or under bushes close to the beach. The female usually lays two eggs, and both parents take turns sitting on them. After about five weeks the chicks hatch, and both parents feed them. At night the birds in the colonies are quite loud, because they communicate with calls.

On **Phillip Island** near Melbourne in Australia, you can watch the famous penguin parade every evening. At dusk, hundreds of little penguins waddle there in groups from the sea to their nests. Visitors watch from stands and walkways. Taking photographs is banned there so that the birds are not disturbed.

On land, little penguins are hunted by introduced **foxes**, dogs and cats. Cars on coastal roads and oil pollution are also a danger. On the Australian island of Middle Island, Maremma sheepdogs guard the penguin colony against foxes. Thanks to such protective measures, some colonies have recovered.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of birds that breed in the same place.
All the feathers of a bird together.
Keeping the eggs warm until the chicks hatch.
A young bird shortly after hatching.

gewusst: The biggest penguin, the emperor penguin, is more than twice as big as the little penguin.
The story of the sheepdogs that guard little penguins was made into a film in Australia in 2015.

teile.einleitung: The brimstone is a butterfly whose males are a bright lemon yellow. It is one of the first butterflies you see flying in spring, often already in February or March. This is because it spends the winter outdoors as an adult butterfly.
wichtigste: The brimstone is a bright yellow butterfly that is common in Switzerland too.
Only the males are lemon yellow, and the females are pale greenish white.
On each wing it carries a small orange dot.
It spends the winter as an adult butterfly hidden in bushes or in leaf litter.
It can survive frost far below zero degrees.
With a life of up to about a year, it is one of the longest-lived butterflies in central Europe.
Its caterpillars feed on alder buckthorn and buckthorn.

abschnitte.text: The **brimstone** (Gonepteryx rhamni) has a wingspan of about five to six centimetres. Its wings end in small points at the tips and look almost like leaves. The males are bright **lemon yellow**, and the females pale greenish white. Both carry a small orange spot on each wing.

Unlike most butterflies, the brimstone spends the winter as an adult animal without a protective hiding place in houses or caves. It simply sits on twigs in bushes, on bramble stems or in the leaf litter. In its body, **antifreeze substances** form, and it loses water so that it does not freeze. In this way it survives temperatures down to about minus 20 degrees, sometimes even covered by snow.

On the first warm days in February or March the butterfly wakes up and flies off. That is why it is regarded as a **herald of spring**. It sucks nectar from early flowers such as pussy willow, coltsfoot and lungwort. With a life of up to about twelve months, it is one of the longest-lived butterflies in central Europe.

In spring the female lays her eggs singly on young leaves of **alder buckthorn** or buckthorn. That is also where its scientific name rhamni comes from, because buckthorn is called Rhamnus in Latin. The green caterpillar is very well camouflaged on the leaves. After pupation, the new butterflies hatch in summer and live until the next spring.

The brimstone is widespread all over Switzerland, from the Central Plateau to the mountain valleys. You see it at woodland edges, in hedges, gardens and parks. It is not endangered, but it needs shrubs such as alder buckthorn for its caterpillars. Anyone who plants native **hedges** in their garden helps it and many other insects.

begriffe.erklaerung: The larva of a butterfly, which eats and grows.
A resting stage in which the caterpillar changes into a butterfly.
Substances in the body that prevent freezing.
The sweet juice in flowers that insects drink.

gewusst: A brimstone can spend the winter covered with snow and simply fly on in spring.
The brimstone almost always settles with its wings folded together, which is why you rarely see the upper side at rest.

teile.einleitung: Vibrissae are especially long and stiff tactile hairs, like the whiskers of a cat. They are very sensitive and report even the finest touches and movements of the air to the brain. In this way animals can sense obstacles, distances and prey even in the dark.
wichtigste: Vibrissae are long, stiff tactile hairs in many mammals.
Well-known examples are the whiskers of cats, mice and seals.
A cat feels obstacles and distances in the dark with its whiskers.
Dogs also use their tactile hairs to sense their immediate surroundings.
At the root of every vibrissa lie many nerve cells.
Vibrissae are found not only on the muzzle, but also above the eyes and on the front legs.
You should never cut off vibrissae.

abschnitte.text: **Vibrissae** are thick, long hairs that are anchored deeper in the skin than normal hairs. They sit in a **follicle** that is surrounded by a small cushion of blood. Very many nerves end there. The word comes from the Latin vibrare, which means to tremble or swing.

When a vibrissa touches something or the air moves, the hair bends slightly. This movement is strengthened at the root and reported by **nerve cells** to the brain. The brain builds a picture of the surroundings from it, almost as if with the fingertips. Some animals such as mice and rats move their vibrissae back and forth actively in order to feel.

A **cat** usually has twelve whiskers on each side of the muzzle. With them it feels obstacles and distances in the dark and checks whether it fits through an opening. It also has tactile hairs above the eyes and on the back of the front paws. In the **dog**, vibrissae sit on the muzzle, chin and above the eyes and help it to sense its immediate surroundings.

**Seals** can feel the water swirls of a swimming fish with their whiskers in murky water and follow it. Walruses find mussels on the sea floor with hundreds of tactile hairs. Rats can even recognise the surface of objects with their vibrissae. Manatees also have tactile hairs spread over the whole body.

Vibrissae should never be cut, because without them the animal is unsure and finds its way around less well. If single whiskers fall out, they normally grow back. Some cats do not like it when their whiskers bump against a narrow bowl while eating. A flat, wide **food bowl** can then help.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, stiff tactile hair in mammals.
The ability to feel touches.
A small pocket of skin in which a hair grows.
A cell that passes signals on to the brain.

gewusst: The whiskers of a cat are about as wide as its body, so they serve as a measuring tool for narrow gaps.
A blindfolded seal can follow the trail of a fish with its whiskers alone.
People have no vibrissae, and our eyebrows and eyelashes are ordinary hairs.

teile.einleitung: Aldosterone is a hormone made in the adrenal cortex. It makes the kidneys keep salt and water in the body. In this way it helps to keep blood pressure and the body’s salt balance steady.
wichtigste: Aldosterone belongs to the mineralocorticoids.
Like all steroid hormones, it is made from cholesterol.
A raised potassium level directly prompts the adrenal gland to make it.
It works mainly in the late distal tubule and the collecting duct of the kidney.
It works through a receptor inside the cell.
Spironolactone blocks its effect at the receptor.
If there is too much aldosterone for a long time, blood pressure rises.

abschnitte.text: Aldosterone is made in the outermost layer of the **adrenal cortex**. Like all **steroid hormones**, it is made **from cholesterol**. It belongs to the group of **mineralocorticoids**, because it controls the balance of the minerals sodium and potassium. It was isolated in the early 1950s. The Basel chemist **Tadeus Reichstein** helped with this. In 1950 he had received the Nobel Prize for his research on hormones of the adrenal cortex.

abschnitte.titel: How it works in the kidney
abschnitte.text: Aldosterone works mainly in the **kidney**, in the **late distal tubule** and the **collecting duct** of the nephrons, the kidney’s tiny filtering units. There it makes sure that **sodium** is taken back into the blood and **potassium** is passed out. Together with the sodium, **water** is also kept back. This increases the amount of blood, and blood pressure rises. As a steroid hormone, aldosterone passes through the cell membrane and works through a **receptor inside the cell**.

A **raised potassium level** in the blood prompts the adrenal gland **directly** to make aldosterone, so that extra potassium can be passed out. A second important trigger is the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system**: if blood pressure falls, **angiotensin II** is made in several steps, and it boosts the production of aldosterone. If someone eats **a great deal of table salt** for a long time, the body has enough sodium, and the **aldosterone level falls**.

If the body makes **too much aldosterone** for a long time, for example in **Conn’s syndrome**, **blood pressure rises**, and the potassium level often falls. The medicine **spironolactone** blocks the effect of aldosterone at the receptor and is used, for example, for high blood pressure and heart failure. With **too little aldosterone**, for example in **Addison’s disease**, it is the other way round: the typical sign is **sodium too low and potassium too high** in the blood. People with it are given a replacement hormone.

gewusst: Tadeus Reichstein is still one of the few Swiss people to have won the Nobel Prize in Medicine.
People who sweat a lot and lose a lot of salt make more aldosterone, so that the body saves sodium.

teile.einleitung: The European bison, or wisent, is a mighty wild bovine and the heaviest land mammal in Europe. It is the European relative of the American bison. It almost died out, but thanks to zoos it lives again today in the wild.
wichtigste: The wisent is the heaviest land mammal in Europe.
It is the European relative of the American bison.
Compared with the bison it has less mane and looks longer-legged.
Bulls can weigh up to about 900 kilograms.
The last free-living wisent was killed in Poland in 1919.
The species was bred back from a few zoo animals.
In the canton of Solothurn, a trial with wisents in the forest has been running since 2022.

abschnitte.text: The **wisent** has a large head, short horns and a high hump above the shoulders. Its fur is dark brown, and in winter dense and long. Bulls reach a shoulder height of almost two metres and weigh up to about 900 kilograms. Compared with the American **bison**, it has longer legs and a less mighty mane, and carries its head higher.

Wisents live mainly in open woods with meadows and clearings. They eat grasses, herbs, leaves, shoots and also tree bark. A large wisent eats many kilograms of plants a day. By their feeding they keep clearings open and so create habitat for other species.

Wisents live in small **herds** of cows and young animals, usually led by an experienced cow. Adult bulls often live alone or in small groups and join in at the mating season. After a pregnancy of about nine months, usually a single calf is born. It can walk soon after birth.

In the past, wisents lived in large parts of Europe, in Switzerland too. Through hunting and the felling of forests they became ever rarer. In 1919 the last free-living wisent was shot in the **Białowieża Forest** in Poland, and in the Caucasus they died out a few years later. Only about a dozen animals in zoos and enclosures formed the basis for the **rescue** of the species.

abschnitte.titel: Return to Europe and to Switzerland
abschnitte.text: Thanks to breeding programmes, there are again several thousand wisents today, many of them in the wild in Poland, Belarus and other countries. In Germany a free-living herd has lived in the Rothaargebirge since 2013. In Switzerland, in 2022, wisents were brought into a large forest enclosure in the **Solothurn Jura** near Welschenrohr. There it is being studied how wisents and people could live together in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wild-living species of cattle, for example the wisent or bison.
A group of animals that lives and travels together.
Animals from enclosures are brought into the wild.
A list of all the animals of a species in zoos, so that suitable pairs can be found.

gewusst: All wisents alive today descend from only about twelve animals.
Despite its weight, a wisent is surprisingly fast and can also jump well.
In enclosures, wisents can live to over 20 years old.

teile.einleitung: Ammonia is a compound of nitrogen and hydrogen with the chemical formula NH₃. It is a colourless gas with a sharp smell. Ammonia is also constantly produced in the human body. It is poisonous to the brain and therefore has to be made harmless quickly.
wichtigste: Ammonia has the formula NH₃ and has a sharp smell.
In the body it is made mainly when amino acids are broken down.
In the blood, at normal pH, it is mostly present as the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺).
The most important harmless way of carrying it in the blood is the amino acid glutamine.
The liver turns ammonia into urea, which is passed out in the urine.
In liver failure, too much ammonia can damage the brain.

abschnitte.titel: A gas with a sharp smell
abschnitte.text: Ammonia consists of one **nitrogen** atom and three **hydrogen** atoms. The gas is colourless and has a very sharp smell. In industry, ammonia is made in huge amounts, mainly for **fertiliser**. If you dissolve it in water, you get a solution known as household ammonia.

abschnitte.titel: Where it comes from in the body
abschnitte.text: Our body is constantly breaking down **proteins** and their building blocks, the **amino acids**. This releases nitrogen, and ammonia is formed. Bacteria in the **gut** also make ammonia. In the blood, most of it is present at normal pH as the **ammonium ion (NH₄⁺)**. Even small amounts of free ammonia are poisonous to the brain.

So that ammonia does no harm, the body binds it to other substances. The enzyme **glutamine synthetase** attaches ammonia to the amino acid glutamate. This makes **glutamine**, the most important harmless transport form in the blood. In the **liver**, the nitrogen is finally turned into **urea**. The kidneys pass the urea out in the urine.

The **kidney** also releases ammonium into the urine itself. In doing so it removes acid from the body at the same time. In this way it helps to keep the **pH** of the blood steady. This process is especially important when the blood threatens to become too acidic.

If the liver is seriously ill, it can no longer break down enough ammonia. Then a lot of it reaches the brain, and **hepatic encephalopathy** develops. People with it become tired and confused and, in the worst case, can lose consciousness. Doctors then often give the sugar **lactulose**, which reduces the uptake of ammonia from the gut. In addition, the **antibiotic rifaximin**, which is hardly absorbed, can slow the gut bacteria that make ammonia.

gewusst: Smelling salts, which used to be held under the nose of someone who had fainted, gave off ammonia.
In 1932 the German researcher Hans Krebs worked out how the liver makes urea.

teile.einleitung: A billy goat is a fully grown male goat. In Switzerland people often also say Geissbock. He is bigger than the female goats, usually carries strong horns and a long beard, and stands out in the mating season through his strong smell.
wichtigste: A fully grown male goat is called a billy goat.
The female is called a nanny goat, and the young a kid.
Billy goats are bigger and heavier than nanny goats.
They usually have a long beard and large horns.
In the mating season in autumn, billy goats smell very strong.
Billy goats fight with butting of heads for rank in the herd.
One billy goat can mate with many nanny goats, so farmers usually keep only a few billy goats.

abschnitte.text: The **billy goat** is built clearly more strongly than the nanny goat. He has a broad neck, a long **beard** and often long horns curving backwards. Many billy goats also have a kind of mane on the neck and on the back. As with the nanny goats, there are billy goats in many coat colours, depending on the breed.

Behind the horns, billy goats have **scent glands** that smell strongly in the mating season. They also spray themselves with urine, especially beard and front legs. For people this smells unpleasant, but for the nanny goats it is attractive. That is why billy goats are usually kept apart from the dairy goats, so that the milk does not take on a smell.

At the **rut**, the mating season in autumn, billy goats fight for rank. They rear up on their hind legs and let themselves fall with full force onto the opponent, so that the horns clash with a crack. A thick skull protects them as they do so. Usually the fight ends without serious injury when one gives up.

A **breeding billy goat** can mate with many nanny goats in a season. That is why goat keepers usually keep only one billy goat for a whole herd. The kids are then born about five months later in spring. For breeding, billy goats with good qualities are chosen, for example from mothers that give a lot of milk.

A close wild relative is the **Alpine ibex**, which is the heraldic animal of the canton of Graubünden. Its males carry mighty horns that can grow over a metre long. They too fight with butting of heads in the rut. The ibex had been wiped out in Switzerland and was reintroduced from 1911.

begriffe.erklaerung: The male animal in goats, sheep, deer and ibex.
The mating season in hoofed animals such as goats and deer.
A gland in the skin that gives off smelling substances.
A billy goat that is used to increase the herd.

gewusst: The German word “bockig”, meaning stubborn, comes from the billy goat.
The billy goat Hennes is the living mascot of the football club 1. FC Köln.

teile.einleitung: Pygmy seahorses are the smallest seahorses in the world and often grow only about as big as a fingernail. They live in warm coral reefs and are so well camouflaged that even experienced divers can hardly find them. As in all seahorses, the father carries the young.
wichtigste: Pygmy seahorses are the smallest seahorses.
Some species grow only about 1.5 to 2 centimetres, about as small as a fingernail.
The best-known pygmy seahorse lives on gorgonian sea fans in the western Pacific.
Their colour and small bumps match their coral exactly.
Seahorses are fish and breathe with gills.
The male carries the eggs in a brood pouch.
Pygmy seahorses eat tiny crustaceans.

abschnitte.text: The name pygmy seahorses is given to several tiny **species of seahorse**. The best known is *Hippocampus bargibanti*, which usually stays smaller than two centimetres. Slightly smaller still is Satomi's pygmy seahorse, at about 1.4 centimetres. Despite their appearance, seahorses are true **fish** with gills and fins.

*Hippocampus bargibanti* lives in coral reefs in the western Pacific, from the Philippines and Indonesia to the Great Barrier Reef in Australia and New Caledonia. It stays at depths of about 10 to 50 metres. It usually spends its whole life on a single **gorgonian**, a branching fan coral. With its prehensile tail it holds on to its branches.

Pygmy seahorses have the same colour as their coral, for example pink or yellow. On their body sit small bumps that look exactly like the polyps of the coral. This **camouflage** is so good that the species was discovered only in 1969, by chance. The researcher Georges Bargibant found the animals in New Caledonia on a coral that he had collected for an aquarium.

In seahorses, the female lays the eggs in a **brood pouch** on the belly of the male. There the young develop until the father releases them into the water. In pygmy seahorses, the newborn young are only a few millimetres in size. The parents often stay together as a pair.

Pygmy seahorses eat tiny crustaceans that drift past them. They suck in the prey in a flash with their tube-shaped mouth. Because they are tied to particular corals, the destruction of reefs harms them. Divers should not photograph them with a harsh flash, because that disturbs the animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A coral that looks like a branching fan or bush.
A pouch on the belly of the male seahorse in which the young grow.
An animal looks so like its surroundings that you can hardly make it out.
The breathing organs of fish, with which they take oxygen from the water.

gewusst: Seahorses are poor swimmers and are among the slowest fish.
Seahorses can move their eyes independently of each other.

teile.einleitung: Anaesthesia makes sure that people feel no pain during operations and examinations. For this there is general anaesthesia and various kinds of local anaesthesia. Anaesthesia is what made modern surgery possible in the first place.
wichtigste: “Anaesthesia” comes from Greek and means roughly “without sensation”.
In general anaesthesia, you sleep deeply and feel no pain.
In local anaesthesia, only a small part of the body goes numb.
In spinal anaesthesia, the lower half of the body is numbed by an injection in the back.
In 1846 the first public anaesthetic with ether was shown in Boston.
A pulse oximeter on the finger measures the oxygen in the blood during anaesthesia.
A tube is a pipe used for artificial breathing.

abschnitte.text: In **general anaesthesia** you sleep deeply and feel no pain. Afterwards you do not remember the operation. The drugs are given through a drip into a vein or as a gas to breathe in. Because your own breathing weakens in deep anaesthesia, you are often ventilated. For this the team puts in a **tube**, a pipe that goes into the windpipe.

Sometimes it is enough to numb only part of the body. In **local anaesthesia**, only a **small part of the body** goes numb, for example at the dentist’s. In **spinal anaesthesia**, an anaesthetic is injected into the **back**, close to the spinal cord. Then the **lower half of the body** goes numb, but you stay awake. In this way, operations can be done, for example, on the leg or the hip.

In the past, people had to endure operations fully conscious. That changed in the 19th century. On **16 October 1846**, the dentist **William Morton** showed the first public anaesthetic with **ether** in **Boston**. A patient was operated on without feeling pain. The news spread quickly, and soon anaesthetics were being used all over the world.

Before an anaesthetic, the **anaesthetist** has a **preliminary talk** with you. In it, they ask especially about **allergies**, **earlier illnesses** and medicines. Usually you are not allowed to eat for some hours beforehand: you have to be **fasting**. This stops stomach contents from getting into the lungs during the anaesthetic.

Throughout the anaesthetic you are watched closely. A **pulse oximeter**, a small clip on the finger, measures the **oxygen in the blood** and the pulse. Blood pressure and heartbeat are measured as well. The anaesthetic team stays with you the whole time and keeps adjusting the drugs. After the operation you usually wake up in the recovery room.

gewusst: 16 October is still celebrated today as “World Anaesthesia Day”.
The pulse oximeter measures oxygen with light, with no needle prick at all.

teile.einleitung: The electric eel is a fish from South America that can give off strong electric shocks. Although it looks like an eel, it is not a true eel at all, but belongs to the New World knifefishes. Since 2019, three different species of electric eel have been distinguished.
wichtigste: The electric eel is a fish of South America that can give off electric shocks.
It belongs to the order of New World knifefishes (Gymnotiformes) and usually to the family Gymnotidae.
It is more closely related to catfish than to true eels.
Since 2019, three species have been distinguished.
In the Volta electric eel, around 860 volts were measured, a record in the animal kingdom.
The electric eel has to come to the surface regularly to breathe air.
It can grow to about two and a half metres long.

abschnitte.text: The **electric eel** has a long, round body and can grow to about 2.5 metres long. It has no dorsal or belly fins, but a long fin fringe on the underside with which it swims forwards and backwards. Like other **New World knifefishes**, it is more closely related to catfish than to true eels. Its eyes are small, because in cloudy water it finds its way mainly by electricity.

abschnitte.titel: The power station in the body
abschnitte.text: Almost the whole body is made of **electric organs** made of thousands of converted muscle cells. Each cell produces only a tiny voltage, but connected one behind another they add up like batteries. With weak electric pulses, the fish finds its way and finds prey. With strong shocks it stuns fish and fends off enemies. Most other New World knifefishes, by contrast, produce only weak electric fields.

For a long time only one species was known, **Electrophorus electricus**. In 2019, researchers showed that there are three species. E. electricus lives on the Guiana Shield and reaches around 480 volts. The **Volta electric eel** (E. voltai) lives in rivers of the Brazilian Shield and manages around 860 volts, and E. varii was named after the fish researcher Richard Vari.

Electric eels live in rivers, streams and swamps in the north of South America, for example in the Amazon region. The water there is often warm, cloudy and poor in oxygen. That is why the electric eel breathes mainly **air**: about every few minutes it comes to the surface and gulps air through the mouth. An electric eel that cannot surface drowns.

The researcher **Alexander von Humboldt** observed around 1800 in Venezuela how electric eels attacked horses with electric shocks. The Volta electric eel is named after Alessandro Volta, who built the first battery around 1800. Volta was also inspired by the structure of the electric organs of such fish. Today researchers study electric eels to develop new, soft batteries.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of measurement for electric voltage.
A part of the body made of special cells that produces current.
A group of fish from South America that produce electric fields.
An ancient area of rock in the north of South America.

gewusst: A household socket in Switzerland has 230 volts, and a Volta electric eel can produce almost four times as much.
Electric eels can leap out of the water to hit an attacker with current.
The current of an electric eel lasts only fractions of a second.

teile.einleitung: Wasps are insects with black and yellow stripes that like to come to cake and lemonade in summer. Many people fear them because of their sting. Yet wasps are useful hunters that eat many pests.
wichtigste: Wasps are insects and are closely related to bees.
Their yellow and black colour warns enemies.
There is poison in the sting of the females.
A wasp colony normally has one queen.
The cells in the nest are mostly six-sided.
In autumn most of the wasps of a colony die.
Anyone who stays calm and does not wave their arms is rarely stung.

abschnitte.text: Wasps have a narrow **wasp waist** between the thorax and the abdomen. Their body is patterned in yellow and black but, unlike bees, hardly hairy. These **warning colours** show enemies that they can defend themselves. Wasps are closely related to bees and ants. Here the German wasp and the common wasp are the most frequent, and the hornet is the biggest species.

Wasps build their nests from chewed wood that looks like paper. They especially often build in attics, in roller shutter boxes or in hollows in the ground. The small **comb** cells are mostly six-sided. In spring the queen builds the first combs alone and lays her eggs there.

A wasp colony normally has one **queen**, who lays all the eggs. The workers build, hunt and feed the larvae. In summer a colony can number thousands of wasps. In autumn most wasps of the colony die, and only the young queens spend the winter hidden. The next spring each one founds a new colony.

Wasps catch many insects such as flies, mosquitoes and caterpillars. They feed these to their larvae and so help against pests in the garden. Adult wasps themselves drink mainly sweet juices. That is why in late summer they like fruit, cake and sweet drinks.

Only females have a **sting**, which contains poison. Unlike bees, wasps can sting several times. When a wasp flies around you, it is best to stay calm and not wave your arms. If it lands, it usually flies off again after a short time. If their nest is threatened, wasps defend it together, which is why you keep your distance from nests. If you drink from bottles outdoors, you should look inside first.

begriffe.erklaerung: The very narrow place between the thorax and the abdomen of a wasp.
A striking colour that shows enemies: careful, I am dangerous.
A structure of many small cells in which the larvae grow up.
The only female in the colony that lays eggs.

gewusst: Wasps, so to speak, invented paper, because their nests are made of a kind of paper from wood fibres.
A hornet is big, but usually more peaceful than the smaller wasps at the cake.
For people with an allergy, a wasp sting can be dangerous, and then medical help is needed at once.

teile.einleitung: The backbone is the flexible axis in the back of all vertebrates. It is made of many single bones, the vertebrae, which lie one behind the other like beads on a chain. It carries the body, makes it flexible and protects the delicate spinal cord.
wichtigste: The backbone is made of many bones lying one behind the other, the vertebrae.
All vertebrates have a backbone, which is where their name comes from.
In the backbone runs the spinal cord, an important nerve cord.
Humans have 33 to 34 vertebrae.
Cats have more vertebrae than humans and are therefore especially flexible.
Almost all mammals have exactly seven neck vertebrae, even the giraffe.
In mammals, elastic discs lie between the vertebrae as buffers.

abschnitte.text: The backbone is not a single bone, but a chain of many **vertebrae**. Each vertebra has a strong body and an arch that together form a hole. These holes lie on top of one another and form the **spinal canal**. Between the vertebrae in mammals sit the **discs**, which cushion shocks like small pillows.

In the spinal canal lies the **spinal cord**, a thick cord of nerves. It carries commands from the brain to the muscles and reports back, for example, pain or touch. Because the spinal cord is very delicate, it needs the hard protection of bone. If it is badly injured, a living thing can be paralysed.

Humans have 7 neck vertebrae, 12 chest vertebrae and 5 lumbar vertebrae. Below these come the **sacrum**, made of 5 vertebrae fused together, and the small **coccyx**. Seen from the side, the human backbone is shaped like a double S. This shape cushions the shocks in upright walking and jumping.

A house cat has about 52 to 53 vertebrae, so clearly more than a human. Many of them are in the long tail, which helps with balancing. Its backbone is especially **flexible**, and the discs are very elastic. That is why a cat can curl up, stretch out far and turn in the air when falling, so as to land on its paws.

Snakes have especially many vertebrae, and in some species there are several hundred. That is why they can slither so smoothly. The giraffe, despite its long neck, has only seven **neck vertebrae**, just like humans, but each of them is up to about 25 centimetres long. In birds, many vertebrae are fused together, which makes the body stable for flight.

Muscles and ligaments keep the backbone upright and stable. Anyone who moves a lot strengthens the **back muscles** and prevents back pain. Lifting correctly with a straight back and bent knees also protects the backbone. Sitting hunched for a long time at the phone or computer, by contrast, strains the neck.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single bone of the backbone.
An elastic disc between two vertebrae that absorbs shocks.
A nerve cord inside the backbone that connects the brain and the body.
A tube made of the holes of the vertebrae in which the spinal cord lies.

gewusst: A giraffe has as many neck vertebrae as a human, namely seven.
In the evening a person is about one to two centimetres shorter than in the morning, because the discs are squeezed together during the day.
Some snakes have more than 300 vertebrae.

teile.einleitung: Adenosine is a small molecule that occurs in all cells. It arises mainly when ATP, the energy carrier of cells, is broken down. Adenosine plays a part in the need for sleep, explains the effect of coffee and is used as a medicine in emergency medicine.
wichtigste: Adenosine is made of the building blocks adenine and ribose.
It arises in cells mainly when ATP is broken down.
Caffeine keeps you awake because it blocks adenosine receptors.
In the brain, caffeine acts mainly at the receptors A1 and A2A.
Alexander Borbély of the University of Zurich developed the two-process model of sleep.
Process S stands for the homeostatic sleep pressure.
In emergency medicine, adenosine ends certain forms of racing heart.

abschnitte.text: Adenosine is what is called a **nucleoside**. It is made of the base **adenine** and the sugar **ribose**. If three phosphate groups hang on adenosine, **ATP** arises, the most important energy carrier of cells. When cells use a lot of energy, ATP is broken down step by step, and adenosine arises in the process. Outside cells it acts as a signalling substance and binds to various **adenosine receptors**.

In the brain, adenosine has a calming effect. According to the present view, it increases over the course of a long day awake and so contributes to our becoming tired. The researcher **Alexander Borbély** of the **University of Zurich** developed the **two-process model** of sleep regulation. **Process S** describes the **homeostatic sleep pressure**: the longer you are awake, the greater it becomes, and in sleep it is broken down again. **Process C** is the internal clock, which varies with the daily rhythm.

How strong the sleep pressure is can be seen in the **sleep EEG**, that is, in the recording of brain waves. The marker is the **activity of slow waves** in deep sleep. After a night without sleep, these slow waves are especially strong the next night. In the course of the night they then decrease, because the sleep pressure falls.

**Caffeine** looks chemically similar to adenosine. It sits on the **adenosine receptors**, mainly on the types **A1** and **A2A**, and **blocks** them without activating them. The calming signal then does not arrive, and you feel more awake. In healthy adults, the **half-life** of caffeine is around **5 hours**. After this time only half has been broken down, which is why a coffee in the evening can disturb sleep.

In emergency medicine, adenosine is quickly **injected into a vein** to end **certain forms of racing heart**. It briefly slows the conduction in the AV node of the heart. In this way a circling electrical impulse can be interrupted, and the heart finds its way back to its normal beat. The effect lasts only a very short time, because adenosine is broken down in the blood within seconds.

gewusst: The two-process model from Zurich has been used in sleep research all over the world since the 1980s.
Caffeine acts much longer in some people than in others, because the liver breaks it down at different speeds.

teile.einleitung: ADHD is the abbreviation for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. People with ADHD find it hard to stay attentive, to sit still or to hold back spontaneous actions. ADHD is not a matter of laziness, but has to do with how the brain works.
wichtigste: The three core symptoms are inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity.
The form without marked hyperactivity is called ADD in everyday speech.
According to DSM-5, the first symptoms appear before the age of 12.
The greatest influence on its development is genetic predisposition.
The messenger substances dopamine and noradrenaline are the focus of research.
A common active substance is methylphenidate, first made in Basel.
In many adults the symptoms persist.

abschnitte.text: Experts describe three **core symptoms**. In **inattention**, thoughts wander easily, tasks are left undone, and things are forgotten. **Hyperactivity** means great physical restlessness, for example constant fidgeting. **Impulsivity** means that you act or speak before you have thought. Not all those affected have all three features equally strongly. If the marked hyperactivity is missing, people speak in everyday language of **ADD**.

According to present knowledge, **genetic predisposition** has the greatest influence, and ADHD therefore occurs more often in some families. Research looks especially at the messenger substances **dopamine** and **noradrenaline**, which pass on signals in the brain. A diagnosis is made by specialists after detailed conversations and tests. According to the **DSM-5** manual, the first symptoms must have appeared before the age of 12 and occur in several areas of life, for example at school and at home.

Treatment often includes counselling, behavioural therapy and support at school, for example fixed routines and short breaks. The active substance **methylphenidate**, known under the name Ritalin, is also often used. It was first made in 1944 at the chemical company **Ciba in Basel**. Whether and for how long a medicine makes sense is decided by doctors together with the family.

In the past people thought ADHD was only a childhood illness. Today we know that the **symptoms often persist**, even if the restlessness in adulthood often shows itself more as inner restlessness. Many people with ADHD learn with time to cope well with it. Some also describe strengths such as plenty of energy, enthusiasm and a wealth of ideas.

The Frankfurt doctor **Heinrich Hoffmann** wrote the children's book “Struwwelpeter” in 1845. In it appears **Fidgety Philip**, a boy who cannot sit still at the table and finally tips over together with the tablecloth. The figure is often seen as an early picture of behaviour that recalls ADHD. A doctor at that time, however, could not yet make such a diagnosis.

gewusst: The name Ritalin goes back to Rita, the wife of the chemist who first made methylphenidate in Basel.
The German expression “Zappelphilipp”, meaning fidgety Philip, is still used for restless children.

teile.einleitung: Wild guinea pigs are the wild-living cavies of South America. People bred the domestic guinea pig from them thousands of years ago. Wild guinea pigs are smaller, slimmer and much shyer than their tame relatives.
wichtigste: The wild guinea pig is the wild-living ancestor of the domestic guinea pig.
It comes from South America.
Its fur is usually grey-brown, well camouflaged.
It eats grasses and herbs.
The young are born well developed.
In the Andes, guinea pigs were kept thousands of years ago.

abschnitte.text: Wild guinea pigs are about 20 to 30 centimetres long and have no visible tail. They usually weigh between 400 and 700 grams, less than many domestic guinea pigs. Their fur is grey-brown to olive-brown and well camouflaged. Bright colours and long hair are found only in bred animals.

Wild guinea pigs live in **South America**, from Colombia and Venezuela as far as Argentina. They inhabit grassland, woodland edges, swamps and the high plateaus of the **Andes**. They mostly do not dig burrows of their own, but use dense plants and trampled paths as hiding places. They are most active at dusk.

They eat grasses, herbs and leaves. Like domestic guinea pigs, they cannot make **vitamin C** themselves and have to take it in with their food. They live in small groups and communicate with squeaks and whistles. Enemies are birds of prey, owls, snakes and wild cats.

After a long pregnancy of about two months, usually two to three young are born. They are **precocial**, so they already have fur and open eyes and can run at once. After only a few days they eat plants. At about two months old they can breed themselves.

In the Andes, people tamed guinea pigs about 5,000 to 7,000 years ago, as a supply of meat. The original form is thought to be mainly the **montane guinea pig**, a wild species from the Andes. In Peru, guinea pigs are eaten to this day and are called “cuy” there. They came to Europe in the 16th century with Spanish sailors. In Switzerland you may keep guinea pigs only in pairs or in groups.

begriffe.erklaerung: Taming and breeding a wild animal into a domestic animal.
Young animals that are born already well developed and can run at once.
A long mountain chain on the west coast of South America.
A colour that makes an animal hard to see in its surroundings.

gewusst: Guinea pigs are not pigs and do not live in the sea, and the German name Meerschweinchen, meaning little sea pig, probably comes from their squeaking and the journey over the sea to Europe.
Young guinea pigs can run about already on the first day of life.

teile.einleitung: Anaphylaxis is a very severe allergic reaction that affects the whole body. It usually develops within minutes and can be life-threatening. Anyone who knows the signs can help quickly.
wichtigste: In children, food is the most common trigger of anaphylaxis.
It usually develops within minutes.
Dangerous signs are difficulty breathing and a tight throat.
In anaphylactic shock, blood pressure falls sharply.
The most important emergency medicine is adrenaline.
Afterwards the person must go to hospital, because the reaction can come back hours later.
In Switzerland, you call 144 in an emergency.

abschnitte.text: In an allergy, the defence system reacts far too strongly to a substance that is actually harmless. In **anaphylaxis** this happens in the whole body. In children, **foods** are the most common triggers, for example peanuts, nuts, milk or egg. In adults, **insect stings** from bees or wasps and **medicines** also play a big part. Anaphylaxis is especially dangerous in people with **poorly controlled asthma**.

The reaction usually starts **within minutes**. Often the skin shows it first: it turns red and comes up in **itchy wheals**, as after touching stinging nettles. There can also be tummy ache, nausea and vomiting. It becomes dangerous with **difficulty breathing**, wheezing and a **tight throat**. In **anaphylactic shock**, **blood pressure** falls sharply, and you can lose consciousness.

People who have a known severe allergy often carry an **adrenaline auto-injector**. You press this pen firmly against the outer side of the thigh. At the same time, you call the ambulance on **144**. You stay with the person and watch their breathing and consciousness. If the adrenaline does not help enough, a second dose may be needed after a few minutes.

How you position the person depends on their symptoms. If they mainly have **circulation problems** but are breathing well, you lay them **flat and raise their legs**. If they mainly suffer from **difficulty breathing** and are conscious, you let them **sit** or put them with the **upper body raised**. This makes breathing easier. An unconscious person who is breathing normally is put in the recovery position.

Even if the person is feeling better again, they must go to **hospital**. The reaction can **come back hours later**. Doctors often divide the severity of anaphylaxis into four grades according to **Ring and Messmer**. Grade I mainly affects the skin; the highest, **grade IV**, means **breathing or circulation has stopped**. After anaphylaxis, an allergy specialist works out the trigger exactly.

gewusst: Adrenaline is a hormone made by the body that narrows the blood vessels and widens the airways.
In an insect venom allergy, treatment over several years with small amounts of venom can make the body less sensitive.

teile.einleitung: Zurich Zoo is one of the biggest and best-known zoos in Switzerland. It lies on the Zürichberg and shows animals in near-natural enclosures that re-create whole habitats, from the rainforest of Madagascar to the African savanna. Here you can also see rhinos.
wichtigste: Zurich Zoo was opened in 1929.
It lies on the Zürichberg in the city of Zurich.
At the end of 2023 about 350 species of animal lived there.
Every year over a million visitors come.
In the Lewa Savanna live white rhinos, giraffes and zebras.
The Masoala Hall shows a rainforest from Madagascar.
The zoo supports nature conservation projects in the animals' countries of origin.

abschnitte.text: **Zurich Zoo** lies on the Zürichberg in the east of the city of Zurich and is easy to reach by tram. It was opened on 7 September 1929. Today it is about 27 hectares in size, which is almost 40 football pitches. At the end of 2023 about 350 species with more than 6,000 animals lived there.

In 2003 the **Masoala Hall** opened, a huge glasshouse with a real rainforest. It recreates the Masoala National Park in Madagascar. In it live lemurs, chameleons, fruit bats, birds and tortoises among tropical plants. It is always warm and damp there, as in the tropics.

The **Lewa Savanna** was completed in 2020 and is named after a protected area in Kenya. There **white rhinos**, reticulated giraffes, zebras, antelopes and ostriches live together in one large enclosure. Anyone who wants to see rhinos in Switzerland will find them here. In the past, black rhinos also lived in Zurich Zoo.

In 2014 the **Kaeng Krachan Elephant Park** opened, with a large house and a wooden roof that looks like a leaf from the air. Asian elephants live there in a herd. In the Australia enclosure you can watch koalas, kangaroos and wombats. Lions, tigers, snow leopards, penguins and great apes also live in the zoo.

Modern zoos such as Zurich Zoo do not want only to show animals, but also to protect nature. The zoo supports, for example, the Masoala National Park in Madagascar and the Lewa conservancy in Kenya. It takes part in **breeding programmes** for endangered animal species. With guided tours and offers for schools, it explains to children and adults why protecting species is important.

begriffe.erklaerung: A park in which wild animals are kept and shown.
Cooperation between zoos to breed rare animal species in a healthy way.
A grassy landscape with single trees, for example in Africa.
A dense forest in the tropics with a great deal of rain.

gewusst: In the Masoala Hall, many animals live free, without bars, among the visitors.
Zurich Zoo is among the most visited leisure destinations in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The kestrel is the most common falcon in Switzerland and a small, elegant bird of prey. You can easily recognise it by the way it “stands” in the air in one spot and hovers when hunting. It often lives near people and likes to nest on church towers, barns and in nest boxes.
wichtigste: The kestrel is a small falcon with a reddish brown back spotted with dark.
Typical of it is hovering flight, in which it hangs in one place in the air.
From pylons and posts it watches for mice in the grass nearby.
Besides mice, it occasionally eats small birds, insects and lizards.
Its legs and feet are yellow, and the claws are sharp and curved.
Both parents take part in looking after the young.
In Switzerland it is fairly common and is currently not regarded as badly endangered.

abschnitte.text: The kestrel is about 31 to 37 centimetres long and has a wingspan of around 70 to 80 centimetres. The male has a **grey head** and a grey tail with a black band at the end, and the back is reddish brown with dark spots. The female is browner overall and more strongly barred. Young kestrels are more plainly coloured and look more like the female. Legs and feet are yellow, and the **claws** are sharp and curved for holding prey.

The kestrel lives in open landscapes with meadows, fields and pastures, where it can hunt mice. It is found in almost all of Europe, Asia and Africa. Very often it nests in **towns and villages**, on church towers, tall buildings and bridges, which is also where its German name, Turmfalke or “tower falcon”, comes from. In Switzerland you can see it from the Central Plateau up to over 2000 metres in the Alps.

Its main prey is **field voles** and other small rodents. It hunts from a perch, such as a pylon, or in **hovering flight**: it beats its wings quickly and holds its head quite still over one spot. When it spots a mouse, it dives down and grabs it with its claws. In addition it occasionally eats small birds, insects such as grasshoppers, and lizards.

The kestrel does not build a nest of its own, but uses wall niches, rock ledges, old crows' nests or **nest boxes**. The female usually lays 4 to 6 eggs and sits on them for about a month. The male brings food during this time, and later both parents look after the young. Shortly before they fly for the first time, the young birds practise flapping their wings at the edge of the nest. At about a month old they are ready to fly.

The kestrel is fairly common in Switzerland and is currently not regarded as badly endangered. Problems are the disappearance of meadows rich in species and a lack of nesting places on modern buildings. Many people therefore put up special **nest boxes** on barns, silos and houses. Nature conservation societies and the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach support such projects.

In the past the kestrel was regarded in **falconry** as a falcon for beginners, because it was easier to train. For hunting larger game, however, it was too small. Today, because of its hovering flight, it is one of the best-known birds of prey of all. Even children can easily watch it from the roadside on a car journey.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of flight in which a bird stays in one spot in the air with quick wingbeats.
A bird that grabs its prey with the claws of its feet.
A raised seat from which a bird looks out for prey.
When a young bird can fly and leaves the nest.

gewusst: Kestrels can see ultraviolet light and so can spot the urine trails of mice.
A kestrel needs about four to eight mice a day.
Some kestrels nest in the middle of big cities such as Zurich or Basel.

teile.einleitung: Goat's cheese is cheese that is made from goat's milk. It comes as soft fresh cheese, as soft cheese with a white rind or as hard, matured cheese. It has a typical, slightly spicy taste that some people love and others find takes getting used to.
wichtigste: Goat's cheese is made from goat's milk.
In France it is called chèvre, which simply means goat.
It is usually very white, because goat's milk contains hardly any yellow pigment.
Its typical taste comes from certain fatty acids in the milk.
There are fresh cheese, soft cheese and hard cheese from goat's milk.
In Switzerland too, many goat's cheeses are made, especially in Ticino and in the mountains.
For goat's cheese, as for other cheese, you need rennet or lactic acid bacteria.

abschnitte.text: **Goat's cheese** is any cheese that is made wholly or mostly from goat's milk. The milk is curdled with **rennet** or lactic acid bacteria, so that solid parts, the curd, separate from the liquid **whey**. From the curd the cheese is formed. Depending on the kind, it is eaten fresh or matured for weeks to months.

Cow's milk contains the yellow pigment **beta-carotene**, which colours cheese and butter yellowish. Goats turn this substance almost completely into vitamin A. That is why goat's milk and goat's cheese are almost snow white. In long-matured goat's cheese, however, the rind becomes darker.

Goat's milk contains more of certain short **fatty acids** than cow's milk. They give the cheese its typically spicy, sometimes slightly sour taste. Some of these fatty acids even carry the Latin name of the goat, Capra, in their name, for example caproic acid. Young fresh cheese tastes mild, and matured cheese clearly stronger.

France is famous for goat's cheeses such as Sainte-Maure, Crottin de Chavignol or Valençay. Some kinds are rolled in wood ash, which forms a grey layer. In Greece, **feta** often contains a little goat's milk as well as sheep's milk. In Switzerland there are, for example, Ticino **formaggini** and many alpine cheeses made from goat's milk.

Fresh goat's cheese tastes good on bread, in salad or with honey and nuts. Baked warm, it is a popular starter. Many cooks combine it with figs, red cabbage or beetroot. Goat's cheese is also gladly used on pizza or in quiches.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance from the stomach of young calves or from micro-organisms that makes milk curdle.
The greenish yellow liquid that is left over in cheese making.
Storage time in which cheese develops taste and firmness.
The French word for goat and goat's cheese.

gewusst: For one small Crottin de Chavignol you need only about a quarter of a litre of milk.
Some goat's cheeses are covered with wood ash, which in the past was meant to protect the rind.

teile.einleitung: Catfish are a huge group of fish with long barbels at the mouth that remind you of a cat's whiskers. There are over 3,000 species, from tiny aquarium fish to giants. The European catfish is the biggest freshwater fish in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Catfish make up an order of bony fish with over 3,000 species.
The barbels at the mouth are typical.
Most catfish have no scales.
The armoured catfish is a close relative of the catfish.
The European catfish can grow to over 2 metres long.
Many catfish are active at night.
Catfish live almost everywhere in the world, mainly in fresh water.

abschnitte.text: Catfish have a long body and a broad, flat head. At the mouth they carry **barbels**, which are long threads for feeling and tasting. Most catfish have no scales, but a slimy skin. Some groups, such as the **armoured catfish**, instead wear bony plates like armour.

Worldwide there are over 3,000 species of catfish, which makes them one of the richest-in-species groups of fish. They live on all continents except Antarctica. Especially many species are found in South America, for example in the Amazon. Most live in **fresh water**, and some also in the sea.

The **European catfish**, also called the wels, is the biggest freshwater fish in Europe. It can grow to over 2.5 metres long and weigh over 100 kilograms. In Switzerland it lives, for example, in Lake Murten, Lake Biel, Lake Neuchâtel and in the Rhine. Because the waters are getting warmer, it is spreading in Switzerland.

Many catfish are **nocturnal** and hide on the bottom by day. With their barbels they find food even in cloudy water. Large catfish eat fish, frogs, crayfish and sometimes even waterbirds. Small species such as armoured catfish search the bottom for worms and scraps of food.

Armoured catfish and suckermouth catfish are popular aquarium fish. They root about in the sand and eat scraps that other fish leave lying. Armoured catfish like to live in groups. Some species of catfish can even swallow air at the surface of the water when there is little oxygen in the water.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thread-like growths at the mouth with which fish feel and taste.
Another name for the European catfish.
A small South American catfish with bony plates on its body.
An animal that is out and about at night and rests by day.

gewusst: Catfish have taste buds all over their skin and so taste, you might say, with the whole body.
The electric catfish from Africa can deliver electric shocks.

teile.einleitung: The ABC scheme helps in first aid to check the most important things in the right order. The three letters stand for airway, breathing and circulation. In this way you first deal with what is most dangerous.
wichtigste: Before anything else you pay attention to your own safety.
Swiss first aid courses sum up the procedure as “Look, Think, Act”.
A stands for airway, B for breathing, C for circulation.
The terms come from English: Airway, Breathing, Circulation.
The greatest danger to life is dealt with first.
At B you check whether the person is breathing normally.
Rescue services often use the extended ABCDE scheme.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who comes to the scene of an accident is often agitated. Swiss first aid courses therefore set three simple steps: **Look, Think, Act**. First you look at the situation. Then you think: are there dangers for yourself, such as traffic, fire or electricity? Your **own safety** always comes first, because an injured helper can help no one any more. After that you act: secure the accident site, get help, for example by the emergency number **144**, and give first aid.

The letters come from **English**. **A** stands for “Airway”, that is, the **airway**. **B** stands for “Breathing”, the **breathing**. **C** stands for “Circulation”, the **circulation**. The order is no accident: without a clear airway nobody can breathe, and without breathing the blood gets no oxygen. That is why the greatest danger to life is dealt with first.

abschnitte.titel: A and B: airway and breathing
abschnitte.text: If a person does not speak and does not react, their airway may be blocked, for example because the tongue falls back. You clear it by **tilting the head carefully back** and lifting the chin. Then at B you check whether the person is **breathing normally**: you look to see whether the chest rises, and listen and feel for the breath, but only for a few seconds. If they are breathing normally, they are put into the recovery position.

C is about the **circulation**, that is, whether the blood is flowing through the body. If the person is not breathing normally, **chest compressions** are needed, and a **defibrillator** if one is available. This device explains with a voice exactly what is to be done. Circulation also includes stopping heavy bleeding, for example with pressure on the wound.

Rescue services and hospitals often use an extension, the **ABCDE scheme**. The D stands for “Disability”, in which it is checked how awake the person is and whether the nervous system is working well. The E stands for “Exposure” or “Environment”: the whole body is examined for further injuries and the person is protected from the cold.

gewusst: Children too can do a lot at the scene of an accident: getting help and calling 144 is already very important.
A defibrillator is built so that even lay people without training can use it.

teile.einleitung: A bird bath is a shallow place with water in a garden or on a balcony where birds can drink and bathe. Especially in hot summers and in towns, birds often find hardly any open water. With a simple dish, any child can help the birds and watch them from close up at the same time.
wichtigste: A bird bath offers birds water to drink and bathe in.
Great tits and many other birds like to take a bird bath in summer to keep clean.
The bath should be shallow so that no bird drowns.
The water has to be changed often and the dish cleaned regularly.
A good place is one with a clear view, so that cats cannot sneak up.
Insects such as bees and animals such as hedgehogs also drink at watering places.
In winter ice-free water helps, but you must never add salt or antifreeze.

abschnitte.text: A bird bath is a container of water that people put out for wild birds. It can be a dish of clay or stone that you buy, but also an upturned **flowerpot saucer**. In the past there were puddles, streams and pools everywhere. Today many soils in towns are covered with asphalt, and rainwater flows quickly into the drains.

Birds bathe to keep their **plumage** clean and healthy. Great tits, blackbirds and sparrows hop into the water, dip their bellies in and shake their wings. Afterwards they clean every feather with the beak. Many birds spread oil from the **preen gland** as they do so, so that the feathers stay water-repellent.

The dish should be only a few centimetres deep at the edge and slope gently towards the middle. A rough bottom or a few flat stones give the birds a good grip. It is best if the bath stands raised on a base or hangs from a branch. A distance of about two metres from dense bushes protects against **cats**, which could hide there.

At a dirty bath, diseases such as **trichomonads** or salmonella can spread from bird to bird. That is why it is best to change the water daily in summer. The dish is scrubbed regularly with hot water and a brush. Washing-up liquid or cleaning products do not belong in a bird bath.

A bath does not help only birds. Bees, bumblebees and butterflies also need water and like to land on a stone that sticks out of the water. A shallow dish on the ground is also used by hedgehogs at night. In this way the garden becomes a small habitat for many animals.

At a bird bath you can watch birds very well. With an identification book or an app, you can tell great tit, blue tit, robin and chaffinch apart. Anyone who sits quietly behind a window often sees many different species in a single day. Some families note down their observations and report them in bird counts.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the feathers of a bird together.
A gland above the tail that makes oil for oiling the feathers.
Tiny germs that can spread among birds at dirty watering places.
The daily cleaning and arranging of the feathers with the beak.

gewusst: Some birds such as sparrows take not only water baths but also dust baths in dry sand.
Blackbirds sometimes bathe so thoroughly that afterwards they can hardly fly properly and first have to dry off.

teile.einleitung: Winter rest is a way of getting through the winter in which animals sleep a lot, but not as deeply as in hibernation. Their body temperature falls only slightly. Well-known examples are the brown bear, the badger and the squirrel.
wichtigste: In winter rest, animals sleep for a long time but do not fall into torpor.
The body temperature falls only slightly.
The brown bear's long winter sleep is really a winter rest.
The bear's heart rate falls markedly.
Animals in winter rest wake up fairly often.
Squirrels and badgers take a winter rest.
The animals live from fat reserves or stores.

abschnitte.text: In winter there is little food, and it is cold. Some animals therefore sleep through a large part of the cold time. In **winter rest** they sleep for a long time, but their body temperature falls by only a few degrees. They can therefore wake up quickly and move about. In **hibernation**, by contrast, the temperature falls very sharply.

The **brown bear** withdraws in late autumn into a cave or a pit it has dug itself. Its heart rate falls markedly, to only about 10 to 20 beats per minute. The body temperature, however, falls by only a few degrees. That is why its long sleep is correctly called winter rest. For months it does not eat, drink or need the toilet, but lives from its fat.

Female bears give birth to their cubs during the winter rest in January or February. The cubs are tiny, weighing only about 300 to 500 grams. They drink their mother's milk in the den and grow fast. In spring they leave the den with their mother.

The **badger** also takes a winter rest in its sett and eats up a layer of fat beforehand. The **squirrel** sleeps in its drey, but wakes up again and again. Then it fetches nuts from its hiding places laid out in autumn. The raccoon and the beaver also spend the winter more quietly.

In Switzerland, badgers and squirrels take a winter rest every winter. The few brown bears that migrate into Switzerland from Italy also withdraw in winter. If you disturb animals in winter rest, they use up valuable energy. That is why there are **wildlife quiet zones** in the mountains that you should not enter in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long sleep in winter in which the body temperature falls only a little.
The number of heartbeats per minute.
A store of fat in the body on which an animal lives in times of need.
The round nest of the squirrel.
An area that protects wild animals from disturbance in winter.

gewusst: A brown bear can lose a quarter to a third of its weight during the winter rest.
Squirrels by no means find all their nuts again, and so new trees grow from forgotten hiding places.

teile.einleitung: A truffle pig is a specially trained domestic pig that finds hidden truffle fungi in the ground. Truffles grow underground on tree roots and are very expensive edible fungi. Pigs can smell them with their fine noses even through the soil.
wichtigste: Truffle pigs are used to find hidden truffle fungi in the ground.
Truffles grow underground in partnership with trees such as oaks and hazel bushes.
The scent of ripe truffles resembles a scent signal given off by boars, so it is mainly sows that like to search for them.
One problem is that the pigs most like to eat the truffles themselves.
Today dogs are mostly used for the search.
In Italy, truffle hunting with pigs has been banned since 1985.
Truffles also grow in Switzerland, for example the Burgundy truffle.

abschnitte.text: A truffle pig is not a breed of its own, but a **domestic pig** that has been trained to search. Pigs have an excellent **sense of smell** and by nature root around in the ground with their snouts. People have used these abilities for centuries. Searching with pigs was especially well known in France, for example in the Périgord.

**Truffles** are fungi whose fruiting bodies grow underground, mostly 5 to 30 centimetres deep. They live in partnership with tree roots, which is called **mycorrhiza**. Well-known kinds are the black Périgord truffle and the white Alba truffle from Italy. Because they are so rare and smell so strongly, they often cost several thousand francs per kilogram.

Ripe truffles give off a strong scent so that animals dig them up and so spread their spores. A substance in the scent of truffles recalls a **scent signal** from male pigs. That is why female pigs in particular are very eager in the search. They can smell truffles even through several centimetres of soil.

Pigs are big and heavy and hard to stop once they have found a truffle. Often they eat the valuable fungus straight away. They also churn up the forest floor a lot and damage the web of fungal threads. That is why today it is mostly trained **truffle dogs** that are used, which only point out the find.

In Switzerland mainly the **Burgundy truffle** grows, for example in woods in the Jura, on the Central Plateau and in western Switzerland. In some cantons you need a permit for collecting, and there are limits on amounts. In this country the search is done almost only with dogs. Some municipalities even hold truffle markets in autumn.

begriffe.erklaerung: An expensive, strongly scented fungus that grows underground.
A partnership between fungi and tree roots from which both benefit.
The ability to notice scents.
Tiny particles from which new fungi grow.

gewusst: A single large white truffle has been sold at auction for more than 100 000 euros.
Pigs have such a good sense of smell that they can keep up with sniffer dogs.
Wild boar also like to dig for truffles in the forest.

teile.einleitung: Adult stem cells are special cells in the bodies of children and adults. They can renew themselves and form new, specialised cells. In this way they constantly replace cells that are worn out or injured, for example in the blood, the gut or the skin.
wichtigste: Every stem cell can renew itself and form specialised cells.
Adult stem cells usually form only cells of their own tissue.
Haematopoietic stem cells constantly replace all blood cells.
Most blood-forming stem cells lie in the red bone marrow.
Bone, cartilage and fat cells arise from mesenchymal stem cells.
The lining of the gut is renewed by stem cells at the base of the intestinal crypts.
For decades leukaemia has been treated with stem cell transplants.

abschnitte.text: Most cells in the body are **specialised**: a skin cell stays a skin cell, a muscle cell a muscle cell. **Stem cells**, on the other hand, have two special properties. They can **renew themselves** by dividing, so there are always stem cells left over. And they can **form specialised cells**. Adult stem cells usually form **only cells of their own tissue**, for example only blood cells or only gut cells.

Blood cells do not live long, red blood cells for example about four months. That is why the body makes huge numbers of new ones every day. This is done by the **haematopoietic stem cells**, the blood-forming stem cells. In adults they sit mainly in the **red bone marrow**, for example in the pelvis and the breastbone. From them arise red and white blood cells as well as platelets.

From **mesenchymal stem cells**, **bone, cartilage and fat cells** can arise. The lining of the gut is renewed every few days. The stem cells needed for this lie protected **at the base of the intestinal crypts**, small hollows in the gut wall. Skin and hair roots also have their own stem cells. For a stem cell to keep its state, it needs a special surrounding, the **stem cell niche**. There it receives signals from neighbouring cells.

For decades **leukaemia**, a form of blood cancer, has been treated with the **transplantation of blood-forming stem cells**. The sick person receives healthy stem cells, which build up a new blood system. In the past they were usually taken directly from the bone marrow. Today, in most donors they are obtained **from the blood**: first the donors are given a **growth factor** for a few days, which lures many stem cells into the blood. Then a machine filters them out.

Anyone who wants to donate stem cells can have themselves entered in a **register**. In Switzerland this register is kept by Blutspende SRK Schweiz. Finding a suitable donor is difficult, because certain tissue features have to match. That is why registers all over the world work together.

gewusst: The body of an adult makes several million new red blood cells every second.
For the first successful bone marrow transplants, E. Donnall Thomas received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1990.

teile.einleitung: True bugs are a large group of insects that all have a pointed piercing beak. Some suck plant sap, others hunt small animals, and some even run over the water.
wichtigste: True bugs are insects with six legs and a piercing beak for stabbing and sucking.
There are about 40 000 known species of bug worldwide.
Their front wings are half hard and half membranous.
Bugs develop without a pupal stage, and the larvae already look similar to the adults.
Many bugs can give off an unpleasant smell when in danger.
There are bugs on land and in water, for example the pond skater.
Most bugs are harmless to people.

abschnitte.text: Like all insects, bugs have six legs and a body made of a head, thorax and abdomen. Typical is the **piercing beak**, which at rest is folded back under the body. The front wings are called **hemelytra**, because they are hard at the front and thin and transparent at the back. This is also where the scientific name Heteroptera comes from, which means roughly “different wings”. Many species are built flat and have a triangular little shield on the back.

Most bugs pierce plants and suck their sap. Others are **predators** and suck out insects, caterpillars or larvae. The pond skater, for example, pierces insects that have fallen on the surface of the water. Only a few species such as the **bed bug** suck the blood of people or animals.

Bugs lay eggs, often in small groups on leaves or stems. Larvae hatch from the eggs that already look like small bugs but do not yet have wings. They usually moult five times and get bigger as they do so. Because there is no pupal stage, this is called **incomplete metamorphosis**. In the pond skater, the young look like small adults without wings.

Some bugs have conquered the water. The **pond skater** glides over the surface of ponds on its long legs. The **backswimmer** swims belly upwards and rows with its long hind legs. The water scorpion lurks on the bottom and breathes through a long breathing tube at the rear end.

Several hundred species of bug live in Switzerland. Very well known is the red and black **firebug**, which in spring often sits in groups on lime tree trunks. The green shield bug is common in gardens. Since the 2000s, the **brown marmorated stink bug**, introduced from East Asia, has been spreading and causes damage to fruit and vegetables.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mouthpart like a drinking straw with pointed bristles, with which bugs pierce and suck.
The front wings of bugs, which are hard at the front and membranous at the back.
Development from the egg through larvae to the adult animal without a pupa.
A gland from which many bugs give off a foul-smelling fluid when in danger.

gewusst: Not every crawling creature that is called a bug in everyday speech is really a true bug: beetles and ticks, for example, do not belong.
Some sea skaters live on the open ocean, far from any coast.
In many bugs you can smell the defensive fluid on your fingers for a long time after touching them.

teile.einleitung: Incomplete metamorphosis is one way in which some insects develop from the egg to the adult animal. There is no pupal stage: the larva already looks similar to the finished animal and gets bigger with every moult. Grasshoppers, dragonflies, aphids and bugs develop in this way.
wichtigste: In incomplete metamorphosis there is no pupal stage.
Development goes in three stages: egg, larva and adult animal.
The larvae are often called nymphs, and they already resemble the parents.
The larvae grow by moulting several times.
Grasshoppers, dragonflies, aphids, bugs and cockroaches go through an incomplete metamorphosis.
Dragonfly larvae live in the water and have a catching mask.
In complete metamorphosis, for example in the butterfly, there is on the other hand a pupa.

abschnitte.text: Experts also call incomplete metamorphosis **hemimetaboly**. A **larva** hatches from the egg that already looks like the adult insect but does not yet have finished wings. It eats, grows and moults several times. After the last moult the insect is adult and can reproduce. There is no pupa.

Insects have a hard **outer skeleton** that does not grow with them. That is why they have to shed it when they get bigger. With every moult the wing buds on the back get a little bigger. A grasshopper larva usually moults four to six times. The shed skin is called an **exuvia**.

In **complete metamorphosis** the larva looks quite different from the adult animal, like a caterpillar and a butterfly. In between lies a pupa, in which the body is completely rebuilt. Beetles, bees, flies and butterflies develop in this way. In incomplete metamorphosis this rebuilding is missing, and the animal changes only step by step.

In the **grasshopper**, the larvae look like small grasshoppers without wings. **Dragonflies** have no pupal phase, but their larvae live for years in the water and look different from the flying dragonflies. Aphids also develop from larva to adult animal without a pupa. Bugs, cockroaches, termites and earwigs belong here as well.

The kind of metamorphosis helps researchers to sort **insects** into groups. Incomplete metamorphosis is regarded as the older form in evolutionary history. Anyone who knows how an insect develops also understands where its larvae live. This is important, for example, in protecting dragonflies, which need clean water.

begriffe.erklaerung: The young form of an animal, which can look different from the adult animal.
The larva of an insect with incomplete metamorphosis.
Shedding the old skin or casing that has become too small.
A resting stage in which a larva rebuilds itself into the adult insect.

gewusst: Dragonfly larvae can live in the water for several years, while the flying dragonfly often lives only a few weeks.
In summer aphids can have offspring without males, and they give birth to live young instead of laying eggs.
