The empty larval casings of dragonflies are often found on reed stems at the bank.

teile.einleitung: The sand lizard is a sturdy lizard that lives on sunny woodland edges, banks and in near-natural gardens. Its scientific name is Lacerta agilis, which means nimble lizard. In Switzerland it is protected and an example of how important warm, varied habitats are.
wichtigste: The sand lizard is called Lacerta agilis scientifically.
Including the tail, it grows about 18 to 24 centimetres long.
At the mating season the males have bright green flanks.
It lays eggs, from which the young hatch after about 6 to 8 weeks.
Besides warmth it needs hiding places such as piles of stones or dense plants.
Its enemies include birds of prey, snakes and cats.
In Switzerland the sand lizard is protected.

abschnitte.text: The **sand lizard** is stockier than other lizards and has a short, strong head. Including the tail it grows about 18 to 24 centimetres long. On the brown back it carries light lines and dark spots with white dots in the middle. At the mating season in spring, the flanks of the males glow bright **green**, while the females stay brownish.

Sand lizards love **sunny**, dry places such as railway embankments, woodland edges, dry meadows, vineyards and gardens. Besides warmth, **hiding places** such as piles of stones, piles of branches or dense vegetation are also important. Loose, sandy soil is needed for laying eggs. In Switzerland it lives mainly on the Central Plateau, in the Jura and at lower altitudes in the Alpine valleys.

As a **cold-blooded** animal, the sand lizard first has to warm up in the sun in the morning before it becomes properly active. Then it hunts insects, spiders, worms and small snails. With its good eyes it sees movement and snaps up quick as a flash. In autumn it withdraws to a frost-proof hiding place and stays in **winter torpor** until spring.

In spring the males fight over females and defend their territory against rivals. Around June the female usually lays 5 to 15 eggs in a small pit in loose, sunny soil. The sun incubates the eggs, and after about 6 to 8 weeks the young hatch. Unlike the common lizard, which gives birth to live young, the sand lizard therefore lays true **eggs**.

Enemies include birds of prey such as the kestrel, snakes such as the smooth snake, crows and house cats. In danger, the sand lizard usually flees quickly to a hiding place. If it cannot flee, it stays motionless or tries to bite. If it is grabbed by the tail, it can **shed** it and so escape, and it grows back shorter afterwards. If need be, it can even swim.

Like all reptiles, the sand lizard is legally **protected** in Switzerland. It has become rarer in recent decades because hedges, fallow land and piles of stones have disappeared. You can help it by making piles of stones, piles of branches and unmown corners in the garden. Many nature conservation projects create such small structures deliberately, which also benefits insects and other animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: The body temperature depends on the surroundings.
A resting state of cold-blooded animals in the cold winter.
An area that an animal defends against others of its kind.
A small habitat such as a pile of stones or branches.

gewusst: A shed lizard tail keeps twitching for a while and so distracts the enemy.
The German name Zauneidechse, meaning fence lizard, comes from the fact that it likes to live by fences and hedges.

teile.einleitung: The zander is a large predatory fish from the perch family and so closely related to the perch. It lives in lakes and slow-flowing rivers and hunts mainly at dusk. Its firm, white flesh is very popular with many people.
wichtigste: The zander is a predatory fish from the perch family.
It is closely related to the perch, the river perch.
Zander can grow to about a metre long.
They hunt mainly at dusk and in cloudy water.
Their eyes shine because they have a light-amplifying layer.
The males guard the nest with the eggs.
In Switzerland the zander lives today in several lakes, but it was introduced.

abschnitte.text: The **zander** (Sander lucioperca) has a long, slim body with a greenish grey back and dark cross bands. On the back it carries two dorsal fins, the front one with hard spines as in the perch. In the mouth it has pointed **canine teeth** with which it holds its prey. It usually grows 40 to 70 centimetres long, and large animals reach about a metre.

Zander have large, glassy-looking eyes. Behind the retina lies a reflecting layer, the **tapetum lucidum**, which makes better use of little light. That is why zander hunt especially well at dusk, at night and in cloudy water. They eat mainly smaller fish such as roach, bleak or young perch.

The zander likes larger, nutrient-rich lakes and slow-flowing rivers with somewhat cloudy water. Originally it lived in eastern Europe and in the area of the Baltic Sea. People took it to many countries, including **Switzerland**. Here it occurs, for example, in Lake Murten, Lake Biel and Lake Neuchâtel.

In spring, when the water is about 12 to 15 degrees warm, the zander spawn. The male cleans a spot on the bottom and builds a kind of **spawning pit**. The female lays thousands of sticky eggs there. The male guards the nest and fans fresh water over the eggs until the larvae hatch.

Zander is a prized **food fish** with firm, white and almost bone-free flesh. Many zander on Swiss plates come from abroad or from fish farms. Among anglers it is a popular catch. For the zander, as for other fish, closed seasons and minimum sizes apply.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fish that hunts other fish or animals.
A family of fish with spiny dorsal fins, which includes the perch and the zander.
Laying eggs, in fish.
A time when a species of fish may not be caught.

gewusst: In the past the zander was also called the pike perch, because it looks like a mixture of pike and perch.
Its eyes glow in the light of a torch, rather like cats' eyes.

teile.einleitung: The white-handed gibbon is a small ape from the rainforests of South-East Asia. It has white hands and feet, swings through the treetops on its long arms and sings loud duets with its partner.
wichtigste: The white-handed gibbon belongs to the gibbons, the small apes.
Its name comes from the white hands and feet.
Its range includes Thailand, Malaysia, Myanmar, Laos and the north of Sumatra.
It has no tail and very long arms.
It moves by swinging from branch to branch.
White-handed gibbons live in pairs and sing together in the morning.
The species is regarded as seriously endangered.

abschnitte.text: The white-handed gibbon grows to about 45 to 60 centimetres in height and weighs around 5 to 6 kilograms. Its fur is either light cream or dark brown to black. Typical are the **white hands and feet** and a white ring around the face. Like all apes, it has no tail.

The white-handed gibbon lives in tropical **rainforests** and mountain forests of South-East Asia. Its range includes Thailand, the Malay Peninsula, parts of Myanmar and Laos, and the north of Sumatra. It spends almost its whole life high up in the trees. It only rarely comes down to the ground.

Gibbons get about by **brachiation**: they swing on their long arms from branch to branch. In doing so they can make leaps several metres wide. Their hands are shaped like hooks, and the thumb is short. On branches they sometimes walk upright and hold their arms up for balance.

The white-handed gibbon eats mainly ripe **fruit**, and especially likes figs. Young leaves, flowers and insects are added. Because it passes the seeds of the fruit out again in its droppings, it helps to spread new trees in the forest. In this way it plays an important role for the rainforest.

White-handed gibbons live in small **family groups** made up of a pair and their young. Every morning the male and female sing a loud **duet** together that can be heard for kilometres. With the song they show other gibbons that the territory is taken. The female usually has a young one only every two to three years.

begriffe.erklaerung: Monkey-like animals without a tail, which include gibbons, orang-utans, gorillas and chimpanzees.
A way of moving in which an animal swings from branch to branch with its arms.
An area that an animal or a family defends against others.
Singing by two partners who take turns or sing together.

gewusst: In the white-handed gibbon the colour of the fur has nothing to do with sex, and in one family there can be light and dark animals.
Gibbons are among the fastest climbers of all mammals.
Gibbons are also called lesser apes, because they are much lighter than gorillas or orang-utans.

teile.einleitung: A pasture is an area of grass on which animals such as cows, sheep, goats or horses feed directly. Pastures shape the landscape of Switzerland, from the Central Plateau to the alpine pastures high in the mountains.
wichtigste: A pasture is grassland that is grazed by animals.
When a cow eats grass directly from the pasture, this is called grazing.
A meadow, by contrast, is mown to make hay or fodder.
Cows, sheep and goats are ruminants and can digest grass well.
In Switzerland, many animals spend the summer on alpine pastures.
Pastures provide a habitat for many plants, insects and birds.
Grazing animals are kept in the pasture with fences.

abschnitte.text: A pasture is an area covered with grass and herbs on which **farm animals** eat their food themselves. People also speak of **grassland**. A meadow, by contrast, is mown, and the fodder is brought to the animals in the barn. Many areas are mown and grazed in turn.

A cow wraps its tongue around the grass and tears it off, which is called **grazing**. Sheep and horses bite the grass off lower down, and goats also like to eat leaves and shrubs. Cows are **ruminants**: they first swallow the grass quickly and later chew it through again in peace. A dairy cow eats about 60 to 80 kilograms of fresh grass a day.

In summer, many cows, young cattle, sheep and goats are taken up to the **alp**. The festive climb up is called the Alpaufzug, and the return in autumn the Alpabzug. On the alp, the animals eat grasses and herbs, and their milk is used to make alpine cheese, for example. Grazing stops the areas from becoming overgrown with bushes and forest.

Pastures that are not fertilised too heavily are often very rich in species. Clover, ox-eye daisies, orchids and many other flowers grow there. In a **cowpat** live beetles and fly larvae, which in turn serve as food for birds. Plants that animals do not eat, such as the poisonous white false hellebore or thistles, spread strongly on some pastures.

So that the animals do not run away, pastures are fenced in, often with an **electric fence**. Walkers should keep their distance from cows with calves in pastures and keep dogs on a lead. Grazing is good for the health of the animals, because they move about and are out in the fresh air. In Switzerland there are support programmes for farmers whose animals regularly get to go outside.

begriffe.erklaerung: Land on which mainly grass grows, that is, meadows and pastures.
A plant eater such as a cow that chews its food twice.
A summer pasture in the mountains with huts for herders and animals.
A fence with a weak current that holds animals back with a small shock.

gewusst: A large part of the area of Switzerland consists of meadows, pastures and alps.
Cows spend many hours every day eating and chewing the cud.
On some pastures, sheep or goats help to keep nature reserves open.

teile.einleitung: The winter cluster is a dense ball of thousands of honey bees with which the bee colony gets through the winter. The bees warm each other inside it. In this way the colony survives frost and snow too.
wichtigste: In winter, honey bees form a winter cluster.
It is made of bees pressed closely together that warm each other.
The queen sits protected in the middle.
The bees make heat by shivering their flight muscles.
Outside and inside, the bees keep swapping places.
The honey store serves as food.
Winter bees live much longer than summer bees.

abschnitte.text: Honey bees do not hibernate. When it gets colder than about 10 degrees outside, they draw close together in the beehive. This produces a ball-shaped **winter cluster** between the combs. It is made of thousands of bees pressed closely together that warm each other. The **queen** sits protected in the middle.

The bees make heat by making their **flight muscles** shiver without moving the wings. This is similar to shivering in us. Inside the cluster it is clearly over 20 degrees warm. The bees at the edge form a dense covering like a coat and keep the warmth in.

The bees on the outside freeze more than those inside. That is why they keep swapping places. When it gets colder, the cluster moves closer together, and when it gets warmer, it loosens. In this way the colony survives even frost of minus 20 degrees and more.

For heating, the bees need energy from **honey**. The cluster moves slowly over the combs and eats the stores. Over the winter a colony needs about 10 to 20 kilograms of food. Because the beekeeper takes honey in summer, he usually feeds sugar water in late summer to make up for it.

The bees in winter are called **winter bees**. They hatch in late summer and live for several months, while a summer bee lives only a few weeks. In winter a colony has about 10,000 to 20,000 bees. On mild days they fly out briefly on a cleansing flight to empty their gut. In spring, when the first willows and hazels bloom, the winter cluster breaks up.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ball of bees pressed closely together that warm each other in winter.
A long-lived honey bee that brings the colony through the winter.
A short outing on a mild winter day to empty the gut.
Strong muscles in the thorax that move the wings.

gewusst: In winter, bees do not relieve themselves in the hive, but wait for weeks for a warm day.
Beekeepers can hear a faint buzzing with an ear to the hive and so check whether the colony is alive.

teile.einleitung: A weathercock is a weather vane in the shape of a cockerel that often sits on church towers. It turns with the wind and so shows where the wind is blowing from. The weathercock has been a well-known sign on churches in Europe for centuries, and in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: A weathercock is a weather vane in the shape of a cockerel.
You find it mainly on church towers.
It turns so that it shows the wind direction.
It is usually made of metal such as copper or sheet iron.
In Christianity the cockerel stands for watchfulness.
It recalls the story of Peter and the crowing cockerel.

abschnitte.text: The **weathercock** is a special form of the **weather vane**. It usually sits right at the top of the spire of a church tower, often above a ball. It is made of sheet metal, mostly copper or iron, and is sometimes gilded. Because it is mounted so that it can turn, it moves with every gust of wind.

The tail of the cockerel is broader than the head. That is why the wind pushes the tail away, and the head points in the direction the wind comes from. Under the cockerel there are often the **points of the compass** with the letters N, E, S and W. In this way, people in the past could read off the **wind direction** without an instrument.

The cockerel is an old sign of watchfulness, because in the morning it announces the day. In the Bible a cockerel crowed after Peter had denied Jesus three times. The cockerel on the church is therefore meant to recall remorse and watchfulness. Weathercocks have existed on church towers since the early Middle Ages.

In Switzerland it is mainly many **Reformed** churches that carry a cockerel on the tower. Catholic churches, by contrast, usually have a cross at the top. So in some areas you can tell from far away which denomination a church belongs to. This rule does not apply everywhere, however.

The wind direction helps to forecast the weather. In Switzerland a west wind often brings rain, and the bise from the north-east usually brings cool, dry weather. Today weather stations measure the wind with **wind vanes** and anemometers. The weathercock has nevertheless remained a popular symbol.

begriffe.erklaerung: A piece of sheet metal that can turn and shows the wind direction.
The point of the compass from which the wind blows.
An instrument that measures wind speed.
A branch of belief within a religion, for example Reformed or Catholic.

gewusst: Someone who often changes their mind is sometimes mockingly called a “weathercock”.
The weathercock points its head into the wind, not away from the wind.

teile.einleitung: Our senses adapt constantly to their surroundings. This adjustment of sensitivity to the strength of a stimulus is called adaptation. It explains why we can see again after a while in the dark, or soon no longer feel clothes on the skin.
wichtigste: Adaptation is the adjustment of sensitivity to the strength of the stimulus.
The pupillary reflex is the fastest adjustment of the eye to brightness.
In sunlight you are dazzled because the retina is still set to dark.
The Kohlrausch kink shows the change from cone vision to rod vision.
Many touch receptors adapt quickly.
Pain receptors hardly adapt, and that protects us.
After a long look at red, you see a greenish afterimage.

abschnitte.text: Our sense cells, the **receptors**, report stimuli to the brain. If a stimulus stays the same for a long time, the report becomes weaker. The senses set their **sensitivity** to the strength of the stimulus, and this is called **adaptation**. In this way there is room for something new: what matters is usually what changes, not what always stays the same. Without adaptation we would be constantly flooded by unchanging stimuli.

The eye can adapt to very different brightnesses. The fastest is the **pupillary reflex**: in bright light the pupil becomes narrower in fractions of a second. The adjustment of the **retina** takes much longer. If you come from a dark room into sunlight, you are **dazzled**, because the retina is still set to darkness. The other way round, **dark adaptation** takes up to half an hour until you see well in the dark.

In the retina there are two kinds of visual cell. The **cones** see colours and work in brightness. The **rods** are much more sensitive and make it possible to see at dusk. If you measure how sensitivity increases in the dark, the curve shows a kink after a few minutes. This **Kohlrausch kink** shows the **change from cone vision to rod vision**: the cones are used to the limit, and now the rods take over.

You hardly feel your clothes any more after a short time, because many **touch receptors adapt quickly**. The nose also gets used to things: the scent in a room is no longer smelled after a while, because the **sense of smell adapts**. Quite different are the **pain receptors**: they **hardly** adapt. This is a protective function, because pain is meant to warn us until we have removed the cause.

If you stare for a long time at a **red surface** and then look at a white wall, a **greenish afterimage** appears there. The visual cells that react especially to red are tired, that is, adapted. On the white surface, the signals of the other colours therefore briefly predominate. In this way you see roughly the **opposite colour**.

gewusst: After half an hour in the dark, the eye is many thousands of times more sensitive than in bright daylight.
If you step into a warm bath, the water feels less warm after a short time, although it stays just as warm.

teile.einleitung: Migratory fish are fish that travel back and forth between the sea and fresh water in the course of their lives. The best known is the salmon, which grows up in the sea and returns to spawn in the river where it hatched. The eel does exactly the opposite and swims from our rivers as far as the Atlantic in order to spawn.
wichtigste: Migratory fish travel between the sea and fresh water, like the salmon.
Fish that go from the sea into rivers to spawn are called anadromous.
Fish that go from fresh water into the sea to spawn are called catadromous migratory fish.
The salmon is anadromous, and the eel is catadromous.
The European eel spawns in the Sargasso Sea in the Atlantic.
In the past, salmon swam up the Rhine as far as Switzerland.
Dams and power stations block the way for many migratory fish.

abschnitte.text: Migratory fish are fish that change between **sea and fresh water** for breeding or finding food. Their bodies have to be able to adapt to salt water and fresh water, and only a few kinds of fish manage this. Experts call such fish **diadromous**. They include salmon, sea trout, sturgeon, shad, lampreys and eels.

abschnitte.titel: Anadromous: from the sea into the river
abschnitte.text: **Anadromous** fish grow up in the sea and swim upstream to spawn. The Atlantic salmon swims hundreds of kilometres against the current to do this and even leaps over small waterfalls. It probably finds its home river again by the smell of the water. The young salmon grow for a few years in the river and then swim into the sea.

abschnitte.titel: Catadromous: from the river into the sea
abschnitte.text: **Catadromous** fish live in fresh water and travel to the sea to spawn. The best-known example is the European **eel**. It lives for many years in rivers and lakes and then swims thousands of kilometres as far as the Sargasso Sea in the Atlantic. The tiny larvae drift back to Europe with the Gulf Stream and reach the coasts as transparent glass eels.

In the past, many salmon swam up the Rhine every year as far as Basel and on into the Aare and its tributaries. At places like Laufenburg and Rheinfelden, catching salmon was an important craft. Through power stations, pollution and straightening of rivers, the salmon disappeared from Switzerland around the middle of the 20th century. Today the countries along the Rhine are trying together to **resettle** it.

Dams and hydroelectric power stations block the way for migratory fish upstream and downstream. So that the fish can get on, **fish ladders** and bypass channels are built. The turbines of power stations are also dangerous for eels migrating downstream. The European eel is regarded today as critically endangered.

For a long time nobody knew where eels breed. Only at the beginning of the 20th century did the Danish researcher **Johannes Schmidt** find out that they spawn in the Sargasso Sea. To this day, however, nobody has yet watched a spawning eel in the wild. Researchers now follow migratory fish with small transmitters.

begriffe.erklaerung: The laying of eggs in fish and amphibians.
Fish that go from the sea into rivers to spawn.
Fish that go from fresh water into the sea to spawn.
A staircase of small pools by which fish can get past a weir.

gewusst: On its way upstream, a salmon can leap over obstacles more than three metres high.
Glass eels are so transparent that you can see right through them.

teile.einleitung: The wild rabbit is the wild ancestor of all domestic rabbits. It lives in sociable colonies and digs large underground burrows. Although it looks like the brown hare, it is a quite different species.
wichtigste: The wild rabbit usually has grey-brown fur.
It lives in groups called colonies.
It digs underground systems of tunnels, the rabbit warren.
It can run as fast as about 50 km/h.
Many predators such as the fox, birds of prey and weasels hunt it.
In winter it eats bark, twigs and roots.
In Australia it became a plague.

abschnitte.text: The European wild rabbit is usually grey-brown, and the belly and the underside of the tail are white. It is smaller than the **brown hare** and has shorter ears without black tips. A grown animal weighs about 1.5 to 2 kilograms. The hind legs are strong, and with them it can run as fast as about 50 km/h and dart sideways.

The wild rabbit originally comes from the Iberian Peninsula, that is, Spain and Portugal. Today it lives in large parts of Europe and has been taken to many countries. It likes best to live in earth burrows that it digs itself, in open landscapes with hedges. The underground system of tunnels is called a **warren** and can be one to two metres deep. In Switzerland it occurs only in a few places, mostly low-lying ones.

Wild rabbits eat grasses, herbs, leaves and field crops. In winter, when there is little grass, they gnaw bark, twigs and roots. Their gnawing teeth keep growing all their lives. They eat part of their droppings again, to get out all the nutrients.

Wild rabbits live in groups called **colonies**. In danger they drum on the ground with their hind legs and so warn the others. A female can have young several times a year, each time about 4 to 8. The young are born naked and blind in a nest chamber, and are **altricial**.

Rabbits are important **prey animals**, because many predators eat them. Here the fox, birds of prey, the eagle owl and the weasel hunt them. In Australia rabbits were released in 1859, and they multiplied strongly and did great damage. Diseases such as myxomatosis have also greatly reduced the populations in Europe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals that live closely together.
An underground system of tunnels and chambers.
Young animals that are born helpless and stay a long time in the nest.
An animal that is hunted and eaten by other animals.

gewusst: Hares are born furry and with open eyes, rabbits by contrast naked and blind.
In Western Australia a fence over 1,800 kilometres long was built to keep rabbits out.

teile.einleitung: The spotted hyena is the largest species of hyena and lives in Africa south of the Sahara. It is known for its giggling call and is often wrongly seen as a pure scavenger. In truth it is a tireless hunter that lives in clans in which the females are in charge.
wichtigste: The spotted hyena is the largest of the four species of hyena.
It is a mistake that spotted hyenas only eat carrion, and they hunt the greater part of their food themselves.
Their jaws are so strong that they can crush thick bones.
Because it digests many bones, its droppings are often pale.
It runs up to about 60 kilometres per hour and hunts with great stamina over long distances.
The gestation lasts about 110 days, and the young are nursed for over a year.
Lions are their most important competitors for food.

abschnitte.text: The spotted hyena has a sandy to grey-brown coat with **dark spots**. Its front legs are longer than its hind legs, so the back slopes downwards towards the rear. It grows to about 1 to 1.6 metres long and can weigh around 40 to 85 kilograms. The females are bigger and heavier than the males. With its enormously strong **jaws** it can crack even thick bones.

Spotted hyenas live in Africa south of the Sahara, mainly in **savannahs** and semi-deserts. The clans in the Ngorongoro Crater and in the Serengeti in Tanzania are very well known. But they are also found in mountain forests up to about 4000 metres. By day they often rest in burrows in the ground or in the shade.

Contrary to a widespread mistake, spotted hyenas do not eat only carrion. They hunt wildebeest, zebras and gazelles in groups and chase their prey with great **stamina** over long distances. In doing so they reach up to about 60 kilometres per hour. They use almost everything, including skin and bones, which is why their droppings are often pale from all the calcium. In quarrels over food they bite and threaten as a pack and can even drive off single lions.

Spotted hyenas live in groups called a **clan**, which can include up to 80 animals. At the top are the females, and even the highest ranking male ranks below the females. The hyenas communicate with many sounds, and their loud, **giggling** call is famous. A long drawn-out whooping call can be heard for kilometres.

After a gestation of about 110 days, the female usually gives birth to two young in a den. The young are born with their eyes open and with teeth. The **mothers** raise the young mainly alone, and the males hardly help. The young are nursed for over a year, longer than in most other predators.

The spotted hyena's most important competitor is the **lion**, which often takes prey from it and the other way round. Lions also kill hyenas if they catch them. The species is still widespread overall, but is declining outside protected areas. The reasons are persecution by people, traps and the loss of habitat.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large family group of hyenas with a fixed ranking.
The flesh of animals that are already dead.
The time in which a young animal grows in the mother's body.
An animal that eats the same food and disputes it with another.

gewusst: Hyenas look like dogs, but are more closely related to cats and mongooses.
A spotted hyena can eat about a third of its body weight in one meal.
Young spotted hyenas often fight for their rank soon after birth.

teile.einleitung: The vicuña is the smallest of the South American camels and lives high up in the Andes. It is a slender, delicate animal with light brown fur. Its wool is regarded as one of the finest and most expensive in the world.
wichtigste: The vicuña is the smallest of the South American camels.
It lives in the high Andes of Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina.
It is usually found at heights of 3500 to 5000 metres.
The vicuña is the wild form of the alpaca.
Its wool is extremely fine and very valuable.
In the 1960s the vicuña was almost extinct.
Today it is the national animal of Peru and appears on the country's coat of arms.

abschnitte.text: The vicuña is about 80 to 90 centimetres high at the shoulder and weighs only 35 to 65 kilograms. That makes it smaller than the **llama**, the alpaca and the guanaco. Its coat is cinnamon brown on top and white on the belly, and on the chest it has long white hairs. It has a long, slender neck and big eyes. Like all camels it has soft **pads** on its feet.

Vicuñas live on the **puna**, a barren grassland in the high Andes. Here the air is thin, and it is sunny by day and often icy cold at night. Their blood can take up oxygen especially well, which helps them at altitude. Their dense coat protects them from the cold.

Vicuñas eat short grasses and herbs. Their lower incisors keep growing all the time, as in rodents, which is a special feature among even-toed hoofed animals. They live in **family groups** of one stallion, several females and young. Young males form groups of their own. In danger the stallion warns with a shrill whistle.

The hairs of the vicuña are only about 12 micrometres thick, much finer than human hair. The **Incas** already prized this wool, and only nobles were allowed to wear it. They rounded up the animals, sheared them and let them go again, which is called **chaccu**. This tradition is being kept up again today, because that way the vicuñas stay wild and healthy.

Because of hunting for their fur, there were only a few thousand vicuñas left in the 1960s. Strict **protection laws** and protected areas have brought the numbers back up strongly. Today several hundred thousand animals live in the Andes again. The vicuña is the national animal of Peru and decorates the country's coat of arms.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal family with long necks that includes the dromedary, Bactrian camel, llama and vicuña.
The wild species from which a domestic animal was bred.
A long mountain range on the western side of South America.
A thousandth of a millimetre.

gewusst: A scarf made of vicuña wool can cost several thousand francs.
Vicuñas use shared dung heaps that they visit again and again.
The alpacas that you see on pastures in Switzerland are descended from the vicuña.

teile.einleitung: Our eye can switch in a flash from a distant mountain to a book in the hand. This adjustment is called accommodation. In it the lens of the eye changes its shape and with it its refractive power.
wichtigste: Accommodation is the adjustment of the lens's refractive power to the distance.
The ciliary muscle is responsible for it.
The lens hangs on fine zonular fibres.
When looking at something near, the ciliary muscle tightens and the lens becomes rounder.
Near accommodation is triggered by the parasympathetic nervous system.
It is accompanied by convergence and narrowing of the pupil.
Presbyopia arises because the lens loses its elasticity.

abschnitte.text: For us to see sharply, the light has to be focused exactly on the **retina**. The cornea and the **lens** bend the light for this. The nearer an object is, the more strongly the lens has to bend the light. **Accommodation** is the adjustment of the **refractive power of the lens** to the distance. It happens all by itself, without our thinking about it.

The lens is suspended on fine fibres, the **zonular fibres**. These are attached to the ring-shaped **ciliary muscle**. When looking into the distance the muscle is relaxed, the fibres are taut and pull the lens flat. When **looking at something near**, **the ciliary muscle tightens**, the ring becomes narrower, and the fibres go slack. The elastic lens then becomes **rounder** and bends the light more strongly. Near accommodation is triggered by the **parasympathetic nervous system**, a part of the autonomic nervous system.

The refractive power of a lens is measured in **dioptres** (D). It is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres. A lens with a focal length of 0.25 m therefore has 1 divided by 0.25, which is **4 D**. The **range of accommodation** states by how much the eye can change its refractive power. If the far point is at infinity and the near point at 0.1 m, it is 1 divided by 0.1 minus 0, so **10 D**.

When we look at something near, more happens besides accommodation. Both eyes turn a little inwards towards the nose, which is called **convergence**. In this way both look at the same point. In addition the **pupil becomes narrower**. This makes the image sharper, much as in a camera with a small aperture. Together this is called the **near response**.

With the years the lens loses its **elasticity** and becomes harder. It can then no longer make itself round so well, even when the ciliary muscle is working. This is the main cause of **presbyopia**. Many people notice from about the age of 45 that they have to hold the newspaper further away when reading. **Reading glasses** make up for this.

gewusst: Children have an especially large range of accommodation and can still see things sharply very close in front of their eyes.
Fish focus by moving their lens back and forth instead of changing its shape.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach is the most important centre for the study of birds in Switzerland. It lies on Lake Sempach in the canton of Lucerne and studies how the birds of the country are doing. That also includes monitoring the numbers of species such as the grey heron and protecting birds.
wichtigste: The Ornithological Institute was founded in 1924 as a ringing centre.
It is a non-profit foundation based in Sempach in the canton of Lucerne.
It studies and monitors the populations of Swiss birds, for example the grey heron.
More than 130 employees and over 2000 volunteers work for it.
Since 2015 there has been a visitor centre made of clay in Sempach.
The Institute cares for sick and injured birds.
It is financed mainly by donations.

abschnitte.text: The Institute began in **1924** as a ringing centre, in order to study bird migration over the Alps. At first it was housed in the home of Alfred Schifferli in Sempach. Since **1954** it has been an independent foundation under Swiss law. Unlike in many other countries, the Ornithological Institute therefore does not belong to the state.

The Institute watches how the number of birds in Switzerland changes. For this, experts and many **volunteers** count breeding birds and winter visitors every year. In the grey heron, for example, it is followed how many breeding colonies there are and how big they are. The results go into the **breeding bird atlas** and into the Red List of threatened bird species.

In **ringing**, a bird is given a light ring with a number on its leg. If it is found again somewhere later, we know where it has travelled and how old it became. Since 1958 the Institute has run a ringing station on the Col de Bretolet in the Valais at a height of 1923 metres. There thousands of birds cross the pass in autumn.

The Institute includes a **care station** for sick, injured and orphaned birds. There, for example, birds that have flown into a pane of glass are looked after. Where possible, the animals are released again after they have recovered. Anyone who finds an injured bird can get advice from the Institute.

Since **2015** there has been a visitor centre in Sempach that is regarded as the first three-storey clay building in Switzerland. In the exhibition, children and adults experience the world of birds with games, films and mounted animals. Outside there is a garden with a pond and nesting places. Many school classes visit the centre every year.

Besides the head office there are regional offices in Sion, Contone, Chur and Yverdon-les-Bains. The Institute advises authorities, farmers and municipalities on how to protect birds. It helps, for example, to improve habitats for the skylark, lapwing and little owl. It also works internationally, for example on an action plan for migratory birds between Africa and Eurasia.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird is given a ring with a number so that it can be recognised later.
An organisation that serves a particular good cause and does not belong to the state.
The number of animals of a species that live in an area.
A list that shows which species are threatened.

gewusst: Every year the Institute gets many calls from people who have found young birds that often need no help at all.
Hundreds of thousands of birds have already been ringed on the Col de Bretolet.

teile.einleitung: Yellowstone National Park in the USA is the oldest national park in the world. It is famous for its geysers, hot springs and free-living bison. Beneath the park lies a huge sleeping volcano.
wichtigste: Yellowstone National Park was founded in 1872 and is regarded as the first national park in the world.
It lies mostly in the US state of Wyoming, with small parts in Montana and Idaho.
The park is known for free-living bison.
There are more geysers here than anywhere else on Earth.
The best-known geyser is called Old Faithful.
Beneath the park lies a mighty volcano, a so-called supervolcano.
In 1995 wolves were reintroduced in the park.

abschnitte.text: **Yellowstone National Park** lies in the north-west of the USA in the Rocky Mountains. It is about 9,000 square kilometres in size, so almost a quarter as big as the whole of Switzerland. The largest part lies in the state of Wyoming. The park gets its name from the Yellowstone River, the river of yellow stones.

In the park there are thousands of hot springs, mud pots and steam vents. A **geyser** is a hot spring that at intervals hurls water and steam high into the air. The geyser **Old Faithful** erupts about every hour and a half and is very reliable. The Grand Prismatic Spring glows in blue, green, yellow and orange, because tiny bacteria live in the hot water.

Beneath Yellowstone lies a huge chamber of hot, molten rock. About 640,000 years ago there was a mighty eruption here that left behind a large crater, the **caldera**. The heat from the depths heats the water of the geysers. Researchers monitor the volcano constantly, and a large eruption in the near future is regarded as very unlikely.

Yellowstone is one of the few places where **bison** have lived free without a break since primeval times. There are also elk, grizzly bears, black bears, moose and pronghorn. In 1995 **wolves** were brought back, which had been wiped out before. Since then they eat many deer, which has let plants on riverbanks recover.

Every year several million people visit the park. Visitors must stay on the paths, because the ground near hot springs can be thin and the water boiling hot. Bison are dangerous too, and you must keep a large distance. Since 1978 the park has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large protected area in which nature may develop freely.
A hot spring that regularly spurts water into the air.
A large crater that collapses after a volcanic eruption.
A large North American wild bovine.

gewusst: The Swiss National Park in the Engadine was founded in 1914 and is the oldest national park in the Alps.
In Yellowstone there are about half of all the geysers on Earth.
Several thousand bison live in the park.

teile.einleitung: Water fleas are tiny crustaceans that hop about in large numbers in ponds and lakes. They have nothing to do with fleas, but they are one of the most important sources of food for fish such as whitefish.
wichtigste: Water fleas are small crustaceans and not insects.
Most are only about 1 to 5 millimetres in size.
They get their name from their hopping way of swimming.
They filter tiny algae and bacteria out of the water.
Fish such as whitefish like to eat water fleas.
Many water fleas multiply for a long time without males.
The best-known water flea is the genus Daphnia.

abschnitte.text: Water fleas live in a transparent **shell** that consists of two halves. Through the shell you can see the beating heart, the gut and sometimes eggs under the microscope. On the head sits one big, dark eye. For swimming they use two long, branched **rowing antennae**.

Water fleas beat their antennae strongly downwards and shoot a little way upwards as they do so. Then they sink slowly again until the next beat. This produces the jerky, hopping movement that is reminiscent of a flea. Many species migrate to the surface of the water at night and into the depths by day, to escape fish.

Water fleas are **filter feeders**. With their fine, hairy legs they create a current of water through the shell. In doing so they sieve out tiny algae, bacteria and floating particles. Because they eat so many algae, they can even make the water of a pond clearer.

In good conditions there are almost only females, which have young without males. This **parthenogenesis** means that water fleas multiply very fast in spring. When it gets cold or the pond dries out, males also arise. Then the females make especially tough **resting eggs** that survive winter and drought.

Water fleas belong to the **zooplankton**, that is, the small animals that float in the water. They are an important link between algae and fish. In Swiss lakes, whitefish for example eat large amounts of them. Dried water fleas are also sold as food for aquarium fish.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny animals that float in the water and are carried by the current.
An animal that sieves its food out of the water.
Breeding in which females have young without males.
An especially protected egg that can survive cold or drought for a long time.

gewusst: Because you can see their heart through the shell, water fleas are often watched under the microscope at school.
Some water fleas grow a pointed helmet when predators are near.
Water fleas are used in laboratories to test whether a substance is poisonous to living things in the water.

teile.einleitung: The pygmy hippopotamus is a much smaller relative of the hippopotamus. It lives hidden in the forests of West Africa and weighs only about as much as a large motorbike. Because it is rare and shy, even researchers know little about its life in the wild.
wichtigste: The pygmy hippopotamus is the small relative of the hippopotamus.
It lives in the forests of West Africa, mainly in Liberia.
A fully grown animal weighs about 180 to 275 kilograms.
It is active mainly at night and usually lives alone.
It eats leaves, ferns, herbs and fruit.
The pygmy hippopotamus is regarded as endangered.
Basel Zoo is known for breeding pygmy hippopotamuses.

abschnitte.text: A pygmy hippopotamus is about 1.5 to 1.75 metres long and just under a metre high at the shoulder. It weighs only about a tenth of a large hippopotamus. The head is smaller in proportion, and the eyes sit more at the sides. The skin is dark and smooth and gives off a reddish fluid that protects against sun and drying out, often called **blood sweat**.

Pygmy hippopotamuses live in the **rainforests** of West Africa, in swamp areas and by streams. Most animals are in Liberia, with smaller populations in Sierra Leone, Guinea and Côte d'Ivoire. An important protected area is the Taï National Park in Côte d'Ivoire. Unlike the large hippopotamus, it spends a lot of time on land in the dense forest.

The pygmy hippopotamus is a **plant eater** and eats leaves, ferns, herbs, roots and fallen fruit. By day it rests in the water or in dens on riverbanks. At night it walks along fixed paths through the forest to look for food. It usually lives alone or as a mother with a young one.

After a pregnancy of about six to seven months, the mother gives birth to a single young one. The newborn weighs only about four to six kilograms. It is suckled for several months and hides in the first weeks while the mother feeds. In zoos, pygmy hippopotamuses can live to over 40 years old.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature, IUCN, classes the pygmy hippopotamus as **endangered**. It suffers from the felling of forests, mining and hunting. In the wild, probably only a few thousand animals are left. Zoos all over the world, including Basel Zoo, take part in breeding programmes so that the species is preserved.

In 2024 a young pygmy hippopotamus called **Moo Deng** from a zoo in Thailand became famous all over the world. Videos of the cheeky youngster were watched millions of times. As a result, many people heard for the first time of this rare animal species. Conservationists hope that this will also help to protect wild pygmy hippopotamuses.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that feeds only on plants.
The time in which a young one grows in the mother's belly.
A dense forest in warm areas in which it rains a great deal.
Zoos work together so that rare animals get healthy young.

gewusst: Outside Africa, the pygmy hippopotamus was known only from the 19th century.
Pygmy hippopotamuses have less webbing between the toes than their large relatives, because they walk more on land.

teile.einleitung: The bridle is the equipment on a horse's head with which the rider steers the horse. It is made of leather straps, usually a bit in the mouth and the reins. A well-fitting bridle is important so that the horse feels comfortable.
wichtigste: The bridle is the gear on the horse's head with which you steer it.
With the reins you give the horse signals.
The bit is a part made of metal or plastic that lies in the horse's mouth.
The simplest and most common bridle is the snaffle bridle.
There are also bitless bridles with no part in the mouth.
A halter is not a bridle, it serves only for leading and tying up.
The bridle must be well fitted so that it does not press or rub.

abschnitte.text: The **bridle** is a harness of straps that sits on the head of the horse. To it are fixed the **reins**, which the rider holds in the hands. Through the reins the horse feels fine signals to stop, turn or slow down. Together with the saddle, the bridle is the most important equipment in riding.

The **headpiece** lies behind the ears, and the browband runs across the forehead. The cheekpieces run down the sides of the head to the **bit**. The noseband and the throatlatch hold everything in place. The straps are usually made of leather, sometimes of plastic.

The **snaffle** is the most common bridle, especially for beginners and young horses. Its bit often consists of a jointed bar with rings at the sides. The **curb** works more strongly through leverage and is used by experienced riders, for example in dressage. The bit lies in a toothless gap in the horse's mouth, which is called the bars.

Some horses are ridden **bitless**, for example with a bosal or a hackamore. Here the pressure acts on the nose and chin instead of in the mouth. Such bridles are also widespread in western riding. With or without a bit, what always matters is a soft and calm hand on the part of the rider.

When bridling, you slip the bridle calmly over the head and let the horse take the bit into its mouth. Between throatlatch and neck there should be about a fist of room. The noseband must not be too tight, so that the horse can chew. After riding, the bit is cleaned and the leather regularly cared for with **leather grease**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Long straps with which the rider steers the horse.
A part made of metal or plastic that lies in the horse's mouth.
A simple, common form of bridle.
A headpiece without a bit for leading and tying up.

gewusst: Horses have a natural gap between the incisors and the molars in which the bit lies.
Several thousand years ago, people were already steering horses with simple bridles of leather or rope.

teile.einleitung: A zoonosis is a disease that can be passed from animals to humans, and sometimes the other way round. Well-known examples are rabies, Lyme disease or echinococcosis, a tapeworm disease that can come from foxes and dogs. Anyone who knows how such diseases are passed on can protect themselves well with simple rules.
wichtigste: Zoonoses are diseases that can be passed between animals and humans.
They are triggered by viruses, bacteria, fungi or parasites such as tapeworms.
Transmission happens through bites, scratches, droppings, food or insects and ticks.
About six in ten of the known infectious diseases of humans are zoonoses.
Echinococcosis is caused by tapeworms that live in dogs and foxes.
Washing your hands after contact with animals is an important protection.
Since 1999, Switzerland has been regarded as free of classic rabies.

abschnitte.text: The word **zoonosis** comes from Greek: “zoon” means animal and “nosos” means disease. The term was coined in the 19th century by the German doctor Rudolf Virchow. What is meant are diseases whose germs can travel back and forth between animal and human. The germs can be viruses, bacteria, fungi or parasites.

In **echinococcosis**, people are infected with the tiny eggs of tapeworms. The fox tapeworm lives in the gut of foxes, and sometimes of dogs and cats. Its eggs reach the outside with the droppings, for example onto berries, grass or into the fur of pets. In humans, the larvae can damage the liver over many years. That is why dogs should be wormed regularly.

Some germs travel with small animals that suck blood. The **tick**, the castor bean tick, can pass on Lyme disease and the brain infection TBE in Switzerland. The germs often come from mice or other wild animals on which the tick has sucked beforehand. In the Middle Ages, fleas from rats spread the plague, from which millions of people died.

Zoonoses can also be passed on through food. Bacteria such as **salmonella** and campylobacter are found, for example, in raw poultry meat or raw eggs. In Switzerland, campylobacter is the most common bacterial cause of diarrhoeal illness from food. Cooking meat through well and keeping chopping boards clean helps against it.

Many new diseases of recent decades originally come from animals. Examples are bird flu, Ebola or HIV, which jumped from monkeys to humans. Experts suspect that the coronavirus too, which from 2019 triggered the Covid-19 pandemic, came from the animal world. The **One Health** approach therefore says that the health of humans, animals and the environment belong together.

After stroking animals and after playing outdoors, you should wash your hands with soap. Wild berries and windfall fruit are washed well or cooked. After an outing in woods and meadows, it is worth checking your body for ticks. Wild animals that seem tame or lie dead are never touched.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny living thing or virus that can trigger a disease.
A living thing that lives in or on another and harms it, for example a tapeworm.
The animal or human in which a parasite lives.
Giving an animal a medicine that kills worms in the gut.

gewusst: Humans can also infect animals, for example great apes with cold viruses.
Bats carry many viruses in them without getting ill themselves.
The fox tapeworm is only a few millimetres long.

teile.einleitung: The bald eagle is a large bird of prey from North America with a white head and a yellow bill. It is the national emblem of the USA and likes to catch fish, especially salmon.
wichtigste: The bald eagle lives in North America, mainly in Canada, Alaska and the USA.
Since 1782 it has been the national emblem of the United States.
Adult birds have a white head and a white tail.
Its wingspan is about 1.8 to 2.3 metres.
It eats mainly fish and likes to catch salmon.
It builds the largest bird nests in North America.
Because of the poison DDT it almost died out, but today it is doing well again.

abschnitte.text: Adult bald eagles have a dark brown body, a white head and a white tail. The strong, curved **bill** and the feet are yellow. Young birds are speckled all over brown and get their typical plumage only at about five years old. The females are bigger and heavier than the males.

The bald eagle lives near lakes, rivers and coasts in **North America**. It needs tall, old trees for its nest and waters rich in fish. Especially many live in Alaska and on the west coast of Canada. In winter, some eagles move to areas where the water does not freeze.

Its most important food is **fish**, which it grasps out of the water with its talons. When in autumn the **salmon** swim up the rivers to spawn, hundreds of eagles often gather on one river. It also eats waterbirds, small mammals and carrion. Sometimes it chases other birds such as the osprey to steal their prey.

A pair often stays together for many years and uses the same nest, called an **eyrie**, again and again. Each year the eagles build it up further with branches. As a result, nests can become several metres deep and weigh over a tonne. The female usually lays one to three eggs.

In the 20th century the bald eagle became rare because it was hunted and the insect poison **DDT** made its eggshells thin. The eggs broke during incubation, and hardly any young hatched. After DDT was banned in the USA in 1972 and strict protection laws came in, the populations recovered. In 2007 it was removed from the list of threatened species in the USA.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that seizes its prey with sharp talons, for example eagles and falcons.
An animal that stands as a symbol for a country or a city.
The nest of a large bird of prey.
An insect poison once widely used, which did great harm to birds.

gewusst: Its close relative in Europe is the white-tailed eagle, which turns up as a rare winter visitor in Switzerland too.
The bald eagle is shown on the Great Seal of the USA.
Despite its mighty appearance, it has a surprisingly high, squeaky voice.

teile.einleitung: The water louse, or water slater, is a small crustacean that lives on the bottom of lakes, ponds and streams. It is a close relative of the woodlouse that you know from the garden, but lives entirely in the water.
wichtigste: Water lice are crustaceans and not insects.
They grow to about 1 to 2 centimetres long and are coloured grey-brown.
A woodlouse relative that lives in lakes and streams is called a water louse.
It feeds mainly on rotting leaves and algae.
Water lice breathe with gills on the abdomen.
Many water lice in a stream often show that the water is heavily loaded with organic material.
The females carry their eggs in a brood pouch on the belly.

abschnitte.text: The **common water louse** has a flat, elongated body made of many segments. It has seven pairs of legs, that is, fourteen legs, and two pairs of antennae. At the rear end sit two forked appendages. The males are usually bigger than the females and can grow about 2 centimetres long.

Water lice live in still and slow-flowing **waters** all over Europe, also in Switzerland. You find them under stones, among water plants and in heaps of leaves on the bottom. They avoid strong currents and prefer to crawl about slowly. They can hardly swim.

The water louse eats mainly **rotting leaves**, algae and other dead plant remains. In this way it helps to break down dead material in the water, like earthworms in the soil. Such animals are called **decomposers**. It is itself eaten by fish, dragonfly larvae and waterbirds.

Water lice need less oxygen than many other stream dwellers. That is why they also survive in water that is heavily loaded with leaves, waste water or fertiliser. If you find very many water lice in a stream but hardly any stonefly larvae, the water is often polluted. Such animals are called **bioindicators**.

At pairing, the male often carries the female around with him for a few days. After that the female lays her eggs in a **brood pouch** on the underside of her body. There the young develop and hatch as tiny water lice. They moult several times until they are fully grown.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal group with a hard shell and many legs, which includes crabs, crayfish and woodlice.
A living thing that eats and breaks down dead plants and animals.
A living thing whose presence reveals something about the state of the environment.
A pocket on the belly of the female in which the eggs and young are protected.

gewusst: Woodlice are the only crustaceans that can also live entirely on land, but the water louse stayed in the water.
In stream studies at school, the water louse is one of the most common animals in the net.
With fourteen legs, a water louse has exactly as many legs as an insect and a spider put together.

teile.einleitung: Box jellyfish are jellyfish with a cube-shaped bell, from whose four corners long tentacles hang. Some species are among the most poisonous animals in the world. They live in warm seas, especially off the coasts of Australia and South-East Asia.
wichtigste: Box jellyfish have a cube-shaped bell with four sides.
Some species, especially the sea wasp, are life-threatening to humans.
They live in warm, tropical and subtropical seas.
Box jellyfish can swim actively and quite fast.
They have 24 eyes, some of them with a lens.
After a sting, vinegar is used as first aid on some beaches.
There are no box jellyfish in Swiss waters.

abschnitte.text: The bell of a **box jellyfish** looks, from the side, like a cube with four side faces. At the four lower corners hang one or more **tentacles**, that is, catching threads. In the biggest species, the sea wasp, the bell becomes about as big as a basketball, and the tentacles can grow around three metres long. The body is transparent, which is why you can hardly see the animals in the water.

Although box jellyfish have no brain like ours, they have 24 eyes. These sit in four groups on small clubs at the edge of the bell. Some eyes even have a **lens** and can make out images. In this way box jellyfish dodge obstacles and find their prey.

On the tentacles sit millions of tiny **stinging cells**. On contact they shoot poison into the skin like small harpoons. The poison of the **sea wasp** (Chironex fleckeri) can kill a person within a few minutes, because it attacks the heart and nerves. The tiny Irukandji jellyfish, which are only about a centimetre across, are also very dangerous.

Box jellyfish live in warm coastal waters, mainly in the Indo-Pacific and around northern Australia. There, at certain times of year, swimming is banned. On some beaches **nets** protect the bathers, and swimmers wear special full-body suits. On many beaches there are bottles of **vinegar** ready, which makes the stinging cells that have not yet fired harmless.

Unlike many jellyfish, box jellyfish do not just drift, but swim purposefully by contracting the bell. They eat small fish and crustaceans, which they catch with the tentacles. Biologists place them as a class of their own among the **cnidarians**, like corals and sea anemones. Their life begins as a small stationary polyp, from which the jellyfish then develops.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny poison capsule in the skin of jellyfish that fires on contact.
A long catching thread of a jellyfish.
An animal group with stinging cells, which includes jellyfish and corals.
The stationary young form of many cnidarians.

gewusst: Box jellyfish have 24 eyes, but no central brain.
The sea wasp is regarded as one of the most poisonous animals in the world.
Sea turtles eat box jellyfish without the poison harming them.

teile.einleitung: The wolverine is the largest land-living member of the weasel family in the world and lives in the cold forests and tundras of the north. It looks like a small, shaggy bear and is known for its strength and stamina. Despite its German name Vielfrass, meaning glutton, it does not eat more than other animals, but it makes use of any food it finds.
wichtigste: The wolverine is the largest land-living member of the weasel family in the world.
It is clearly bigger and heavier than most other members of the weasel family.
It lives in cold northern regions such as Scandinavia, Siberia, Canada and Alaska.
Besides prey it has killed itself, it likes to eat carrion, that is, animals that are already dead.
Another name for it is Järv, and in English it is called the wolverine.
It has broad paws with which it can walk well over snow.
The wolverine does not occur in the wild in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The wolverine grows to about 65 to 105 centimetres long, plus a bushy tail. Males usually weigh 11 to 18 kilograms, and females less. That makes it clearly bigger and heavier than most other **mustelids** such as the stone marten or weasels. Its thick, dark brown coat often has a light band on the sides. It has strong legs, big **claws** and powerful jaws.

The wolverine lives in the cold regions around the North Pole, in **coniferous forests** and in the tundra. It is found in Norway, Sweden, Finland, Russia, Siberia, Canada and Alaska. It needs very large territories, sometimes several hundred square kilometres. Its thick coat and broad paws, which work like **snowshoes**, protect it in winter.

The wolverine is an **omnivore** with a liking for meat. It hunts hares, rodents and birds and can even catch reindeer in deep snow. Very often it eats **carrion**, for example the leftovers of wolf kills. With its strong teeth it also cracks frozen meat and bones. It hides stores in the snow for later.

Wolverines are mostly loners and cover long distances in search of food. They are brave and can even drive wolves or bears away from a carcass. In late winter the female usually gives birth to two or three young in a **snow den**. The deep snow protects the young from cold and enemies.

In Scandinavia the wolverine is unpopular with reindeer herders, because it sometimes kills reindeer. In the past it was heavily hunted, and today it is protected in many countries. In Switzerland it does not live in the wild, but you can see it in some **wildlife parks**. The German name Vielfrass probably comes from the Old Norse fjallfress, which means mountain cat, and was later misunderstood.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of predators with a long body, such as the badger, otter and weasel.
The flesh of animals that are already dead.
An animal that lives alone most of the time.
The area in which an animal lives and which it defends.

gewusst: The comic character Wolverine from the X-Men is named after the wolverine.
A wolverine can walk dozens of kilometres through snow in a day.
The wolverine's fur hardly ices up, which is why the Inuit used it in the past for the edges of hoods.

teile.einleitung: The wolf is a predator from the dog family and the ancestor of all domestic dogs. Wolves live in family groups, the packs, and hunt together. After it was wiped out in Switzerland, the wolf returned in the 1990s.
wichtigste: A group of wolves that lives and hunts together is called a pack.
A typical pack has about 5 to 11 animals.
A fully grown wolf weighs about 30 to 50 kilograms.
Wolves howl to communicate over long distances.
The wolf marks its territory with urine and droppings.
The first returning wolves came to Switzerland from Italy, later also by way of France.
In Australia the wolf originally never occurred naturally.

abschnitte.text: The **wolf** (Canis lupus) looks like a large, long-legged dog with a bushy tail. Its fur can be grey, brown, black or white depending on the region, and polar wolves in the Arctic are almost entirely white. In Europe a wolf usually weighs 30 to 50 kilograms. There are many **subspecies** of different sizes, and in parts of North America especially large wolves live.

Wolves live in Europe, Asia and North America, in forests, steppes, mountains and in the tundra. In Australia there were never any wolves naturally, and the dingo there is a dog gone wild. A wolf territory is often several hundred square kilometres in size. Young wolves sometimes travel hundreds of kilometres to find a territory of their own.

A **pack** is usually a family made of a pair of parents and their young of the last one to two years. After a pregnancy of about two months, the she-wolf gives birth in spring, usually to four to six pups in a den. Right after birth the pups have blue eyes, which later turn yellowish. With **howling**, wolves keep in contact and show other packs that the territory is taken.

Wolves hunt mainly hoofed animals such as roe deer, red deer, chamois and wild boar. They often take young, old or sick animals and so keep the game populations healthy. A wolf can eat several kilograms of meat at once. Unfortunately wolves also kill unprotected **sheep** and goats, which leads to conflicts with farmers.

At the end of the 19th century the wolf was wiped out in Switzerland. In 1995 the first wolves appeared again in the Valais, and they came from Italy. In 2012 the first pack formed on the **Calanda** in Graubünden. In about 2024 around 300 wolves lived in Switzerland in over 30 packs, which is why there is strong debate about **livestock protection** and regulation.

From tamed wolves, the **domestic dog** arose many thousands of years ago. In fairy tales such as Little Red Riding Hood the wolf is often the villain, but in reality he mostly avoids people. Wolves living in the wild rarely live longer than about 8 to 13 years. Livestock guardian dogs and electric fences help to protect sheep from wolves.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family group of wolves that lives and hunts together.
An area that a pack lives in and defends against strange wolves.
A young wolf or young dog.
Measures such as fences and dogs that protect farm animals from predators.

gewusst: Under good conditions, the howl of a wolf can be heard several kilometres away.
All breeds of dog, from the chihuahua to the Great Dane, descend from the wolf.
When hunting, a wolf can briefly run as fast as about 50 to 60 kilometres per hour.

teile.einleitung: The wild ass is the wild ancestor of our domestic donkey. It lives in hot, dry regions where few other animals can cope. Today it has become very rare.
wichtigste: The African wild ass is the ancestor of the domestic donkey.
Wild asses today live mainly in dry regions of Africa and Asia.
In Asia live the related half-asses such as the kulan and the onager.
Wild asses usually live in small, loose groups.
They can go a long time without water.
The African wild ass is critically endangered.

abschnitte.text: The **African wild ass** has grey to sandy fur and a light belly. It has long ears, a short, upright mane and a dark stripe on its back. The Somali subspecies has zebra stripes on the legs. It stands about 1.2 to 1.3 metres high at the shoulder and weighs around 230 to 280 kilograms.

Wild asses today live mainly in dry regions of Africa and Asia. The African wild ass now occurs only in Eritrea, Ethiopia and perhaps Somalia. In Asia live the closely related **half-asses**, such as the kulan and the onager. They inhabit deserts, semi-deserts and stony high plateaus.

Wild asses eat tough grasses, herbs and leaves of bushes. They can get by for a very long time without water and drink a lot at once. Their long ears help to give off heat and to hear others of their kind over long distances. On stony ground they are very sure-footed.

In the wild, wild asses mostly live in small, loose groups. The make-up of the groups often changes. Strong stallions defend a **territory** around waterholes. With a loud “hee-haw” they call over long distances. After a pregnancy of about a year, a mare has a foal.

The African wild ass is regarded as **critically endangered**, and only a few hundred animals still live in the wild. The reasons are hunting, wars and mixing with domestic donkeys. More than 5,000 years ago it was tamed in North Africa to become the **domestic donkey**. In Switzerland, donkeys used to be important pack animals in the mountains, and Somali wild asses live, for example, in Basel Zoo.

begriffe.erklaerung: Asian wild asses such as the kulan and the onager, which stand between horse and donkey.
When people make a wild animal into a domestic animal over many generations.
An area that an animal defends against others of its kind.
A female horse or female donkey.

gewusst: A donkey can lose up to a quarter of its body weight in water and drink it up again quickly.
The call of a donkey can be heard for kilometres.

teile.einleitung: Miniature donkeys are especially small breeds of donkey that are often no bigger than a child of kindergarten age. The best-known breed originally comes from the island of Sardinia and from Sicily in the Mediterranean. With their long ears and friendly nature, they are popular today on many farms and in animal parks.
wichtigste: Miniature donkeys are especially small domestic donkeys.
The well-known breed originally comes from Sardinia and Sicily.
They are usually less than about 90 centimetres tall, measured at the shoulder.
Donkeys descend from the African wild ass.
Miniature donkeys eat mainly hay, straw and grass.
Donkeys are herd animals and must not be kept alone.
They can live to be 25 to 35 years old.

abschnitte.text: Miniature donkeys look like small versions of normal donkeys. The best-known breed, the **Mediterranean miniature donkey**, usually measures less than about 90 centimetres at the shoulder. Typical are the long ears, the grey to brown fur, and a light belly and a light muzzle. Across the back there often runs a dark stripe, the **dorsal stripe**, which joins a cross stripe at the shoulders to form a cross.

All domestic donkeys descend from the **African wild ass**, which lives in dry areas of north-east Africa. On the islands of Sardinia and Sicily, small donkeys were kept a long time ago. Farmers used them as pack animals and for turning grain mills. In the 1920s some of these animals were brought to the USA, where the breed was bred on deliberately.

Donkeys are frugal plant eaters and need mainly hay, straw and a little grass. Because they come from barren regions, they cannot tolerate food that is too rich. Too much juicy grass or bread makes them fat and ill quickly. They also always need fresh water and something to nibble, for example branches.

Donkeys like to live in a group and are very sociable. They are regarded as cautious and in danger tend to stand still instead of running away, which is wrongly taken for stubbornness. A jenny carries her foal for about a year. With the loud call **“hee-haw”**, donkeys communicate over long distances.

In Switzerland you see miniature donkeys on farms, in petting zoos and in animal parks. The Swiss **Animal Welfare Act** requires that donkeys, horses and ponies have contact with others of their kind. Donkeys need a shelter, because their coat is not as water-repellent as that of horses. Their hooves have to be cared for regularly and trimmed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dark stripe that runs along the back in many donkeys.
A female donkey.
A young horse or young donkey.
The hard foot of horses and donkeys, made of horn.

gewusst: A newborn miniature donkey foal is often only about as tall as a large dog.
A donkey can remember the faces of other donkeys for many years.

teile.einleitung: The wood mouse is a small, nimble mouse with big eyes, big ears and a long tail. It lives almost everywhere in Switzerland, in woods, fields and gardens. Because it is out and about mainly at night, you still only rarely get to see it.
wichtigste: The wood mouse likes living best in woods, fields and gardens.
In Switzerland it is found almost everywhere.
It is active mainly at night and avoids bright light.
Its big eyes show that it can see well in the dark.
The tail is almost as long as the body.
On the belly it has light, almost white fur.
In the wild, a wood mouse usually lives only about a year.

abschnitte.text: Without the tail, the wood mouse is about 8 to 11 centimetres long and usually weighs between 15 and 30 grams. Its back is brown, and on the belly it has light, almost white fur. The tail is almost as long as the body. Big **button eyes** and big ears show that it can see and hear well in the dark.

The wood mouse lives in woods, hedges, fields and gardens and is found in almost all of Europe. In Switzerland you find it almost everywhere, from the lowlands up into the mountains. It digs **burrows** with tunnels and nest chambers or uses hollows under roots. In winter it sometimes also comes into garden sheds and cellars.

The wood mouse eats mainly seeds and fruits such as acorns, beechnuts, hazelnuts and berries. It also likes to eat buds and young shoots, and also insects, caterpillars and snails. When eating, it holds the food cleverly with its front paws. If it finds more than it needs, it makes **stores** and hides them for later.

The wood mouse is active at night and avoids bright light, and in danger it hides in a flash. It has a very good sense of smell and hearing, which helps it to find food. With its strong hind legs it can make long **leaps** and also climbs well. If an enemy grabs it by the tail, the skin of the tail can come off, and the mouse escapes.

From spring to autumn a female has several litters, usually of four to seven young. The gestation lasts only about three to four weeks. The young are born naked and blind and are independent after a few weeks. Because many wood mice die young, the many young make sure that the species survives.

The wood mouse is an important prey animal for the **tawny owl**, fox, weasel, marten and cats. In the wild it therefore usually lives only about a year. Because it leaves forgotten stores in the ground, it helps to spread trees such as oak and beech. It is easy to confuse with the very similar **yellow-necked mouse**, which has a yellowish patch at the throat.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mammal with gnawing teeth that keep growing all its life.
Food that an animal hides in order to eat it later.
An animal that is awake at night and sleeps by day.
All the young that a mother animal gives birth to at once.

gewusst: Wood mice are skilful climbers and even climb into bushes and trees to get at fruit.
Wood mice sometimes mark their way with small leaves or twigs in order to find their way around.

teile.einleitung: Fear is a feeling that everyone knows. It warns us of dangers and gets the body ready to react fast. But sometimes fear is bigger than the danger really is.
wichtigste: Fear is an important feeling that protects us.
When we are afraid, the body releases adrenaline.
The heart beats faster, and the hands often sweat.
Many people feel fear and excitement in their tummy.
Animals such as deer run away when they sense danger.
There are many kinds of fear, for example exam nerves or fear of heights.

abschnitte.text: Fear is really a **protection**. It warns us when something could be dangerous, for example a fast car or a barking dog. Then we take more care. Animals feel fear too. A **deer**, for example, **runs away** as soon as it senses danger. In this way it can save itself from enemies.

When we are afraid, the body releases the substance **adrenaline**. It gets us ready to fight or to **flee**. The **heart** beats faster, and you breathe more quickly. Often the **hands sweat**. The **knees** sometimes feel **weak and shaky**. Many people also feel the excitement clearly **in the tummy**.

There are many different fears. Someone who is afraid of a test at school has **exam nerves**. Someone who does not like looking down from a high tower has a **fear of heights**. Some people are afraid of the dark, of spiders or of thunderstorms. In German, someone who gets scared easily is jokingly called an “Angsthase”, a scaredy-cat. But being afraid is nothing to be ashamed of.

It often helps to **breathe slowly and deeply**. Then the body calms down again. It also does you good to **talk** to someone about your fear, for example your parents, a teacher or friends. Before a test, good practice helps, because then you feel surer. If the fear becomes very big and does not stop, experts can help.

gewusst: When you get goosebumps from fear, the fine hairs on your skin stand up.
Many people are afraid of roller coasters but still like riding them, because the fright can be fun too.

teile.einleitung: Varroa destructor is a tiny mite that attacks honey bees and does them great harm. It sucks on bees and their brood and passes on dangerous viruses. Together with the lack of flowering meadows, it is today one of the greatest threats to honey bees.
wichtigste: Varroa destructor is a mite that lives as a parasite on honey bees.
It is about 1.6 millimetres wide and reddish brown.
The varroa mite and a lack of flowering meadows especially threaten honey bees today.
The mite multiplies in the capped brood cells of the bees.
It originally comes from the Eastern honey bee in Asia.
In Switzerland it was first discovered in 1984.
Without treatment by beekeepers, most infested colonies die within a few years.

abschnitte.text: Varroa destructor is a **mite**, that is, an arachnid with eight legs. The female is about 1.1 millimetres long and 1.6 millimetres wide, reddish brown and flat like a scale. It lives as a **parasite** on honey bees and feeds on the fat body of the bees. The name destructor means destroyer.

abschnitte.titel: How does it harm the bees?
abschnitte.text: The female mites slip into the **brood cells** with the bee larvae shortly before they are capped. There they lay eggs, and the young mites feed on the growing bee. The bees that hatch are weakened and live shorter lives. What is especially bad is that the mite passes on **viruses**, such as the deformed wing virus, which gives bees crippled wings.

Originally the mite lived on the **Eastern honey bee** in Asia, which can defend itself well against it. In the 20th century it jumped to our Western honey bee. Through the trade in bee colonies it spread almost worldwide. It reached Switzerland in 1984, and today there are hardly any colonies without varroa.

Beekeepers have to **treat** their colonies against the mite every year. Natural acids such as formic acid and oxalic acid are often used. They also remove the drone brood, in which especially many mites multiply. With a tray in the beehive, beekeepers count the mites that have fallen down and so check how bad the infestation is.

Besides the varroa mite, bees suffer from the lack of **flowering meadows** and hedges. Pesticides and long spells of bad weather also weaken the colonies. Everyone can help by planting native flowers in the garden or on the balcony.
